Reading notes

Issue Reading note
The latest full year is stale by four to ten margin points FY2025 gross margin was 59.9% and operating margin 50.8%. Q2 2026 printed 67.7% and 60.3%. Every peer table, moat test and driver comparison here shows the recent quarter beside the fiscal year, and any conclusion anchored on FY2025 alone understates the current business.
Two earnings bases, both TSMC's The audited 20-F reports FY2025 net income of NT$1,697,604m and diluted EPS of NT$65.47. Bloomberg, the press and TSMC's own quarterly releases report NT$1,717,883m and NT$66.25 on the Taiwan IFRS basis. Revenue, gross profit, operating income and pre-tax income tie exactly; the whole gap is the income-tax line and it changes sign across years. Annual figures here use the 20-F; quarterly figures use the 6-K; consensus comparisons cross the two bases and say so.
One reported segment TSMC discloses a single operating segment. The three franchises used throughout (leading-edge logic at 7nm and below, mature and specialty at 16nm and above, and the backend "Others" product line) are built from the disclosed node and product tables. Their revenue is filed; every franchise margin, capex and return figure is an estimate and is tagged.
Two currencies, two listings, and a third exposure TSMC reports in NT$ and sells almost entirely in US$. NT$ and US$ growth rates diverge by up to six points in a year. The NYSE ADS has also traded between a 5.1% discount and a 33.4% premium to the Taipei line over twelve years, and that premium moved from +26.2% to +11.5% inside July 2026. A US-dollar return on this company is a TSMC return plus a currency move plus a premium move.
  • TSMC discontinued its billing-utilization disclosure after FY2020. Annual capacity ("exceeded 17 million 12-inch equivalent wafers in 2025") and shipments (15,022 thousand) are measured on different bases, so the ratio between them is not a utilization rate.
  • Advanced packaging was about 8% of FY2025 revenue on the CFO's own figure. The audited "Others" product line was 14.1%. The two are not the same measure: Others also contains wafer probe and final test, mask making, design services and royalties.

1. Business description, model and unit economics

TSMC manufactures integrated circuits to other companies' designs. It owns no product line of its own, sells no chip under its own brand, and competes for the manufacturing step between a customer's finished design and a packaged, tested die.▪ In 2025 it ran 305 distinct process technologies and made 12,682 products for 534 customers (6-K 2026-Q2, About TSMC). Net revenue was NT$3,809,054m (US$122,438m at the disclosed weighted-average NT$31.11), gross margin 59.9% and operating margin 50.8% (20-F FY2025, Item 5).

The company reports one operating segment, so the disaggregation below is built from the three tables it does publish: revenue by product (wafer versus other services), revenue by circuit resolution, and revenue by platform (Note 22a).

What sets price

Price per wafer is set node by node in bilateral negotiation, with no published price book, no indexation and no take-or-pay.▪ The 20-F says only that TSMC "establish[s] pricing levels for specific periods of time with our customers, some of which are subject to adjustment during the course of that period to take into account market conditions" (20-F FY2025, Item 5). Realized price moves with which node a wafer slot is configured for, and that is TSMC's own supply decision taken five to seven years earlier.

The disclosed evidence is the blended wafer ASP series, which is the ratio of two filed numbers.

Year Wafer revenue (NT$m) Shipments (k 12-inch eq.) ASP (NT$/wafer) ASP (US$/wafer) US$ ASP YoY
2018 911,296 10,752 84,756 2,810 —
2019 927,317 10,068 92,105 2,981 +6.1%
2020 1,178,456 12,398 95,052 3,230 +8.4%
2021 1,405,300 14,179 99,111 3,547 +9.8%
2022 1,991,856 15,253 130,588 4,376 +23.4%
2023 1,882,518 12,002 156,850 5,029 +14.9%
2024 2,514,461 12,910 194,768 6,062 +20.5%
2025 3,272,554 15,022 217,851 7,003 +15.5%

Source: 20-F Note 22a (wafer revenue) and Item 5 (shipments), each year.

Blended revenue per 12-inch-equivalent wafer rose 149% in US dollars between 2018 and 2025 while shipments rose 39.7%. Shipments in 2025, at 15,022 thousand, were below the 2022 level of 15,253 thousand while wafer revenue was 64% higher.

Management attributes little of the margin gain to price. Asked on the Q4 2025 call whether 20% annual ASP growth is the new normal, the CFO answered: "in the last few years, the pricing benefits to the profitability was just enough to cover the inflation cost from tools, equipment, materials, labor, et cetera. There are other factors contributing to the higher profitability. The first one will be a high utilization rate... The other one will be our manufacturing excellence" (Q4 2025 earnings call, 2026-01-15). The CEO frames the policy the same way: "we don't [just] increase our price by which I like to have with 4x, 5x if you cannot survive for that kind of a price increase. So we earn our value, and we make sure that our profit, our gross margin is enough for our long-term sustaining expansion" (Q2 2026 call). Reported 2nm pricing landed at roughly US$30,000 per wafer, about 10-20% above 3nm's US$25,000-27,000, against market expectation of a 50% premium (TrendForce, accessed 2026-07-28) [web].

What drives volume

Volume is a supply variable, not a demand variable, for as long as the order book exceeds capacity. Disclosed annual capacity went from roughly 14 million 12-inch equivalents in 2021 to "exceeded 17 million" in 2025, about 22% over four years, against US$167bn of cumulative capital expenditure over 2021-2025 (Q4 2025 call). Most of that spending did not buy new wafer slots; it converted existing slots from mature-node value to leading-edge value and built the shells and long-lead tools for capacity landing in 2026-2028.

The regime changed in the current year. First-half 2026 shipments were 8,510 thousand against 6,977 thousand a year earlier, +22.0%, with revenue per wafer up 12.2%. For the three years to 2025 this business grew on price and mix with volume flat to negative; in the first half of 2026 volume supplied roughly 60% of the growth.

What drives the cost curve

Cost of revenue by nature, FY2025 (20-F FY2025, Note 25a; per-wafer at 15,022 thousand shipments):

Component NT$m % of COGS NT$/wafer US$/wafer
Depreciation of PP&E and right-of-use assets 638,014 41.8 42,472 1,365
Amortization of intangibles 5,362 0.4 357 11
Employee benefits 235,604 15.4 15,684 504
Raw wafers, gases, chemicals, masks, utilities, outsourced services, spares 648,780 42.5 43,189 1,388
Total cost of revenue 1,527,760 100.0 101,702 3,269
Revenue 3,809,054 — 253,565 8,151
Gross profit 2,281,294 — 151,864 4,882

Machinery and equipment depreciate straight-line over five years and buildings over ten to twenty (20-F FY2025, Note 4). That five-year life sets the margin lifecycle of every node: a ramping node runs at a low margin and dilutes the consolidated figure, a node in its fourth year reaches the corporate average (management expects N3 to cross it in the second half of 2026, per the Q1 2026 call), and a node past five years runs at a margin the CFO describes as "generally very high" (Q1 2026 call).▪ The consolidated gross margin is therefore a weighted average of four cohorts, and which way it moves in any period depends mainly on the weight of the ramp cohort. Management quantifies the current one: the N2 ramp dilutes consolidated gross margin by about 3-4 percentage points in the second half of 2026 (Q2 2026 call).

Cash cost per wafer, the residual after depreciation and amortization, ran NT$41,102 in 2023, NT$50,661 in 2024 and NT$58,872 in 2025, a 43% rise in two years against 25% more wafers. That is node complexity, not input inflation: an N3 wafer takes roughly 85-90 mask layers against roughly 35 for a 28nm wafer.

Operating leverage

Incremental operating margin, Δ operating income ÷ Δ revenue, NT$ basis:

Period Δ revenue (NT$m) Δ operating income (NT$m) Incremental operating margin
2016→2017 +29,509 +7,601 25.8%
2017→2018 +54,027 (1,935) (3.6)%
2018→2019 +38,511 (10,923) (28.4)%
2019→2020 +269,270 +194,083 72.1%
2020→2021 +248,160 +83,197 33.5%
2021→2022 +676,476 +471,298 69.7%
2022→2023 (102,155) (199,813) 195.6% decremental
2023→2024 +732,572 +400,587 54.7%
2024→2025 +914,746 +614,039 67.1%
2019→2025 cumulative +2,739,069 +1,563,391 57.1%

The record shows three things. Realized incremental operating margin over the full 2019-2025 cycle is 57.1%, roughly six points above the 50.8% average margin, so operating leverage is real but not extreme, because the fixed-cost base rebuilds itself every five years through capex.▪ The leverage runs as hard in reverse: revenue declined NT$102bn in 2023 and operating income declined NT$200bn. And 2017-2019, the N7 build before volume arrived to fill it, produced negative incremental margins for two consecutive years, which is the base rate for a node transition without demand behind it.

The first half of 2026 is far above that record. Revenue of NT$2,404,484m against NT$1,773,046m added NT$631,438m while operating income added NT$555,065m, an incremental operating margin of 87.9% in the reported half-year. The deck arithmetic on the second quarter alone gives 89.9%, with cost of revenue growing 6.1% year over year against revenue up 36.0% [deck: Q2 2026 earnings conference 2026-07-16, slide 4]. About 0.5 points of the 10.7-point operating-margin expansion is currency at the disclosed sensitivity; the rest is loading and cost.

Unit economics

The economic unit is one 12-inch-equivalent wafer, the unit TSMC prices, ships and measures capacity in. The consolidated figures are arithmetic on filed numbers; the node-level figures are triangulated, because TSMC discloses no node volume, price or cost.

Leading edge — N5/N4 1,993-2,525 ~US$17,000 (US$15,000-19,000) ~US$3,000 ~US$700 ~US$13,300 73-85% [estimate: mix identity back-solve] Five-year machinery life (Note 4); N5 volume production began 2020
Leading edge — N7/N6 1,351-1,818 ~US$9,500 (US$8,100-10,900) ~US$2,200 ~US$150 ~US$7,150 73-85% [estimate: same identity] N7 volume production 2018; tools fully depreciated
Leading edge — N2 (first disclosed quarter) not disclosed; 3% of Q2 2026 wafer revenue ~US$30,000 [web] not disclosed not disclosed not disclosed 10-40%, centre ~25% [estimate: dilution back-solve] "the steep ramp-up of our 2-nanometer technology to dilute our gross margin by about 3 to 4 percentage points" (CFO, Q2 2026 call)
Mature — 16nm and above 8,700-10,500 ~US$2,810 (US$2,580-3,130) [estimate: residual] ~US$1,119 [estimate: layer-weighted] ~US$320 [estimate: capex-share key] ~US$1,371 ~49%, range 45-57% [estimate] GAP on cost; peer gross margins (UMC 29.0%, GlobalFoundries 24.9%) bound it from below
Leading-edge subtotal 4,500-5,800 [estimate] ~US$15,300 [estimate] — — — — Reconciles to the disclosed US$77,843m of advanced wafer revenue

Given the Q2 2026 wafer mix (N2 3%, N3 30%, N5 33%, N7 11%, mature 23%) and a 67.7% consolidated gross margin, the fully-depreciated N5/N7 band has to run somewhere in the 73-85% range across every plausible assumption for the other bands.▪ Under assumptions generous to every other band — N2 already at 40% after two quarters, mature at 60%, the backend at 70% — the identity still requires N5/N7 above 72%. A physical cross-check agrees: an N5 wafer at about US$17,000 with a fully depreciated tool set has cash costs of roughly US$2,500-3,500, giving a cash gross margin of 79-85%.

Node-level cash cost is not disclosed at any level below consolidated cost by nature, so the cost column is an allocation on a mask-layer and process-step basis, not a measurement. The volume split comes from third-party node prices, and the two published estimates for N3 differ by 30% (US$19,500 versus US$25,000-27,000), which alone moves implied leading-edge volume by roughly 25%. The volume range and the mature ASP are therefore the output of one accounting identity with a price assumption, not two independent measurements.

The mature franchise is not a smaller version of the leading edge. On the estimated allocation, depreciation is about 11% of mature revenue against about 20% of advanced revenue, because the fabs running 16nm and above commenced production between 1990 and 2018 and every tool installed before 2021 is fully depreciated. That makes the mature franchise more utilization-tolerant and far more exposed to price than to volume, because an incremental wafer on a depreciated fab costs only cash. Capital intensity follows: at the disclosed ~10% specialty share of the 2026 budget, the mature franchise absorbs roughly US$6.0-6.4bn against roughly US$30.7bn of annualized revenue, about 20-21%, against 37-40% consolidated [estimate: management's capital-budget split applied to the guided budget].

The purchase decision is made two to three years before the wafer ships: "as process technology complexity increases, the engagement lead time with customers is now at least 2 to 3 years in advance" (CEO, Q4 2025 call).▪ By the time price is set, the customer has taped out to TSMC design rules, licensed TSMC-qualified IP through the Open Innovation Platform and committed a mask set. The CEO's framing on the Q2 2026 call: "choosing a technology, ramping it up is not buying a milk from 7-Eleven... it takes about 5 years."

There is no backlog and no revenue-performance-obligation disclosure. The only quantified forward commitment is customer capacity deposits, and they moved the wrong way in 2025:

Year-end Temporary receipts from customers (NT$m) % of that year's revenue
2021 185,994 11.7%
2022 276,123 12.2%
2023 278,295 12.9%
2024 291,102 10.1%
2025 189,858 5.0%

Source: 20-F FY2021 through FY2025, Note 22c. The balance declined 34.8% in a year revenue grew 31.6%. The 20-F says the treatment "either by refund or by accounts receivable offsetting, will be determined by mutual consent" and discloses no roll-forward, so an offset against a much larger receivable base and a real reduction in cash reservations cannot be separated from the filing.

Demand-driver decomposition

Revenue can be decomposed into wafer shipments times revenue per wafer, plus the backend share.

A. Wafer shipments (15,022k in FY2025; +22.0% year over year in H1 2026)

Ultimate exposure: TSMC's own installed leading-edge capacity, set by capital committed three to five years earlier, EUV scanner deliveries from a sole supplier, fab construction, and Taiwan power and water. Measurable in quarterly 12-inch-equivalent shipments (earnings deck slide 4), annual capacity (20-F Item 4) and the capital budget with its 70-80 / 10 / 10-20 allocation. Realized check: shipments were 15,253k in 2022 and 15,022k in 2025, so three years of AI revenue growth came with negative volume. Volume reappeared as a driver only in H1 2026.

The demand that fills it has four sources:

Driver Ultimate exposure Contribution: % of FY2025 revenue Contribution: % of 2023-2025 growth Robustness Realized check
A1. AI accelerator silicon (GPU, custom ASIC, HBM controller) The capital budgets of six to eight hyperscalers and AI labs, roughly US$610-725bn guided for 2026 across the four largest against roughly US$380-410bn in 2025 depending on the aggregation [web], increasingly debt- and lease-funded. Not end-user AI adoption. Measurable quarterly in those four capex lines and their capex/operating-cash-flow ratios. high teens % on management's own band ~32-36% Directionally structural, amplitude unbenchmarked. The nearest analogue in TSMC's own record is the 2021-22 shortage, which reversed inside four quarters: shipments −21.3% in 2023, operating margin 49.5% → 42.6%. Confirmed. HPC revenue NT$934,769m (2023) → NT$2,192,931m (2025); HPC share 43% → 58% → 66% by Q2 2026.
A2. Data-centre CPU, switch ASIC, optical DSP — the HPC residual management does not call AI The same buyers, the same racks, the same budget as A1. Management confirmed the linkage in Q2 2026: "the emergence of agentic AI is leading to a resurgence in the role of CPUs in AI data centers." ~40% [estimate: platform disclosure less management's AI-accelerator band] ~42%, larger than A1 Same cycle as A1, not an independent leg. Confirmed, and invisible in the "AI is high-teens percent" framing.
A3. Premium smartphone application processors and companion silicon Premium-tier handset units, flat at roughly 250-300m a year, times die area, times node price. Not global handset units. 29.2% (FY2025), 22% (Q2 2026) ~18% Structural but low-growth. Its strategic function differs from its revenue function: the premium smartphone customer is the anchor tenant for each new node, taking the first and most dilutive year of production. Confirmed as a decelerator. Smartphone declined 11% QoQ in Q1 2026 and 4% in Q2 2026, roughly 15% over two quarters in absolute terms [deck: Q1 2026 slide 6; Q2 2026 slide 6].
A4. Automotive, industrial and IoT at 16nm and above Semiconductor content per vehicle and per connected device at 16-28nm and above, times the share TSMC wins from IDMs that still fabricate in-house. Not vehicle units, which have been roughly flat since 2018. ~12-14% of the mature franchise, about 3% of revenue [estimate: platform revenue bounded by the per-platform node lists in Item 4] negative Slow and qualification-gated. Not confirmed. IoT platform revenue NT$196,115m (2022) → NT$191,047m (2025), −2.6%; DCE NT$56,159m → NT$47,997m, −14.5%. Flagged as a hypothesis, not a driver.

B. Blended wafer revenue per 12-inch equivalent (US$7,003 in FY2025, +149% since 2018)

Driver Ultimate exposure Contribution Robustness Realized check
B1. Node-mix migration Which node a wafer slot is configured for, which is a TSMC supply decision taken five to seven years earlier, gated by EUV deliveries and fab construction. Advanced share of wafer revenue 41% (2020) → 74.4% (FY2025) → 77% (Q2 2026). Explains 94-110% of wafer-revenue growth depending on the window. Mechanically bounded. 23 points of advanced-mix headroom remain against 33 points already used. Migration within the advanced band continues (N2 prices 10-20% above N3, with A16 and A14 above that). Confirmed as the dominant historical driver and confirmed as decelerating.
B2. Node list-price escalation Whether the customer's design still pays for a 10-20% more expensive wafer given the density and power gain. That is Moore's-Law economics computed on the customer's income statement. Reported at single-digit percent for N3/N4/N5/N7 in 2026 and 5-10% on advanced nodes from January 2027, with a 10-15% surcharge on HPC volume above committed levels [web]. Weak as a margin driver on management's own testimony. Did not show up as a margin driver. The CFO states the pricing benefit covered input inflation and no more. The 54.4% (FY2023) to 67.7% (Q2 2026) gross-margin move traces to utilization, to the N5/N7 cohort passing its depreciation cliff, and to currency.

C. Backend share of net revenue (14.1% in FY2025; 16.0% in Q2 2026, a record)

Driver Ultimate exposure Contribution Realized check
C1. Advanced packaging (CoWoS, SoIC) Total interposer AREA required, not accelerator units. The disclosed reticle roadmap moves package area from 3.3 reticles to 5.5x (2026), 9.5x (2027) and above 14x (2028-29) [web], so CoWoS wafer demand can compound with units flat. ~8% of FY2025 revenue on the CFO's figure, guided to "slightly over 10%" for 2026. Contributed roughly 10% of the 2023-2025 revenue increase against a ~14% weight. The mix shift the market forecast from 2023 arrived in 2026, not 2024.
C2. Wafer probe and final test Test seconds: dies tested times test time per die, which rises independently of unit volume as known-good-die requirements for 3D stacking grow. Measurable in Advantest and Teradyne tester revenue and book-to-bill. Inside the ~6.1% of revenue residual. C.C. Wei on the Q2 2026 call: "as time goes by, some of the customers['] product need more test... so we put more CapEx in the tester."
C3. Mask making, design services, royalties Tape-out count times mask layers per node. Measurable in TSMC's own quarterly boilerplate: 288 process technologies / 11,878 products / 522 customers (2024) → 305 / 12,682 / 534 (2025). C2 and C3 together are roughly 43% of the backend line, NT$231,800m or US$7,500m, and nobody models them. Products +6.8% and technologies +5.9% in 2025 after being flat-to-down in 2024.

Reconciliation to the realized record. Three of the four things management names as drivers appeared. Node-mix migration explains 94-110% of wafer-revenue growth. AI-driven demand appeared, but at roughly double the disclosed "high teens percent" once the non-accelerator HPC residual is included, and it is one exposure, not two. Volume did not appear until H1 2026. Pricing power did not appear as a margin driver, on management's own testimony.▪ Section 6 tests the same tree against industry data and peers.

Working capital in this business scales with the ramp cohort, not with revenue. Inventory days rose from 74 at the end of 2025 to 80 and then 87 through the first half of 2026, which management attributes to the N2 ramp on both 2026 calls. Inventory itself grew 26.7% year over year against 36.0% revenue growth, so the day count rose partly because the denominator, cost of revenue, grew only 6.1%. Accounts receivable grew 87.1% year over year, from NT$235.69bn to NT$440.92bn, and rose from 3.4% to 4.7% of total assets, which the deck does not explain [deck: Q2 2026 earnings conference, slide 7].

2. Key technologies and technical differentiators

The obvious technical candidates do not differentiate TSMC. Nanosheet gate-all-around is an industry-wide transition; Samsung shipped GAA at 3nm in 2022 and Intel shipped RibbonFET at 18A in 2025 [web]. ASML is the sole source of EUV and sells to Samsung and Intel as well.▪ And the FY2025 20-F describes intellectual property only qualitatively: "Since our inception, we have applied for and been issued a substantial number of patents in the United States and other countries, the majority of which are semiconductor related" (20-F FY2025, Item 4, Research and Development). The filing gives no patent count and no licensing revenue line.

The advantage comes from yield learning and process control on nodes TSMC did not invent, advanced packaging capacity and reticle-area scaling, a design-enablement ecosystem funded by third parties, and cadence discipline, in that order of contribution.▪

Leading-edge logic process (N7/N5/N3 FinFET, N2 nanosheet GAA)

Mechanism. A process node is a set of transistor geometry, interconnect and design rules that lets a customer put more switching elements into the same area at lower energy per switch.▪ N2 uses nanosheet gate-all-around transistors, where the gate wraps the channel on all four sides, not three, restoring electrostatic control that FinFET loses below roughly 3nm and letting the designer trade channel width continuously. The disclosed generation deltas, taken from earnings calls:

Node Versus Speed at same power Power at same speed Density Source
N2 N3E 10-15% 20-30% >15% Q2 2025 call
A16 N2P 8-10% 15-20% +7-10% Q2 2025 call
A14 N2 10-15% 25-30% close to 20% Q2 2026 call
A13 A14 optical shrink — >6% die-area saving Q2 2026 call

Why it is hard, from those who tried. Intel spent US$13.8bn on R&D in 2025, US$16.5bn in 2024 and US$16.0bn in 2023 against TSMC's NT$246,427m (US$7,921m) in 2025, and still writes in its own risk factors that it "has been unsuccessful to date in securing any significant external foundry customers for any of our nodes" (INTC 10-K FY2025).▪ Intel Foundry's external revenue in 2025 was US$307m. Intel's 10-K also states the minimum-efficient-scale problem in its own words: "the development and manufacturing of next-generation leading-edge nodes like Intel 14A is highly capital intensive and their cost structure requires wafer volumes beyond what we expect from our own products to achieve economic efficiency." Samsung reached GAA at 3nm three years before TSMC and has not converted the lead into share; TrendForce puts Samsung Foundry at 6.5% of the foundry market in Q1 2026 against TSMC's 72.3% [web].

Differentiation evidence. Wafer revenue growth since 2021 is almost entirely price and mix: wafer volume rose 5.9% between 2021 and 2025 while wafer revenue rose 133%. Advanced technologies went from 58% of wafer revenue in 2023 to 74% in 2025 and 77% in Q2 2026. At the 2026 Taiwan symposium a TSMC vice president stated about 25 finalized 2nm chip designs with more than 70 additional customer projects in development, and 2nm capacity growing at a 70% compound rate over 2026-2028 (Focus Taiwan, accessed 2026-07-28) [web].

Substitution threat. The threat is a customer switching supplier. Intel 18A entered high-volume manufacturing in late 2025 with RibbonFET and PowerVia; Intel expects external 14A commitment decisions in the second half of 2026 into the first half of 2027, and has said publicly it may pause or discontinue 14A without a significant external customer. Samsung SF2 has Tesla's AI5 dual-sourced and AI6 reported as wholly Samsung under a US$16.5bn agreement [web, unverified against any filing]. SMIC is constrained to DUV multi-patterning with reported 7nm yields under 50% [web, unverified].

A16 and backside power delivery

Backside power delivery moves the power network to the reverse side of the thinned wafer, freeing front-side routing tracks for signals and shortening the power path. Intel shipped it first: PowerVia entered high-volume manufacturing with Intel 18A in late 2025 and Intel calls it "our unique industry-first implementation of backside power delivery" (INTC 10-K FY2025). TSMC's implementation, Super Power Rail, is reserved for A16 and guided for volume production in the second half of 2026. On this specific capability TSMC is the follower by roughly a year.▪

The timing is contested and unresolved. TSMC's own speakers said 2H 2026 on the Q3 2025 call, the Q4 2025 call and again at the Taiwan symposium on 14 May 2026; trade press covering the April 2026 North America symposium headlined a slip to 2027, with a reconciling statement attributed to TSMC that A16 "will be ready for production in 2026" but that volume production begins in 2027 [web, unverified]. A16 received no status paragraph in either the Q1 2026 or Q2 2026 prepared remarks, having had one in each of the three prior calls.

EUV and the High-NA decision

ASML is the sole supplier. Its 0.33 NA TWINSCAN NXE:3800E runs at 220 wafers per hour, a 37% improvement over the prior generation; High-NA at 0.55 NA doubles resolution but halves the printable field, forcing designers to stitch large dies, and ASML expects the High-NA platform "to start supporting high-volume manufacturing in 2027" (ASML 20-F FY2025). High-NA tools are reported at US$350-400m installed against roughly US$200m for 0.33 NA [web].

TSMC has deferred High-NA further than either leading-edge rival. At the 2026 North America symposium it signalled that A12 and A13 do not require High-NA, which means no High-NA requirement on any node through 2029 [web].▪ Intel is designing 14A "to potentially incorporate an industry-first use of high-NA EUV lithography in high-volume semiconductor logic manufacturing" (INTC 10-K FY2025). C.C. Wei's framing on the Q2 2026 call was that TSMC works with ASML on cost and maturity and decides "whether we use it or not." If TSMC can hold density and yield with 0.33 NA multi-patterning through 2029 while Intel pays for High-NA at 14A, its capital efficiency advantage widens; if it cannot, A14's density claim is where the strain shows first. It resolves around 2028.

The FY2025 20-F never names ASML or EUV, and equipment sole-source exposure is disclosed only generically.

3DFabric: CoWoS, SoIC, InFO, SoW and COUPE

CoWoS mounts logic dies and HBM stacks side by side on a silicon interposer that provides the wide, short traces HBM bandwidth requires; interposer area is measured in reticle multiples because the interposer itself must be built by stitching lithography fields. SoIC is direct copper-to-copper hybrid bonding with no solder bumps. InFO is the thin fan-out package used in premium smartphone application processors.

Item Now 2028 2029
CoWoS interposer size 5.5 reticles, yields above 98% 14 reticles, ~10 compute dies + 20 HBM stacks >14 reticles, 24 HBM stacks
SoIC bonding pitch 6 µm 6 µm at N2 4.5 µm at A14
System-on-Wafer SoW-P logic-only in production since 2024 — SoW-X targeted 2029; 40+ reticles, 64 HBM stacks
COUPE silicon photonics 200Gbps micro-ring modulator in production 2026 — —

Source: TSMC press release for the 2026 North America symposium and trade coverage of the Taiwan leg, all [web].

This is the franchise where management concedes the least defensible position, and it does so explicitly.▪ Asked on the Q2 2026 call whether Intel's embedded-bridge packaging gaining traction was a threat, C.C. Wei said packaging capacity is so tight that it limits customer growth, that he welcomes the additional alternatives, and "we hope they will be successful." Pressed a second time on whether losing packaging opens the door to losing front-end wafers, he answered that "the front end wafer business and the back end of business are 2 different [things]... since our capacity in the back end is [in] shortage mode, the gap is bigger. And so I welcome that the competitor offers some [flexibility] to my customer so that the [front-end] wafer can be put into the package."

Yield learning and process control

This has no spec sheet. Defect density determines what fraction of dies on a wafer work, and at large AI accelerator die sizes a small difference compounds into a large yield gap that flows straight to cost per good die. TSMC discloses no defect density and no utilization rate. What it does disclose: N2 "entered high-volume manufacturing in 4Q 2025, at both our Hsinchu and Kaohsiung site[s] with good yield" (Q4 2025 call), and an A14 internal product vehicle demonstrated "close to 90% device performance and close to 90%, 256 megabit SRAM [yield]" with customer tape-outs "ahead of schedule" (Q2 2026 call), two years before A14 volume production. Comparative yields for Samsung SF2 (55-60% rising toward 70%), Intel 18A (roughly 65% to over 85% during 2026) and SMIC (7nm under 50%) are trade press only [web, unverified].

The design-enablement ecosystem

A process node is unusable until EDA tools are certified against it, process design kits and SPICE models exist, and a library of silicon-verified IP has been ported. TSMC does not pay for most of that. The Open Innovation Platform organises partners into six alliances who fund their own certification work in order to be on TSMC's list. Ecosystem scale, from TSMC's own materials: more than 70,000 IP titles and more than 3,300 process design kits as of 2023, with over 5,000 attendees across 750 companies at the 2025 forum series [web]. TSMC stopped publishing the IP and PDK counts after 2023.

The lead time is what the ecosystem buys. Synopsys's 2025 OIP award citation is "Joint Development of A14 and A16 Design Infrastructure"; A14 volume production is 2028, so partners were funding certified design flows three years before it ships [web]. A competitor node with no certified flows, no PDKs and no ported IP is not a substitute even if its transistors are equal, which is why Intel's 10-K says potential customers "may be inclined to remain with their current foundry partners and unwilling to make the significant investments of time and resources needed to develop products on our nodes."▪

3Dblox, TSMC's 3D-IC design description language, has moved from a TSMC-hosted specification to IEEE P3537 [web]. Standardisation cuts both ways: it raises adoption and removes exclusivity.

Roadmap delivery record

Reconstructed from the primary filings, each year's 20-F stating what shipped and what is promised next:

Node Promised for Actual Outcome

N7+ 2019 "In 2019, we successfully commenced volume production of 7-nanometer Plus" (20-F FY2019) Delivered
N5 2020 "our 5-nanometer technology successfully entered volume production in 2020" (20-F FY2020) Delivered

Six consecutive leading-edge nodes entered volume production between 2018 and 2025, each confirmed in the following annual filing.▪ The full-node cadence has lengthened from two years to three: N7 (2018) → N5 (2020) → N3 (2022) was a two-year rhythm; N3 (2022) → N2 (2025) → A14 (2028) is three, with the gap filled by derivative nodes delivering single-digit-percent improvements. Management frames this positively, describing A14 and its derivatives as "an even larger and long-lasting node for TSMC than N2" (Q2 2026 call), and a longer node life is good for depreciation and yield; it is also what a slowing scaling cadence looks like. And symposium claims soften on the earnings call: A14 density went from "more than 20%" at the April 2025 symposium to "about 20%" on the Q2 2025 call to "close to 20%" on both 2026 calls, and A16 density from "up to 1.10X" to "7% to 10%." The earnings-call figure is the working number in every case.

Roadmap exposure

Effectively 100% of current wafer revenue comes from shipped technology: N3 30% + N5 33% + N7 11% + N2 3% = 77% of Q2 2026 wafer revenue on nodes in volume production, plus 23% at 16nm and above. Delivering the guided approach to a 25% US$ revenue compound rate from 2024 requires N2 to move from 3% of wafer revenue to a node-class share, A16 and N2P to ship in 2H 2026, A14 in 2028, A13 and A12 in 2029, and CoWoS reticle area to scale from 5.5 to 14 or more between now and 2028-29. Roughly the back half of a five-year growth path depends on technology that is not yet in production, against a record of six consecutive nodes delivered and a two-to-three-year engagement lead time.

3. Competitive advantages and moat assessment

TSMC publishes no per-fab or per-country table of capacity, capex, revenue, government grants or return, despite a US$265bn Arizona commitment, roughly 30% of eventual sub-2nm capacity eventually sitting there, NT$198,968m of grants received over 2023-2025, and guided overseas gross-margin dilution widening from 2-3 points to 3-4 points. That dilution is worth roughly NT$150bn of annual gross profit at FY2026 revenue, and it is unquantified.

The leading-edge franchise holds a structural advantage of the strongest class available in manufacturing, and it is expensive to hold. The mature franchise earns excess returns today and is open to erosion. The backend franchise earns excess returns today and is the one part of the company where rivals are actively attacking the position.▪ Because the leading edge is 63.9% of revenue, 74% of wafer revenue and 70-80% of the capital budget, it sets the consolidated economics, and the company-level assessment follows from it.

Leading edge. TSMC took 72.3% of merchant foundry revenue in Q1 2026, up from 70.4% the quarter before [web], and a bottom-up build of merchant sub-7nm revenue from each player's own disclosure puts its share of that market between 77% and 93% depending on how much of Samsung's and SMIC's revenue is assumed to be leading-edge (Section 4).▪ Consolidated gross margin was 67.7% and operating margin 60.3% in Q2 2026, against 54.4% and 42.6% in FY2023. Return on invested capital was 51.0% in FY2025 against an assumed 9-11% cost of capital. The two attackers with the balance sheets to try are both losing money doing it: Intel Foundry lost US$10,318m on US$17,826m of segment revenue in FY2025, a −57.9% operating margin, of which only US$307m came from external customers (INTC 10-K FY2025); Samsung's combined foundry and System LSI operating loss is estimated at KRW 6tn in 2025 [web], and its foundry revenue declined 5.8% quarter over quarter in Q1 2026 while TSMC's rose 6.3%.▪

The advantage is expensive to hold: capital expenditure was 33.4% of revenue in FY2025 and the 2026 budget was raised from US$52-56bn in January to US$60-64bn in July, with R&D at NT$246,427m. Visa, Google and Meta earn their excess returns without anything resembling this reinvestment. TSMC's returns are of that tier; its capital requirements are not. The reinvestment is what keeps the lead, and the day it stops is the day the lead starts to close. And TSMC does not price at the level its position would support, and says so. In the same calendar quarter TSMC earned 67.7% gross margin while Micron earned 84.6% and NVIDIA 74.9%. An analyst put this to management directly on the Q2 2026 call; C.C. Wei answered that he is "really jealous about the memory companies, 86% gross margin, 68 I will be happy." The margin understates the moat, because the margin is a policy choice, not a market-clearing outcome.▪

Mature and specialty. The franchise is the largest mature-node foundry business in the world, about 3.5x UMC's entire company, 2.9x SMIC's and 4.0x GlobalFoundries', sitting on a largely depreciated asset base and selling qualification-locked specialty processes.▪ Peer gross margins were 29.0% (UMC), 24.9% (GlobalFoundries), 23.2% (Tower), 21.0% (SMIC) and 11.8% (Hua Hong) in FY2025, and the residual arithmetic bounds TSMC's mature franchise at roughly 45-55%, 16 to 43 points above every one of them.▪ But it compounded at 2.0% a year in NT$ from 2018 to 2025 while the company compounded at 20.5%, and at 2.9% a year in US dollars from 2020 to 2025 against SMIC's 19.0% and Hua Hong's 20.1%.▪ TSMC's mature franchise was about 6.0x SMIC's total revenue in 2020 and is about 2.9x today. This franchise does not set price: its revenue peaked in 2022, declined 16.9% in 2023, declined again in 2024 and recovered in 2025 on the same cycle UMC, GlobalFoundries and SMIC rode. And management has held specialty capital spending roughly flat in absolute dollars at about US$4-6.4bn a year since 2023 while total capex more than doubled.

Backend. On returns the advantage is real: ASE's packaging segment earned a 22.1% gross margin in FY2025 and its combined packaging-and- test operation 23.8%; Amkor earned 14.0% at the consolidated line. TSMC does not disclose its packaging margin, but management has described it as approaching but still below the corporate average, which puts the gap to ASE at roughly 25-35 points [estimate: management's language applied to the disclosed FY2025 corporate gross margin]. Most of the evidence against durability comes from TSMC itself. Advanced packaging has been in acknowledged shortage since mid-2023 and the CFO said in January 2026 that the margin is still below the corporate average. Asked in July 2023 whether the CoWoS shortage was an opportunity to reprice, C.C. Wei said "the most important thing for them right now is supply assurance," adding that "we do everything possible to increase the capacity. And of course, at the same time, we share our value"; the then-Chairman said price adjustment was strategically appropriate. So the franchise has repriced selectively, not to parity, and three years into a shortage it still runs below its own company's average. TSMC has also deliberately lowered the switching barriers around its own flows: it contributed 3Dblox to the IEEE, qualified Amkor, ASE, Integrated Service Technology and SK hynix as 3DFabric partners, and signed a ten-year agreement in October 2024 to contract turnkey advanced packaging and test from Amkor's Arizona facility [web].▪

What the company claims

Claim Where How central

"We compete primarily on process technologies, manufacturing excellence, customer trust and service quality, such as earlier technology readiness, better quality, faster yield improvement and shorter cycle time." 20-F FY2025, Item 4, Competition The Competition section names no rival and gives no share figure.

"Through the development, deployment of the differentiated specialty technologies, the profitability of our mature nodes can be around our corporate average gross margin." Q4 2023 call Not repeated for this franchise on any 2024, 2025 or 2026 call, while corporate gross margin rose 13.3 points.

TSMC holds no investor day and no capital markets day, so there is no management document that argues the moat at length. The 20-F's competition section is thin for a company in this position.

What external sources say

Sell-side coverage is two reports, both Buy, both predating the Q2 2026 print, and neither engages with the mature franchise at all. Trade press supplies the share data (TrendForce's Q1 2026 foundry ranking), the yield comparisons and the pricing reports, all of them estimates. Ben Thompson argues TSMC underinvests relative to hyperscaler demand and that if it still is not producing enough chips by 2028 the hyperscalers "will be forgoing billions of dollars in revenue," rising to "potentially in the hundreds of billions of dollars," which is "surely a lot more than whatever expense is necessary to make Samsung and/or Intel into viable competitors for TSMC" (Stratechery, accessed 2026-07-28) [web]. That is a critique of TSMC's effect on the industry, not of its position.

Ground-up industrial organisation

Minimum efficient scale is the barrier at the leading edge. Developing one node and equipping a fab to run it costs on the order of US$20-30bn before a wafer ships, and A14 alone takes five to seven years from development to volume production.▪ That fixed cost is amortised over wafers, and TSMC shipped 15.0 million 12-inch equivalents in 2025 against UMC's 3.87 million. R&D declined from 8.5% of revenue in 2023 to 6.5% in 2025 while absolute R&D rose 35.1%. The fixed cost went up and the intensity went down.

The customer cannot integrate backwards. The largest single leading-edge buyer takes far less than one fab's minimum efficient output at a modern node, and design and manufacturing are separate disciplines. The population of IDMs still at the leading edge has declined from roughly a dozen in 2001 to one, which is losing money. Hyperscaler custom silicon increases TSMC's demand.

Switching cost is a qualification cost denominated in time. Moving a design between foundries means redoing physical design against a different PDK, requalifying IP, rerunning silicon and absorbing a yield-learning penalty. The observable proxy is the design pipeline: about 25 finalized 2nm designs plus more than 70 in development [web].

Entry barriers at mature nodes are low and falling. Depreciated 200mm and older 300mm equipment is available on the secondary market, process recipes at 28nm and above are ten to twenty years old and widely diffused, and the binding leading-edge input does not bind here: 28nm and above use DUV immersion, which ASML, Nikon and Canon all supply and which China can import.▪ SMIC ran a 93.5% annual average utilization in 2025 on roughly 9.7 million wafers and Hua Hong ran above 100% in every quarter of 2025 (102.7%, 108.3%, 109.5%) [web], while UMC's ASP declined 5.0% in 2024 and 5.4% in 2025 and GlobalFoundries' declined 10.4% in 2025 (each company's own 20-F). The highest utilization goes with the lowest margin. Capacity is not scarce in that industry; profitable capacity is.

Supplier power is real and partly offsetting. ASML is the sole EUV source, and C.C. Wei's second reason for the 2026 capex raise, after demand, was "inflation. Now we buy the [tools] with inflation price" (Q2 2026 call). TSMC's answer is to pre-book supplier capacity years ahead, which is itself a scale privilege.

Regulation cuts against TSMC. Every major government subsidises a rival: the US CHIPS Act, the European Chips Act (up to €5bn to ESMC), Japan's METI support for JASM and Rapidus, Korean support for Samsung. TSMC's own risk factor complains about unequal access to incentives. The consequence is quantified: overseas fabs dilute gross margin 2-3 percentage points in early stages, widening to 3-4 points later. Policy, not competition, is eroding this dimension.▪

Standalone returns

Basis:

NOPAT = income from operations × (1 − effective tax rate), where the effective rate is income-tax expense ÷ pre-tax income. Invested capital = total equity + total debt + lease liabilities − cash and cash equivalents − current financial assets. ROIC = NOPAT ÷ average of opening and closing invested capital. ROIIC = (NOPAT_t − NOPAT_t−3) ÷ (invested capital_t − invested capital_t−3). Cost of capital is not disclosed by TSMC and no Bloomberg WACC is used here; 9-11% is used as a stated assumption throughout.

Operating margin 39.9% 39.4% 37.2% 34.8% 42.3% 40.9% 49.5% 42.6% 45.7% 50.8%

The worst year in the decade was 2019 at 46.0% gross margin, 34.8% operating margin and 28.6% ROIC, at the bottom of a smartphone demand trough with 7nm just ramping and capex at 43.0% of revenue. A business whose cyclical trough is a 29% ROIC is not competing away its returns.▪ The level is also rising: five-year average ROIC was 33.0% over 2016-2020 and 41.6% over 2021-2025. Three-year rolling ROIIC of 55.2% over 2022-2025 exceeds the terminal-year ROIC, so the NT$7.0tn of capex spent over the decade earned more than the existing base.

Cash and financial assets were NT$3,202,932m at end-2025, 40.4% of total assets, earning a 3.30% pre-tax yield. Running FY2025 returns on invested capital including and excluding that pool gives 24.9% and 48.7% respectively. The operating business earns roughly 49%; the reported group earns roughly 25%. Half the reported return dilution is a treasury decision, not an industrial one.▪

The latest fiscal year and the most recent quarter diverge. TSMC's own gap is 7.8 points of gross margin and 9.5 of operating margin, explained by loading, cost improvement and mix. Intel's Q1 2026 headline operating margin of −23.1% includes US$4,070m of restructuring; excluding it the quarter was +6.9%, the first meaningfully positive operating quarter in the series, so Intel is improving while remaining nowhere near TSMC. Micron shows the widest gap: FY2025 gross margin 39.8% against 84.6% in the quarter ended 28 May 2026, on revenue of US$41,456m that now exceeds TSMC's quarterly revenue. TSMC is not the most profitable semiconductor manufacturer, and management concedes it. Amkor's Q1 2026 gross margin of 14.2% against a 14.0% full year, on 27.5% revenue growth, shows that revenue growth in the packaging layer is not converting into margin for the specialists.

There is no dimension on which the leading-edge gap is narrowing. The mature franchise is the opposite: the margin gap holds at a high level while the scale gap closes.▪ Intel Foundry's operating loss improving from −77% to −57.9% to −36.2% and Samsung's utilization recovering above 80% are recoveries from catastrophe toward merely loss-making, at a moment when TSMC's own margins are inflecting upward faster.

Where this sits

Against the three reference points, TSMC's leading-edge position is the first: a structural advantage that neither Intel Foundry nor Samsung has narrowed on any dimension in the table above, supporting pricing power the company chooses not to fully exercise and throwing off returns several multiples of any plausible cost of capital.▪ It sits one notch below the Visa, Google and Meta reference because those franchises earn their excess returns without reinvesting a third of revenue every year to defend the position. The mature franchise is the second reference point: it earns excess returns today, is defensible for now, and is open to erosion as Chinese capacity scales and as TSMC itself reallocates the asset base toward the leading edge. The backend is also the second reference point, and it is closer to the boundary, because the incumbent is inviting rivals into it.

Business-model analogues. The shape of the leading-edge moat is a cumulative process-learning monopoly: the roadmap costs more each generation, only the volume leader can amortise it, and customers design into the process years before production, which converts the cost lead into a qualification lock.

Analogue Why it holds Where it breaks
ASML The same industry one layer up: a single scaled supplier of the enabling capability, protected by cumulative know-how and a supply base only it can organise, with customers planning multi-year around its roadmap ASML is additionally protected by patents and physics, and its capital intensity is a fraction of TSMC's. ASML's moat is the stronger of the two
KLA Dominant share of process control, tools qualified into the customer's line, returns above 35% on far less capital. The same designed-into-the-customer's-process lock KLA's addressable market is a fraction of TSMC's and it faces no state-subsidised attacker
Lam Research (for the backend franchise only) A technology leader in an enabling step inside somebody else's product, earning well above the commodity layer beneath it, capacity-tight during a build cycle, with the customer's standing incentive to qualify a second source Lam's customers cannot switch mid-node; a package can be re-sourced within a product cycle

No US-listed company reproduces the combination of monopoly share, 50%+ ROIC and 33%-of-revenue capital intensity. ASML is the closest single name, with the caveat that its protection is patent- and physics-based while TSMC's is volume- and learning-based, and volume can in principle be bought.▪

What would falsify this

In rough order of how early each would appear: Intel or Samsung announcing a named, committed leading-edge external customer at 14A or SF2 with disclosed volume; Intel Foundry external revenue moving from US$307m toward US$2bn annualized; TSMC's advanced share of wafer revenue stalling below about 77% while total shipments grow; a gross-margin gap versus UMC or GlobalFoundries that stops widening for four consecutive quarters; TSMC declining to raise price into a fifth consecutive year; and overseas capacity rising above roughly 25-30% of leading-edge output, at which point the guided 3-4 points of dilution stops being small against the mix tailwind.

4. Competitive landscape and market sizing

The same corporate entity operates in two industries with opposite structures. At 7nm and below the Herfindahl index on merchant revenue is roughly 8,700 out of 10,000, more than three times the threshold US merger guidelines treat as highly concentrated. At 16nm and above it is roughly 2,000, which is the middle of the moderately-concentrated band.▪ The consolidated margin therefore describes the first industry, not the second.

Assuming every dollar of Samsung's, SMIC's and Intel Foundry's external revenue is leading-edge gives TSMC 77.2% of merchant sub-7nm revenue. Who sets price. TSMC does, and states openly that it declines to set it at the clearing level (Section 3). An analyst on the Q2 2026 call floated unconstrained demand for 3nm and below at 30-50% above supply; investor relations explicitly distanced management from the figure and C.C. Wei declined to give a number, saying only that the gap is very big. A supplier who can allocate scarce capacity and still prices below a rival category is choosing not to extract.

TSMC's leading-edge franchise alone is 6.1x Samsung's entire foundry business across all nodes, 7.8x SMIC's entire business and 255x Intel Foundry's external revenue. TSMC targets 100,000-140,000 2nm wafers per month against Samsung's 21,000, a ratio of 4.8x to 6.7x, both figures trade press. On the design pipeline, which predicts 2028-29 share because a win converts to revenue two to three years later, the gap is wider than on today's revenue. On capital, TSMC's 2026 spend on advanced process alone is roughly 2.9-3.5x Intel's entire-company PP&E additions in FY2025 and exceeds Samsung's whole 2026 semiconductor budget. The direction of Intel's spending is the material fact: PP&E additions declined from US$25,750m (FY2023) to US$23,944m (FY2024) to US$14,646m (FY2025), 43.1% over two years, with only US$9,100m of capital-expenditure commitments for 2026 and a stated policy of building 14A capacity only against firm external commitments (INTC 10-K FY2025).

TSMC does not trail on any leading-edge metric in the table above. The two places a rival holds an advantage are outside the franchise: Samsung's memory business earns a higher gross margin than TSMC's foundry, a fact TSMC's own chief executive volunteered, and Intel holds High-NA tools TSMC says it does not require through 2029.▪

Share counter-evidence at the leading edge

  1. Customer dual-sourcing at 2nm, the only threat with observable traction. Qualcomm engaged Samsung for 2nm prototypes and then selected TSMC N2P for its flagship, with Samsung a candidate for mid-tier parts; Tesla dual-sourced AI5 [web]. Sizing: if Samsung reaches 21,000 wafers per month fully loaded at a reported US$20,000 per wafer, that is roughly US$5,000m of annual 2nm revenue, 6.4% of TSMC's FY2025 leading-edge revenue and less than one quarter of TSMC's leading-edge growth in FY2025 alone [estimate: 21,000 × 12 × US$20,000 at 100% utilization and no yield loss].
  2. Intel Foundry's external ramp. External revenue rose 13x year over year to US$293m in Q2 2026, which annualizes to roughly US$1,200m, about 1.1% of TSMC's leading-edge run rate, and the line includes packaging and test. Intel now has the US government as a shareholder plus equity investments from NVIDIA and SoftBank. Its capital trajectory is inconsistent with a rapid external share build.
  3. Advanced packaging as an entry vector, which TSMC actively welcomes (Section 3). Favourable to the wafer franchise, unfavourable to the packaging franchise.
  4. Samsung's 2nm yield progress. Reported at 55-60% for SF2 and around 70% for SF2P, both [web] and conflicting. Capacity, not yield is the binding limit.
  5. China's parallel leading edge. SMIC plans to double 7nm-class capacity in 2026 on DUV multi-patterning at reported 20-40% yields, anchored on Huawei [web]. This is share TSMC cannot compete for: the January 2025 US rules require a licence to ship 16nm-and-below products to specified destinations. It removes a market.
  6. Rapidus. Zero volume customers after a pilot line running since April 2025.

Powerchip's 38.6% decline from peak overstates the foundry decline: its 2021-22 revenue included a large memory component that collapsed with DRAM pricing.

TSMC's mature ASP and where it sits. Deriving mature volume as a residual (total disclosed shipments less advanced volume implied by third-party node prices) gives mature volume of 9,580-10,080 thousand wafers and a blended mature ASP of US$2,675-2,816 per 12-inch equivalent [estimate: residual method; node prices from published foundry pricing compilations, which disagree by up to 30% on N3, so the band is the usable figure]. That is 36-43% above UMC's disclosed US$1,973 and 24-30% above SMIC's implied US$2,164. The comparison with GlobalFoundries is not like-for-like on its headline revenue, because GlobalFoundries' disclosed US$6,791m includes US$769m of non-wafer revenue; stripping that out gives roughly US$2,630 per 300mm equivalent, so TSMC's premium over GlobalFoundries is small and positive.

The mix explains the premium. 16nm (NT$215,722m) and 28nm (NT$225,134m) together are 52.5% of TSMC's mature revenue, and 16nm FinFET is a node UMC does not run at scale. UMC attributes its own ASP decline of 5.0% in 2024 and 5.4% in 2025 to "the nominal price erosion in 2024 and 2025" (UMC 20-F FY2025, Item 5). TSMC's mature franchise is not selling the same wafer as UMC's, and management describes the strategy as competing only in "the higher value-added and strategic segment" (Q2 2026 call).

Who sets mature-node price. Not TSMC, historically. UMC shipped 3,195k, then 3,446k, then 3,870k 12-inch equivalents across 2023-2025 while its ASP declined 5.0% and then 5.4%; GlobalFoundries shipped 10.4% more wafers in 2025 at 10.4% lower prices.▪ Both companies name subsidised competition in their risk factors: GlobalFoundries devotes a named risk factor to "strong government support in China for their domestic capacity expansion." China's share of global mature-process capacity is forecast at 31-39% by 2027 depending on the source, an eight-point spread across TrendForce, DigiTimes and SEMI [web] that is logged.

That mechanism may be turning. TSMC has notified customers of mature-node price increases of up to 10% on 12nm, 16nm, 28nm and other legacy processes effective January 2027, reported as the first mature-node increase in over three years (TechNode, accessed 2026-07-28) [web], and four second-tier foundries were reported in April 2026 to be planning increases of up to 10% or more [web]. These are trade-press reports sourced to customer notifications, not company confirmations.

Where TSMC leads and trails at mature nodes. It leads on absolute scale (2.9x SMIC, 3.5x UMC, 4.0x GlobalFoundries on line revenue), on blended ASP (36-43% above UMC), on breadth (305 process technologies, 12,682 products, 534 customers company-wide), on specialty qualification depth (16nm second-generation MRAM and 22ULL RRAM both passed Automotive Grade-1 in 2025, per 20-F FY2025 Item 4), and on capital commitment: roughly US$6.0-6.4bn of 2026 specialty capex against UMC's US$1.5bn for the entire company, a ratio of about 4.0-4.3x. It trails on growth: +1.9% US$ compound over 2021-2025 against SMIC's +14.4% and Hua Hong's +10.2%, though ahead of GlobalFoundries' +0.8% and Tower's +0.9%. It is below its own 2022 peak, alongside UMC (−14.8%), GlobalFoundries (−16.2%), Vanguard (−11.7%) and Powerchip (−38.6%), while SMIC is at its peak. And it does not disclose utilization at all, in a franchise it is choosing not to fill. Closing the gap fastest are SMIC, on a 14.4% four-year compound rate with 93.5% utilization and US$5.97bn committed to buying out the remaining 49% of its SMNC joint venture (two 300mm 28nm lines) [web], and Nexchip, which reached its highest-ever ranking of eighth in Q1 2026 [web].

Backend: the incumbent holds the profit pool, and the capacity gap is closing

The published advanced-packaging market number does not settle the question. Yole sizes the market at US$55bn in 2025 growing to more than US$120bn by 2031 [web], but that spans flip chip, fan-out, wafer-level CSP and 2.5D/3D and includes captive IDM and memory packaging. TSMC's roughly US$9.8bn of FY2025 advanced-packaging revenue is about 18% of it, which is the wrong headline because the market so defined mixes a commodity with a near-monopoly.

TrendForce puts total 2026 industry 2.5D capacity at roughly 200,000 wafers per month, of which TSMC is 120,000-140,000 and OSAT partners 50,000-60,000 [web], so TSMC is roughly 60-70% of 2.5D capacity▪ [estimate: TrendForce ranges, midpoints]. The revenue can be sized two ways: capacity times price gives TSMC CoWoS revenue of about US$13bn in 2026 (1.3m wafers at a reported US$10,000 ASP [web]); management's guide of "slightly over 10%" of a roughly US$171bn revenue year gives about US$18bn for all advanced packaging. Those are not independent measurements — both lean on the same guided revenue base — but the difference between them is roughly the SoIC and InFO contribution, so US$13-18bn brackets the franchise.

ASE will spend US$7.0bn in 2026 against roughly US$14bn of ATM revenue and Amkor US$2.5-3.0bn against roughly US$8bn, while TSMC's entire backend bucket — packaging plus test plus mask making plus other — is US$6.0-12.8bn against roughly US$25bn of Others-line revenue. On the midpoints TSMC commits about 38% of backend revenue to backend capex where ASE commits about 50%. The OSATs are buying their way in at materially worse capital efficiency than the incumbent.

On a full-year basis TSMC's backend line grew 41% while ASE's ATM grew 20% and Amkor 6%. On the most recent quarter the OSATs grew 28-30% against TSMC consolidated at 34-36%, and Amkor's growth rate quadrupled. The gap is closing because TSMC is outsourcing more, not because the OSATs won business away from it.▪

Where the profit pool sits, on a 45-55% estimated TSMC packaging gross margin: TSMC earns roughly US$4,400-5,400m of gross profit from advanced packaging against ASE's US$2,885m across its whole packaging-and-test operation and Amkor's US$939m — roughly as much as both combined, on about half their combined revenue.▪ At 45-55% against a 59.9% FY2025 corporate gross margin, a rising packaging mix pulls the consolidated number down, and management has never listed packaging mix among the six gross-margin factors it does name.▪

Capital is competing the scarcity away. TrendForce puts the CoWoS supply-demand gap at around 20% currently, narrowing to about 10% by the end of 2026, with TSMC planning to expand CoWoS capacity by more than 60% again by 2027 and total industry capacity approaching 200,000 wafers per month (TrendForce, accessed 2026-07-28) [web]. Attackers are arriving with capital: ASE guided leading-edge advanced-packaging revenue to at least US$3.2bn and later more than US$3.5bn for 2026 from about US$1.6bn in 2025, on record capital spending of US$7bn with about two-thirds earmarked for leading-edge capacity (Taipei Times, accessed 2026-07-28) [web], and Intel's chief financial officer said at a February 2026 conference that Intel is close to closing packaging deals worth billions of dollars per year [web]. Intel packaging margins are reported at around 40% [web, unverified against any filing].

The incumbent openly invites rivals into this franchise, because the constraint costs it more in wafer sales than the packaging margin is worth.

A definitional trap

Three different "foundry share" numbers circulate and all three are correct on their own definition. TrendForce's 72.3% for Q1 2026 is share of top-ten merchant foundry revenue and excludes Intel Foundry entirely because it is 98% internal; Intel Foundry nonetheless produced US$17,826m of segment revenue in FY2025, which would be second-largest in the world on a total-leading-edge-manufacturing basis. TSMC's own "Foundry 2.0" definition (all logic wafer manufacturing plus packaging, testing, mask making and others) puts the industry at roughly US$320bn in 2025 with TSMC at about 35-38%. And the merchant sub-7nm figure computed above is 77-93%. None of the three can be blended with another.

5. Value chain and profit pools

Gap flagged at the top of this section: the non-packaging half of the backend line is not analysed below. Mask making, wafer probe and final test, design services and royalties are NT$231,800m, US$7,500m, 6.1% of FY2025 revenue, larger than either the Automotive or the IoT platform and larger than Amkor's entire company. It enters the model as a residual with no revenue driver, no growth series and no margin estimate, even though ASE's disclosed testing gross margin of 31.0% against 22.1% for packaging suggests it may be the higher-margin half. That mis-centres the 45-55% backend margin band the profit-pool table below uses.

Ranked by gross margin: memory first, then the chip designers, then TSMC, then process control, then lithography, then general equipment, then mature foundry, then packaging services. TSMC out-earns every one of its own suppliers on gross margin and is beaten only by memory and by its own customers.

The AI accelerator dollar, per unit

Epoch AI's published breakdown of a NVIDIA B200 module gives a total manufacturing cost of roughly US$6,400 (Epoch AI, accessed 2026-07-28) [web]:

Component Cost Share of manufacturing cost Captured by
HBM3E ~US$2,900 45% SK hynix / Micron / Samsung
CoWoS-L advanced packaging ~US$1,100 17% TSMC
Packaging yield loss ~US$1,000 16% —
Logic die (TSMC 4NP) ~US$900 14% TSMC
Balance (substrate, test, other) ~US$500 8% OSAT / ODM / substrate
TSMC total ~US$2,000 ~31% —

A disclosed-figure cross-check runs the other way and lands nearby: TSMC's Customer A revenue of US$23,263m in calendar 2025 is 37.3% of NVIDIA's FY2026 cost of revenue of US$62,406m. The two methods bracket TSMC's share of the customer's manufacturing cost at roughly 31-37%. The Customer A identification is an inference, since TSMC names nobody.

Reported B200 street pricing is roughly US$30,000-40,000 [web]. TSMC's roughly US$2,000 of content is therefore 5.0-6.7% of what the end buyer pays.▪ At TSMC's FY2025 gross margin that is about US$1,198 of TSMC gross profit per accelerator against NVIDIA's roughly US$21,000-28,000.

Evidence against: memory suppliers capture more of the accelerator bill of materials than TSMC does, 45% against 31%, on a component TSMC does not make, and TSMC's packaging capture on the most supply-constrained input in the AI build-out is about 3-4% of what the accelerator sells for. Owning the bottleneck has not translated into owning the profit.

Evidence for: packaging is roughly 55% of what TSMC collects per B200 (US$1,100 of US$2,000) against about 8% of consolidated revenue, because the consolidated figure is diluted by smartphone and mature-node revenue where packaging attach is low or zero.▪ On the products driving growth, the backend is several times larger a share of TSMC's take than the corporate mix suggests, which the Q2 2026 print of a record 16.0% backend share of revenue has begun to show.

Inside TSMC's own dollar

Per NT$100 of FY2025 revenue, roughly 34 cents is paid, now or earlier, to suppliers: 17 cents of raw wafers, chemicals, gases, masks, utilities and outsourced services, plus 16.8 cents of depreciation, which is a deferred payment to the equipment and construction layers. Same-year cash flow to suppliers is larger: FY2025 capital expenditure of NT$1,272,411m was 33.4% of revenue, and the 2026 budget of US$60-64bn against an implied US$170bn of revenue is 35-38% paid straight back up the chain.

The binding constraint

Near-term, packaging: confirmed by the company, with a caveat. C.C. Wei on the Q2 2026 call: "our packaging capacity is so tight, that now is [limiting] customers growth." This constraint is being relieved. CoWoS capacity moved from roughly 35,000 wafers per month at the end of 2024 to about 75,000 at the end of 2025, with 120,000-140,000 projected for the end of 2026, and TrendForce projects the supply-demand gap narrowing from about 20% to about 10% over 2026 [web].▪

Near-term, ABF substrate: the successor constraint, and TSMC does not control it. An advanced AI accelerator uses roughly ten times the ABF build-up film of a standard PC processor. Ajinomoto, the effective sole supplier of the film, notified substrate makers in May 2026 of a roughly 30% price increase effective in the third quarter of 2026, and the ABF supply gap is projected at about 10% in the second half of 2026 widening to about 21% in 2027 (DigiTimes, accessed 2026-07-28) [web]. TSMC does not buy the film; the substrate vendors do. Its exposure runs through its customers' ability to obtain substrates for parts TSMC has already packaged. C.C. Wei confirmed the dependency without naming it: "we also work with substrate vendor so that our customer can have their product be in the market."

Near-term, memory: the largest price signal in the chain, and TSMC has no position in it. Micron's gross margin moved from 37.7% in the quarter to May 2025 to 84.6% in the quarter to May 2026 on revenue up 346%. Microsoft's chief financial officer attributed US$25bn of a US$190bn calendar-2026 capital budget to memory and component price inflation, not to capacity (The Register, accessed 2026-07-28) [web]. That is 13.2% of one buyer's budget consumed by input price.

Multi-year, EUV: not confirmed as a hard constraint. ASML recognised 48 EUV systems in 2025 against 44 in 2024 and said in July 2026 that it plans to raise Low-NA EUV production capacity by about 30% in 2027 from roughly 65 systems in 2026 [web]. TSMC's own view is that it collaborates with tool suppliers well in advance and does "not foresee any bottlenecks to our capacity expansion plans" (CFO, Q2 2026 call). The multi-year constraint management does name is time, not tools: five to seven years from technology development to volume production.

What TSMC has locked up. Capital purchase and other purchase obligations at 2025-12-31 were NT$1,534,575m (about US$49.3bn), of which NT$1,220,393m is due within one year, for construction or purchase of equipment, raw material and other property or services not recorded on the balance sheet (20-F FY2025, Item 5). That is close to a full year of capital budget placed forward, and it is a larger and nearer claim on cash than the entire bond stack.

Customer-side economics

Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft guided to roughly US$610-725bn of 2026 capital expenditure depending on the aggregation, against roughly US$380-410bn in 2025 [web]. TSMC's entire consolidated revenue at management's guided growth is roughly US$170bn, or about a quarter of the four largest buyers' capital budgets alone.

Two disclosed facts bound whether the customer's spend makes sense without requiring an assumed AI revenue forecast. NVIDIA's outstanding inventory purchase and long-term supply and capacity obligations were US$95.2bn at 2026-01-25 against FY2026 cost of revenue of US$62,406m, so more than 1.5 years of cost of revenue is committed forward. And NVIDIA has already taken one large loss on that willingness: a US$4.5bn charge in Q1 FY2026 for H20 excess inventory and purchase obligations after export controls, with full-year provisions for inventory and excess purchase obligations reaching US$7.2bn in FY2026 against US$3.7bn in FY2025, a 2.6-point unfavourable gross-margin effect (NVDA 10-K FY2026). The mechanism by which a demand break reaches TSMC is visible: the customer absorbs the purchase obligation first, which buys one or two quarters and no more.

Customer headroom. TSMC's content is 10.8% of NVIDIA's revenue dollar and 5.0-6.7% of a B200's street price, against a 71.1% NVIDIA gross margin. A 20% TSMC price increase on that content costs NVIDIA about 2.2 points of gross margin. Apple is the counter-case: TSMC's second-largest customer accounted for 17% of FY2025 revenue, about US$20,815m, against Apple's FY2025 revenue of about US$416,207m, so 5.0% of the customer's revenue dollar but against a 36.8% products gross margin, not 71.1%. The smartphone customer has roughly half the headroom of the accelerator customer, and TSMC's allocation has moved accordingly: HPC from 58% of FY2025 revenue to 66% in Q2 2026 while smartphone declined from 29% to 22%.

Bargaining power, and which way it is moving

Supplier to TSMC. TSMC has gained margin against its sole-source lithography supplier. The gross-margin gap, TSMC less ASML, was +4.8 points in FY2024, +7.1 points in FY2025 and +13.7 points on the most recent quarters.▪ TSMC is also the largest single buyer of equipment and exercises that: ASML's largest customer accounted for €7,796.7m, 23.9% of 2025 net sales, up from 16.6% in 2024, and KLA names TSMC as a customer above 10% of revenue in each of FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025. Against a 2026 wafer-fab-equipment market forecast of US$135.2bn [web], TSMC's US$60-64bn budget at an assumed 70-75% equipment share implies US$42-48bn, roughly 31-36% of world equipment spending [estimate: TSMC capex × assumed equipment share; TSMC discloses capex including buildings and does not split tools out]. TSMC used that position against ASML's roadmap: Intel, not TSMC, shipped the first High-NA logic product.

Power is nonetheless shifting toward suppliers on unit price. The CFO on the Q4 2025 call: "the cost of tools are becoming more expensive and process complexity is increasing. As a result, the CapEx dollar required to build 1,000 wafer per month capacity of N2 is substantially higher than 1,000 wafer per month capacity for N3. The CapEx per k cost for A14 will be even higher." On materials, the Q1 2026 call flagged that "given the recent situation in the Middle East, prices for certain chemicals and gases are likely to increase."

TSMC to customer. Realized price is outrunning input cost by a wide and widening margin at the leading edge — gross margin 54.4% (2023) to 67.7% (Q2 2026) — while the mature franchise shows the opposite pattern across the whole peer group. Concentration is rising and management dismisses it: top-ten customers went from 70% to 78% of revenue over two years, and asked directly, C.C. Wei answered "No, that's not our concern... we are very happy about it" (Q2 2026 call).▪ The 20-F says the same fact "may adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition."

The one disclosed measure of customers paying cash to reserve capacity moved the other way: temporary receipts declined 34.8% in 2025, from 10.1% to 5.0% of revenue, in the year management described demand as most acutely exceeding supply. The 20-F permits a benign explanation: treatment is by refund or offset against receivables, "by mutual consent," and an offset against a much larger receivable base would produce exactly this. The filing discloses no gross movement, so the two explanations cannot be separated.

Backward integration by customers is not visible in the numbers. Intel Foundry's external revenue was US$293m in Q2 2026 and US$467m in the first half of 2026, against US$22m and US$53m a year earlier, so 13x growth off a base under 1% of TSMC's quarterly revenue.

Circularity and financing

TSMC has refused to participate in the chain's financing loop, on the record. Asked whether it would invest in or finance its customers' customers, C.C. Wei answered: "So far, no. TSMC don't do this kind of financial arrangement because we think we are working with current customer with the current model smoothly and also successfully" (Q2 2026 call). No vendor financing, no equity in customers and no guarantees to end buyers appear in the 20-F. For contrast, NVIDIA discloses that it has "been asked to offer financing arrangements to support our customers' and partners' buildout of datacenter infrastructure" and states that it "ha[s] not entered into any financing arrangements" (NVDA 10-K FY2026).

What TSMC does have is small relative to revenue. Under the SSMC shareholders agreement it and NXP must in aggregate purchase at least 70% of SSMC's capacity, with TSMC alone not required to take more than 28% — an obligation TSMC owes, not collects. Its equity-method holdings sit upstream and sideways (Vanguard, Global Unichip), not in customers. Performance guarantees through financial institutions were NT$23,375m and unused letters of credit NT$439m at 2025 year-end, together under 0.7% of revenue. Government funding is the one large third-party input: US CHIPS Act support for Arizona, METI support for JASM and up to €5bn of EU state aid for ESMC, all with clawback conditions.

6. Secular and industry trends

Between the 2022 revenue peak and FY2025, TSMC shipped fewer wafers and earned 68% more revenue. Shipments went from 15,253 thousand 12-inch equivalents in 2022 to 15,022 thousand in 2025, a decline of 1.5%, while net revenue went from NT$2,263,891m to NT$3,809,054m. All of the three-year growth came from realized price and product mix; volume subtracted from it.▪ Physical output had still not regained its 2022 level in 2025.

The industry data agrees. Worldwide silicon wafer area shipments were 12,973 million square inches in 2025, still 10.9% below the 14,565 MSI record set in 2022 (SEMI Silicon Manufacturers Group, released 2026-02-10) [web]. The semiconductor industry has been in a dollar boom on a flat physical base.

TSMC's mature and specialty franchise performed like the mature-node cohort, not better than it. Every unit of outperformance is at the leading edge, where the competitive set is Samsung Foundry and Intel Foundry, and where Intel Foundry lost US$10.3bn in 2025.▪ The mature cohort's 2025 was volume up, price down. That is the standard mature-node oversupply pattern and the exact inverse of TSMC's leading-edge pattern. A single "semiconductor cycle" averages the two.

Did the claimed driver show up?

Management claim Where it appears in the realized record
"AI accelerator revenue more than tripled in 2024" (Q4 2024 call) Consistent with HPC platform revenue +58% in 2024. Confirmed indirectly; TSMC never discloses AI revenue in dollars.
"close to mid-teens percent of our total revenue in 2024" → "high teens percent... in 2025" Implies US$11.7-13.5bn in 2024 and US$20.8-23.3bn in 2025, a range of +54% to +99% [estimate: stated percentage bands × reported revenue].
"we forecast our revenue from AI accelerator to double in 2025" (Q4 2024 call) The midpoint of the implied range, about +75%, is below a double. Not resolvable from disclosure; logged as an open question.
"content per wafer is increasing" Fully confirmed. Wafer revenue per 12-inch equivalent went NT$95.1k (2020) to NT$217.9k (2025), +129%.
"unit growth from the four growth platforms" (smartphone, HPC, IoT, automotive) Not confirmed. Smartphone went from 39% of revenue in 2022 to 22% in Q2 2026. IoT and Automotive are 5% and 4%. Only HPC moved.
Foundry 2.0 industry growth of +10% forecast for 2025 (Jan 2025) Actual +16% (Q4 2025 call). Management under-forecast its own market.

Tracing the AI driver to its ultimate exposure gives hyperscaler and AI-lab capital budgets, not end-user AI adoption. Management named the transmission path itself: "our customers' customers who are mainly the cloud service providers are also providing strong signals and reaching out directly to request the capacity" (Q4 2025 call). The ultimate exposure is therefore six to eight balance sheets' capital budgets, and that concentration is the fragility in the driver. It is measurable quarterly from those companies' own guidance, which TSMC's revenue follows with a two-to-three-quarter lag.

Market growth versus company growth

FY2025 US$169.5bn (+26.3%) US$122.54bn (+36.1%) 69.9%

Source: TrendForce via EE Times Asia and TelecomLead, accessed 2026-07-28 [web].

The share gain is mostly price, not units. Among the three foundries that disclose 12-inch-equivalent wafer volume, TSMC's share of shipments rose from 70.0% to 70.9% in 2025, 0.9 points, while its revenue share on the TrendForce measure rose 5.5 points.▪ The difference is realized price: TSMC's wafer revenue per 12-inch equivalent was about US$7,003 in 2025 against UMC's US$1,973 and GlobalFoundries' roughly US$2,630. TSMC is not taking wafers from UMC and GlobalFoundries; both grew wafer volume 10-12% in 2025. What TSMC is taking is the profit pool.

Cyclical versus secular

Measure 2019 trough 2022 peak 2023 trough 2025 Q2 2026
Wafer shipments (k 12-inch eq.) 10,068 15,253 12,002 15,022 4,336 (quarter)
Net revenue (NT$m) 1,069,985 2,263,891 2,161,736 3,809,054 1,270,381 (quarter)
Gross margin 46.0% 59.6% 54.4% 59.9% 67.7%
Operating margin 34.8% 49.5% 42.6% 50.8% 60.3%
