Trough-to-trough shipments went 10,068 (2019) to 12,002 (2023), +19.2% over four years or 4.5% a year. That is the underlying physical growth rate of the business through a full cycle, far below the 20%-plus revenue compound rate. Peak-to-peak gross margin of 59.6% (2022) and 59.9% (2025) is nearly identical despite 68% more revenue, because 2025 absorbed the N3 ramp and overseas-fab dilution that 2022 did not. The new high is Q2 2026's 67.7%, guided down to 65-67% in Q3 2026 with the N2 ramp diluting 3-4 points.

Every conventional cycle indicator is at or near an extreme: record margins, revenue guidance raised three times inside seven months (close to 30% in January, above 30% in April, slightly above 40% in July), the capital budget raised, inventory days at 87 and customer concentration at a record. The one indicator that is not at an extreme is capital intensity, which was 52.9% of revenue in 2021 and 47.8% in 2022 against 33.4% in 2025 and about 36% on the 2026 budget. The growth of the last three years has been unusually capital-light for this company precisely because it came from mix on installed capacity. That is the mechanism behind the margin expansion, and it is what changes from here.▪

The 2026 guide embeds a steep fourth quarter. First-half actuals of US$76.10bn plus the Q3 guide midpoint of US$45.2bn leave an implied Q4 2026 of US$50-53bn at "slightly above 40%" full-year growth, which is +11% to +16% sequentially and +49% to +56% year over year against a Q3 guide of +37% year over year▪ [estimate: full-year guide less first-half actual less Q3 guide midpoint]. The annual guide embeds a year-over-year acceleration into the fourth quarter on a base that has already compounded. It is tested on the October 2026 call.

A measurement trap in the market-size figures

WSTS's Spring 2026 forecast puts the 2026 semiconductor market at US$1.51 trillion, +90%, "overwhelmingly driven by the Memory segment" [web]. TSMC's own Foundry 2.0 market is forecast to grow 14% in 2026. The two describe different things: the WSTS figure is dominated by a memory pricing event in which TSMC does not participate at all. Using "semiconductor market growth" as TSMC's market growth would overstate the denominator by roughly six-fold in 2026 and make a share gainer look like a share loser. Logic is forecast at +37% on the same release, which is closer and still not the same as foundry.

What would show first if the secular story were breaking

Ranked by lead time. TSMC's disclosure cadence is unusually fast for this.

  1. Monthly NT$ net revenue, published around the 10th of each month under Taiwan Stock Exchange rules and furnished on Form 6-K. Two consecutive months of sequential decline outside first-quarter seasonality, arriving roughly five weeks ahead of any US-listed peer's data.
  2. Hyperscaler capital-expenditure guidance, which precedes TSMC's revenue by two to three quarters given the engagement lead time.
  3. The capital-budget revision direction. The 2026 pattern was US$52-56bn, then near the upper end, then US$60-64bn. A mid-year cut is management's clearest available signal and it is published quarterly.
  4. Node mix. 2nm as a percentage of wafer revenue, 3% in Q2 2026, against the guided steep ramp.
  5. Inventory days. 74 at the end of 2025, 80 in Q1 2026, 87 in Q2 2026. A further step-up without a node-ramp explanation is the standard pre-correction signal.
  6. Gross margin against the guided dilution. Q3 2026 is guided to 65-67% with 3-4 points of N2 dilution, implying an underlying 69-70%. A miss that management attributes to utilization, not to the ramp is the first evidence of the demand-supply gap closing from the wrong side.
  7. The Foundry 2.0 forecast versus TSMC's own guidance, both published each January. The gap between them is management's own statement of expected share gain.

7. Critical points

1. Three years of AI-era revenue growth involved no wafer growth at all, and that regime changed in 2026. Between 2022 and 2025 TSMC shipped 15,253 thousand and then 15,022 thousand 12-inch-equivalent wafers, 1.5% fewer, while wafer revenue in US dollars rose 57.6% and disclosed capacity rose from about 15 million to over 17 million. The entire revenue gain was mix and price, and the entire capacity gain went unused. In the first half of 2026 shipments grew 22.0% year over year and volume supplied roughly 60% of the growth. A mix-driven business decelerates when the node ladder runs out; a volume-driven business decelerates when demand stops filling capacity that has already been committed. The 2026 volume arrived on capacity already paid for; 2027-2028 volume requires new capacity, and the incremental margin on the two is different.

2. The gross-margin expansion comes from depreciation and utilization, and management says so. Consolidated gross margin went from 54.4% (FY2023) to 67.7% (Q2 2026), 13.3 points. The CFO, asked directly whether 20% annual ASP growth was the new normal, answered that "in the last few years, the pricing benefits to the profitability was just enough to cover the inflation cost from tools, equipment, materials, labor," attributing the higher profitability to utilization and manufacturing excellence instead (Q4 2025 call). The arithmetic supports him. Under the Q2 2026 wafer mix, reproducing a 67.7% consolidated gross margin requires the N5/N7 band, both past the five-year machinery life, to run at 73-85%. Roughly 44% of wafer revenue is currently in that fully-depreciated band, down from 50% in FY2025 as N2 and N3 take share. That is a mechanical headwind.▪ Depreciation as a share of revenue also declined from 26.3% (2019) to 17.8% (2025), 8.5 points, against 13.8 points of gross-margin expansion over the same window; since foundry depreciation sits almost entirely in cost of revenue, a large part of the margin gain is revenue outgrowing a fixed depreciation base, not price. That reverses when volume stalls, which is exactly what 2023 demonstrated.

3. TSMC's AI exposure is roughly double what its own disclosure says. Management labels AI accelerator revenue at "high teens percent of our total revenue in 2025" and excludes data-centre CPUs by definition. But the HPC platform was 58% of FY2025 revenue and 66% by Q2 2026, and the non-accelerator remainder of HPC grew from about US$26.0bn to about US$48.5bn over 2023-2025, a larger contribution to consolidated growth (roughly 42%) than AI accelerators themselves (roughly 32-36%) [estimate: platform disclosure less management's stated AI-accelerator band]. Data-centre CPUs, switch ASICs and optical DSPs go to the same hyperscalers out of the same budget for the same racks; management effectively conceded the linkage in Q2 2026. AI-data-centre-driven demand is plausibly 35-45% of total revenue and supplied roughly three-quarters of 2023-2025 growth. The diversification implied by "AI is only high-teens percent of revenue" is not there.▪

4. The 22%-of-revenue franchise that is supposed to cushion a downturn was itself declining, and its 2026 recovery is AI-linked, not broad. Mature and specialty wafer revenue went from about NT$936bn (2022) to NT$839bn (2025), −10.4% in NT$ and about −14.0% in US$, and it subtracted 6.3% from the consolidated revenue increase over that window. Over 2021-2025 it compounded at 4.6% in NT$ and 1.9% in US$ while the advanced franchise compounded at 36.4% in NT$ and consolidated revenue at 24.5%. Its share of revenue halved from 44.2% to 22.0% because the denominator more than doubled. In the first half of 2026 it grew 22.3% year over year, but management identifies the cause narrowly: "the mature node cover a lot of different segments only the one is related to AI is in shortage... number one is a power management IC because of all the AI data center needs a lot of power management... And also the sensor portion" (Q2 2026 call). The node detail agrees: 65nm +29% and 28nm +9% over 2022-2025 while seven other node bands declined. The diversification argument for TSMC is therefore weaker than it appears, because the cushion is exposed to the same end demand as the leading edge.

5. The people who attack the moat lose money doing it. Intel Foundry lost US$10,318m on US$17,826m of segment revenue in FY2025, a −57.9% operating margin, with external revenue of US$307m that went US$547m, US$159m, US$307m across three years. Its PP&E additions declined 43.1% over two years to US$14,646m with only US$9,100m committed for 2026, and it has stated it may pause 14A without a significant external customer. Samsung's combined foundry and System LSI operation is estimated to have lost KRW 6tn in 2025 [web] and its foundry revenue declined 5.8% sequentially in Q1 2026 while TSMC's rose 6.3%. Rapidus has 60-plus companies in talks and zero volume agreements. Meanwhile TSMC's 2026 spend on advanced process alone, US$42-51bn, is roughly three times Intel's entire-company PP&E additions in FY2025.

6. Customers stopped paying cash to reserve capacity in the year capacity became scarcest. Temporary receipts from customers, which the 20-F defines as "payments made by customers to the Company to retain the Company's capacity," went from NT$291,102m at end-2024 to NT$189,858m at end-2025, −34.8%, and from 10.1% to 5.0% of revenue, while revenue grew 31.6%. In the same filing TSMC added "If the market demand does not materialize" to the capacity risk factor for the first time. The benign explanation is that reserved capacity was delivered and deposits were offset against a much larger receivable base; the filing gives no roll-forward, so it cannot be separated from the adverse one. The cash-in-hand form of customer commitment is nonetheless at its lowest share of revenue in five years at the point of the largest capital commitment in the company's history.

7. Geographic diversification has not yet reached the asset base; Taiwan concentration rose. Taiwan's share of non-current assets rose from 77.2% at end-2024 to 80.0% at end-2025, and United States non-current assets declined in absolute NT$ terms from NT$541,836m to NT$540,057m. Eighteen of twenty-three fabs are in Taiwan as of 2026-02-28, and management stated on the Q2 2026 call that it is "building 13 leading edge and advanced packaging fab in Taiwan over the next several years." The additional US$100bn Arizona commitment was announced with no schedule: "if you ask me to give you a firm schedule or no, we don't have it today, but we do have a plan." The de-risking is real and it is years out; the announcement and the asset base are not the same thing. Meanwhile the overseas capacity that does arrive comes with 2-4 points of guided gross-margin dilution, roughly US$3,400-6,800m of annual gross profit at 2026 revenue scale.

8. The capital-allocation menu has one growth channel and one return channel, and the cash keeps compounding. Over ten years TSMC deployed 63 cents of every operating-cash dollar into its own plant, 24 cents into dividends, nothing into acquisitions and 0.03% into buybacks, retaining the rest. Cash and marketable securities went from NT$583bn at end-2019 to NT$3,069bn at end-2025 to NT$3.5 trillion at 30 June 2026, while the paid dividend payout ratio compressed from 73.2% (2019) to 27.5% (2025). Management has refused a general buyback on the record three times across seven years. Capital expenditure has absorbed between 48.6% and 76.5% of operating cash flow in twelve years, never all of it, so the stated reason that cash is better kept for capital spending is not what the cash flow statement shows. Half the reported group return is diluted by that pool: ROIC including cash and financial assets is 24.9% against 48.7% excluding them.

9. Value capture per accelerator points in two directions at once. On a roughly US$6,400 B200 manufacturing cost, memory suppliers capture about 45% and TSMC about 31%, and against roughly US$30,000-40,000 of street price TSMC's packaging capture is about 3-4% of what the accelerator sells for. Owning the bottleneck has not translated into owning the profit, and TSMC's own chief executive says so about memory. Yet packaging is roughly 55% of what TSMC collects per accelerator against about 8% of consolidated revenue, so on the products driving growth the backend is several times larger a share of TSMC's take than the corporate mix suggests. That is the mechanical case for the backend share rising as HPC mix rises, and Q2 2026's record 16.0% backend share is the first quarter it is visible.

10. Two forward numbers went qualitative on the same call, at the point of maximum uncertainty. On the Q2 2026 call management declined to update the five-year AI accelerator compound rate ("not a number, but is stronger and stronger and stronger"), declined to quantify multi-year revenue growth ("Next few years is going to be a very good business for TSMC. That's all I can say"), did not restate the through-cycle gross-margin and return-on-equity targets, gave no revised node capacity figure ("Now it's bigger. That's all I say"), and declined for the second time to break advanced-packaging capital spending out of the 10-20% bucket. Each refusal was framed as upside, and every one of them removes a number an external model would otherwise anchor on.

8. Management claim pressure tests

1. "TSMC is exercising monopoly pricing." Consensus framing through 2026 treats four straight years of price increases as the bull case. TSMC prices deliberately below the clearing level and says so: reported 2nm pricing landed at roughly US$30,000 per wafer, +10-20% over 3nm, against a rumoured +50% [web], and C.C. Wei's stated rule is "we don't [just] increase our price by which I like to have with 4x, 5x if you cannot survive." Quantification: in the same calendar quarter TSMC earned 67.7% gross margin while Micron earned 84.6% and NVIDIA 74.9%. Closing half the gap to Micron would add roughly eight points of gross margin, about NT$102bn per quarter at Q2 2026 revenue, before any volume response. Two implications follow, both against the framing: the moat is stronger than the reported margin because the margin is capped by policy, not by competition, and the downside case in which TSMC "loses pricing power" is less dangerous than it appears because a large cushion sits between what TSMC charges and what the market would pay.▪

2. "Mature nodes earn around the corporate average gross margin." The claim was made by the CFO in Q3 2023 and by the CEO in Q4 2023, and has not been repeated for this franchise on any 2024, 2025 or 2026 call. Run the residual arithmetic on FY2023, when corporate gross margin was 54.4% and mature was 41.9% of wafer revenue: setting mature equal to the corporate average implies an advanced-node margin of 55.4-56.7%, entirely consistent. The claim was defensible in 2023. Run the same identity on Q2 2026 at a 67.7% consolidated margin and mature at the corporate average requires TSMC to earn 39 points more than UMC on the same 28nm node. The credible interior of the range is a mature gross margin of roughly 45-55%, 13-23 points below corporate [estimate: residual allocation of Q2 2026 consolidated gross profit across the three disclosed revenue lines, bounded below by peer gross margins and above by the ex-N2 margin implied by Q3 2026 guidance; cross-checked against the 2018-2019 mature-mix anchor, when a TSMC that was 61-71% mature earned 46.0-48.3%]. Applying the 2023 claim forward overstates this franchise's margin by roughly 15-20 points.▪

3. "CoWoS is TSMC's strategic lock on the AI accelerator socket." Asked on the Q2 2026 call whether losing packaging share to Intel's embedded-bridge technology would become an entry point into the front-end wafer business, C.C. Wei said the two are different businesses, that back-end capacity is sold in shortage mode, and that he welcomes a competitor taking packaging load so TSMC's wafers still get packaged and sold. Quantification: advanced packaging is 8-10% of revenue at a gross margin management concedes is below the corporate average, against a leading-edge wafer business at an estimated 69-70% gross margin in Q2 2026. TSMC is roughly seven times more exposed in revenue, and more than that in gross profit, to the wafer than to the package. CoWoS pricing power as a margin driver would require a price increase TSMC has publicly declined to take.

4. "Advanced packaging is less capital-intensive, so it is margin-accretive as it scales." A Goldman Sachs analyst stated this as a premise on the Q2 2026 call and asked TSMC to break packaging capital spending out separately; C.C. Wei declined, saying the bundle is deliberately fungible: "sometimes we have a bottleneck. So we put more money to buy the bottleneck tools and sometimes in the front end, sometimes in the back." Quantification: backend capital spending at the 15% midpoint of the US$62bn 2026 budget is US$9.3bn against roughly US$25.5bn of estimated 2026 backend revenue, 36.5% of revenue, identical to the corporate 36.5%. Only at the 10% floor of the disclosed range (24%) is the premise true; at the 20% top (49%) the backend is more capital-intensive than the company. For comparison, Amkor's FY2025 capital spending was 13.5% of net sales, so the OSAT model really is asset-light and TSMC's backend does not follow that model.

5. "Lower margin but lower capital intensity, so similar returns." The CFO made this defence of the backend precisely once, in October 2020, and repeated it on the Q2 2021 call; it has not been made since, despite analysts raising backend profitability in Q2 2023, Q2 2024, Q3 2024, Q4 2024 and Q4 2025. Quantification: on FY2025 disclosure, advanced packaging at 8-10% of revenue and 8-14% of a NT$1,272,411m capital budget implies capital intensity of 26.7-58.5% against a corporate 33.4% — a band that straddles parity. If margin is below average and capital intensity is at or above average, backend returns are below corporate returns and the franchise is return-dilutive, not return-neutral. The disclosure does not settle it.

6. "The AI packaging boom is lifting the whole packaging layer." Amkor's gross margin went 14.5% (2023), 14.8% (2024), 14.0% (2025), 14.2% (Q1 2026) — flat across the entire boom — while its capital intensity rose from 11.8% to 13.5% of sales. ASE's packaging segment gross margin of 22.1% in FY2025 is 5.0 points below the 27.1% it earned in the pre-AI 2022 cycle peak, and ASE's total revenue in FY2025 was still 3.8% below its 2022 level after three years. The economics of AI packaging accrue to the party holding the scarce capability, not to the packaging step.

7. "The 'Others' line is a CoWoS proxy." Others was 14.1% of FY2025 revenue, NT$536,501m, while management put advanced packaging at about 8%, NT$304,724m. Using the audited line as a CoWoS and SoIC proxy overstates advanced packaging by 40-75%. The residual — mask making, test, design services and royalties — is NT$231,800m, US$7,500m, 6.1% of revenue, up from 4.7% in 2018, and it grew faster than advanced packaging in FY2025. Note that management has itself given two different FY2025 figures: "over 10%" guided in January 2025 and "close to 10%. It's about 8%" reported in January 2026. Either advanced packaging missed its own guided share, or the second statement repeats a stale figure. Both cannot hold, so the FY2025 figure is a range of 8-10%.

8. "TSMC's capital intensity is coming down." Management stated a mid-30s% capital intensity target in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, and the CFO said on the Q1 2026 call that "revenue growth outpaced the CapEx growth... we do not expect in the next several years, a sudden surge in capital intensity." One quarter later the 2026 budget went to US$60-64bn against US$40.9bn spent in 2025, +47% to +57%, while full-year revenue growth was guided to slightly above 40% in US dollars. Capital-expenditure growth outpaces revenue growth in 2026 and US$ capital intensity rises from 33.4% to roughly 35-37%. The reported ratio has improved over the decade — 52.9% in 2021 to 33.4% in 2025 — because revenue per wafer rose faster than cost per wafer; capital intensity per unit of capacity has risen, on management's own statement. Both are true, and the two framings are used selectively.

9. "The margin beats are engineered by a conservative currency assumption." Over the last ten guided quarters TSMC's guidance exchange-rate assumption averaged within 0.2% of the revenue-implied realized rate and explains about +6 basis points of the +157 basis point average gross-margin beat [estimate: implied average rate = reported NT$ revenue ÷ reported US$ revenue; effect = deviation × the disclosed 40bp-per-1% sensitivity]. Roughly 150 basis points per quarter came from utilization and cost improvement, which matches management's own attributions in the releases. The clearest case is Q2 2025, when the NT dollar came in 4.5% stronger than the 32.5 assumption, an estimated 178 basis point headwind, and TSMC still printed 58.6% inside a 57-59% guide.

10. "TSMC guidance is conservative" conflates two different records. The quarterly guide is reliable: revenue has not printed below the low end of its guided range since Q1 2019, twenty-nine consecutive quarters, and every quarter that finished outside its original range did so after a disclosed physical event (the 2016 earthquake, the 2018 computer-virus outbreak, the 2019 photoresist defect), with TSMC pre-announcing a revised guide in three of the four cases. The annual guide is a starting position: in the six up-years the January guide understated realized growth by roughly 5-11 percentage points and in the two down-years overstated it by 5-10, and the number was revised in-year in every one of those years. The 2026 revision is the largest in the sample, from close to 30% in January to slightly above 40% in July.

11. "The systematic beat is a property of the company." In the fourteen guided quarters from Q3 2014 to Q4 2017, gross margin exceeded the high end of the range once and operating margin twice; results clustered inside the range. The 79% / 79% / 82% beat rates on revenue, gross margin and operating margin come almost entirely from 2020 onward. A forward model that assumes TSMC keeps beating its own guide by 150-250 basis points is assuming utilization stays where it is, not assuming anything about how the company forecasts.

12. "The through-cycle gross-margin target is a forward anchor." "56% and higher through the cycle" was set on 15 January 2026 alongside a printed 62.3% and was 1,050 basis points below the run rate within two quarters.▪ It was raised once in four years (53% to 56%) while realized margin moved from 54.4% (FY2023) toward a 66-67% FY2026 trajectory. Every published long-term target has been raised after the realized number passed it, in every instance: revenue compound rate 5-10% (2018) to 10-15% (2021) to about 20% (Jan 2025) to about 25% (Jan 2026); gross margin 50% to 53% to 56%; return on equity above 25% to high-20s. Target-setting here is a lagging indicator of the company's own results, and the targets are a floor management is willing to be held to, not a central case.▪

13. "The de-rating in July 2026 was an earnings event." Between 2026-06-30 and 2026-07-28 the ADR declined 17.9% while consensus twelve-month-forward EPS per ADS rose 9.7%, FY2027 consensus EPS rose 8.6% and FY2028 rose 10.7%. The forward multiple went from 27.0x to 20.3x, a 25.1% compression. One hundred percent of the price decline, and then some, is the multiple. This is the same configuration as the 2022 drawdown, when the price declined 57.1% while forward estimates rose 18.4% and the multiple compressed 63.8%.

14. "TSMC always beats consensus." Across 2014-2026, TSMC beat the pre-print consensus EPS in 45 of 50 announcements, with five misses (Q1 2016, Q1 and Q3 2017, Q1 2019 and Q2 2021 at −1.0%). The current unbroken run is twenty announcements. The magnitude stepped up with the cycle, not with any change in disclosure: mean surprise averaged +1.7% across 2016-2019 and +5.5% across 2022-2025, reaching +9.4% across the two 2026 quarters reported so far. And the configuration has just changed: for Q3 2026 consensus revenue of US$44.87bn is at the 22nd percentile of the guided US$44.6-45.8bn range, below the midpoint, and for the full year the quarterly-consensus sum implies +38.9% against management's "slightly above 40%." Consensus is below the company on the year for the first time in the recent sequence.

15. "Customer concentration is a growing risk." The largest customer's share declined three years running, 25% (2023), 22% (2024), 19% (2025), and the top two combined were 36% in both 2023 and 2025. What rose is the top ten, from 70% to 78%. What changed underneath is correlation: HPC moved from 58% of FY2025 revenue to 66% in Q2 2026 while smartphone declined from 29% to 22%. TSMC's customer base used to span two cycles that moved at different times; it now spans one. What matters for the next annual filing is whether Customers A through J are all exposed to the same six capital budgets.

16. "FY2025 shows a shrinking mature franchise." The reconstructed quarterly series, calibrated to within 1.0% against the disclosed annual figure, puts first-half 2026 mature revenue at about NT$493bn against NT$403bn a year earlier, +22.3%, which annualizes to roughly NT$986bn against FY2025's NT$839bn. The share is falling because the denominator is exploding, not because the numerator is. Two cautions apply. The 23-26% mature residual includes 16nm, at 7% of wafer revenue the single largest node in the bucket, which behaves more like a trailing leading-edge node than a specialty one, and the quarterly disclosure cannot separate a 16nm-led recovery from a 28nm-and-above-led one. And the inference that the growth is predominantly price depends on TSMC winding down a 6-inch and an 8-inch fab and converting 40-90nm tools while simultaneously adding 12-inch specialty capacity at JASM and ESMC, so the volume base is being reshaped, not simply reduced.

17. "TSMC's capital allocation is exemplary." The framing is right about what TSMC did and silent about what it sold. TSMC held 5% of ASML, bought in October 2012 at €39.91 per share, hedged the entire position over 2013-14 at an average €62.59 and disposed of all of it by 8 October 2015 for NT$56,176m and a NT$22,070m book gain, 1.57x in euros over three years. Those same 21.0 million shares at ASML's 28 July 2026 close of €1,388.40 would be worth about €29.2bn. The forgone value of roughly €27.8bn is about 27% of FY2025 revenue and about 80% of FY2025 capital expenditure [estimate: shares × current price less hedged exit proceeds; excludes eleven years of dividends and any tax]. Nothing TSMC ever bought approaches that magnitude. The 2012 purchase was strategic, not financial and the objective was met — EUV entered TSMC production with N7+ in 2019 — and the hedge was placed before EUV's commercial success was established. TSMC monetized its single best non-operating asset three years in.

9. History and inflection points

Date Event Why it mattered
Feb 1987 Incorporated in the R.O.C. as a joint venture between the government and private investors; pioneered the pure-play foundry model The R.O.C. government still holds 6.38% through the National Development Fund and a board seat
Sep 1994 / Oct 1997 Listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange, then on the NYSE as ADSs, five common shares per ADS Two lines, two currencies, and a premium between them that has ranged from −5.1% to +33.4%
Nov 2013 Mark Liu and C.C. Wei appointed co-CEOs; Morris Chang remains Chairman The start of the current management cohort
2015 A flagship application-processor socket is dual-sourced to a rival 14nm process The only competitive loss of scale in the record. Morris Chang, Jan 2016: "16-nanometer turned out to be a discontinuity... And we hated that. And so 1.5 years ago, I vowed that we'll recover it, and we have recovered it"
Aug 2015 Solar manufacturing ceased; TSMC Solid State Lighting sold to Epistar in Feb 2015 The two diversification attempts in the record, both exited within about eighteen months at a disclosed 2014-2016 cost of roughly NT$6.8-7.9bn
Oct 2015 The entire 5% ASML stake disposed of at a NT$22,070m book gain The largest identifiable value-destroying capital decision in the disclosed record, and it concerns what TSMC sold
Jun 2018 Morris Chang retires; Mark Liu Chairman, C.C. Wei sole CEO Split leadership structure begins
Aug 2018 Computer-virus outbreak halts fab tools; cause "misoperation and insufficient firewall controls" About 2% of Q3 revenue and 1 point of gross margin, with ~75% of affected shipments recovered inside the quarter
Jul 2019 2019 capex guidance abandoned mid-year; FY2019 capex +45.9% on 3.7% revenue growth The capital-intensity break (Inflection 1)
May 2020 Arizona fab announced; TSMC stops taking new orders from a customer that was 14% of FY2019 revenue after US export rules Inflection 2
Apr 2021 US$100bn capex over three years, the first multi-year commitment; first explicit pricing statement Inflection 3
Oct 2022 US "October Rules" export controls on advanced computing ICs to China China revenue by customer headquarters declined from 12.4% (2023) to 8.6% (2025)
FY2023 Revenue −4.5% NT$, gross margin −5.2 points, operating margin −6.9 points, EPS −17.5% Inflection 4, the only annual decline in the window
Jun 2024 C.C. Wei becomes Chairman and CEO; the roles are combined Governance change discussed below
Jan-Jul 2026 Every long-term target raised; 2026 capex US$52-56bn → US$60-64bn; Arizona +US$100bn to US$265bn; FY2026 growth guide close to 30% → slightly above 40% Inflection 5
Dec 2025 - Mar 2026 Section 232 concludes with a 25% tariff on certain advanced computing chips; Nanjing VEU replaced by an annual licence; US-Taiwan agreement caps reciprocal tariffs at 15%; the Supreme Court strikes down the IEEPA tariffs and they are replaced under Section 122; USTR opens two Section 301 investigations naming Taiwan The trade paragraph of the 20-F was rewritten from scratch, with every element dated inside fifteen months

The five inflections

  • Inflection 1 (2018-2019): the capital-intensity break, made at the margin trough. In October 2018 the stated model was US$10-12bn of annual capital spending supporting a 5-10% US$ revenue compound rate, and capex had run almost flat in absolute terms for five years while declining from 37.8% to 30.6% of revenue. Revenue compounded at 7.0% over 2014-2019 and operating income at 4.7%; gross margin declined for two consecutive years to 46.0%, and Q1 2019 was guided at 43-45%. In July 2019 management abandoned its own capital guidance mid-year, and FY2019 capex landed at NT$460,422m, +45.9%, on revenue growth of 3.7%. Free cash flow declined 40% to the lowest of the decade while the dividend was raised from NT$8 to NT$10. What followed: revenue compounding at 23.6% over 2019-2025 against 7.0% before, operating income at 31.6% against 4.7%, gross margin 46.0% to 59.9%. The decision was taken on a customer-roadmap signal, not an observed order book, and the same behaviour repeats in April and July 2026.
  • Inflection 2 (2020): a 14%-of-revenue customer removed by regulation, absorbed in two quarters. US export rules stopped new orders from 15 May 2020 and shipments ceased in mid-September. FY2020 revenue nonetheless grew 25.2% in NT$, attributed by the 20-F to "an 8.2% increase in ASP due to higher advanced technology revenue weighting and a 23.1% increase in wafer shipments." The capacity vacated was refilled at a higher price inside two quarters. This is the historical test of the near-sole-supplier position, and the caveat is that 2020 was a supply-short year with a 5G handset cycle and a first-year N5 ramp waiting for capacity. A concentration shock into a slack market has not been observed.
  • Inflection 3 (2021-2022): technology leadership converted into realized price. In April 2021, in the same prepared remarks as the US$100bn commitment, management said "We are looking to firm up our wafer pricing to a reasonable level," justified by cost structure, not scarcity and framed against thirty years of "stable and predictable pricing." Gross margin went 51.6% (2021) to 59.6% (2022) and the long-term target was raised from 50%+ to 53%+. The correction to the standard account is in Section 7: a large share of the margin gain is revenue outgrowing a fixed depreciation base.
  • Inflection 4 (2023): the one down year, and what got protected. Revenue −4.5% in NT$ and −8.7% in US$, gross margin −5.2 points, operating margin −6.9 points, EPS −17.5%, return on equity 26.9%. Operating cash flow declined 22.9%, five times the rate of the revenue decline. Free cash flow collapsed to NT$292,150m against dividends paid of NT$291,722m, 99.9% of it. The response ranks what management protects: R&D was expanded on a falling revenue base, the dividend was raised, capital spending was cut 12.3%, and operating margin declined more than gross margin because operating expenses were not cut. The order is roadmap first, dividend second, capex third, margin last.
  • Inflection 5 (2024-2026): the AI regime, and targets that trail the results. HPC as a share of revenue went 43% (2023) to 51% (2024) to 58% (2025) to 66% (Q2 2026); smartphone 38% to 22%. Every published long-term number has been raised, most twice, and each raise followed. The January 2026 gross-margin target of 56%+ was 11.7 points below the Q2 2026 realized 67.7%, and the CFO declined to revise it when asked in April 2026.

How this company behaves

  1. It spends into a demand signal the income statement has not yet shown, and breaks its own guidance to do it. 2019, April 2021, and April and July 2026.
  2. In a downturn it protects the roadmap and lets margin take the hit. 2023 and, in milder form, 2019.
  3. It answers a competitive loss by accelerating the node and adding an adjacent capability, not by cutting price. The 2015 socket loss was answered with 16FF+ and with InFO, announced for volume production alongside it and shipping more than US$100m in Q4 2016 at "moderate gross margin." That packaging capability is the direct ancestor of the franchise that is 14.1% of FY2025 revenue and the current binding constraint.
  4. It raises price only to fund capacity, and says so in the same breath.
  5. It absorbs external shocks inside a quarter and quantifies them on the next call. The 2018 virus, the February 2016 and April 2024 and January 2025 earthquakes (NT$3.0bn and NT$5.3bn net of insurance).
  6. Its published long-term targets trail its results.
  7. It returns cash through the dividend and only the dividend. Weighted average shares went from 25,927.8m (2013) to 25,928.3m (2025).

What the current account omits

The 70%-of-free-cash-flow dividend policy was never a filed policy. It appears in exactly six earnings calls — Q1, Q2 and Q3 2019, Q4 2020, Q1 2023 and Q1 2024 — and in none of the ten archived annual filings, whose dividend section describes only the Articles of Incorporation mechanics and the board's quarterly authority. The last statement was April 2024. The current formulation is "a sustainable and steadily increasing cash dividend per share." Realized payout was 99.9% of free cash flow in 2023, 41.7% in 2024 and 46.6% in 2025. The language moved toward the behaviour without the change being flagged, and because it was never in a filing there was nothing to withdraw.

The 2015 competitive loss is not part of the story management tells today. It appears in the archived record only in Morris Chang's answer on the January 2016 call. The current framing — "technology, manufacturing and customer trust... this fundamental never changed" — has no room for a period in which a flagship socket was dual-sourced away and took eighteen months to recover. That episode is the historical test of whether customers can leave and how fast they return.

Management welcomed a competitor into its constrained franchise. On the Q2 2026 call, on packaging: "the technology looks good according to the newspaper. And we hope they will be successful." A company describing an unassailable position does not say that about a rival's product.

A downturn the record has not seen

In 2023 a 4.5% NT$ revenue decline produced a 22.9% decline in operating cash flow, because gross margin declined 5.2 points at the same time. Applying that same sensitivity to the 2025 base of NT$2,274,976m gives operating cash flow of roughly NT$1,754,000m. The 2026 capital budget at the US$62bn midpoint, translated at the company's own NT$32 assumption, is roughly NT$1,984,000m. Free cash flow would be about −NT$230,000m before a dividend of roughly NT$622,000m, a combined shortfall on the order of NT$850,000m [estimate: the 2023 operating-cash-flow sensitivity applied to the 2025 base; capex at the guided midpoint and the company's own currency assumption; dividend at the stated 2026 per-share rate]. That is fundable against NT$3.5 trillion of cash and marketable securities, but it is the first time in the window that the arithmetic gets there at all. In 2023 the same shock left free cash flow exactly equal to the dividend. The behaviour the record predicts — cut capex about 12%, raise the dividend, protect R&D, let margin absorb it — does not close a gap of that size.

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

What a foreign private issuer discloses

TSMC is a foreign private issuer. There is no DEF 14A, no compensation discussion and analysis, no say-on-pay vote, no pay-versus-performance table and no chief-executive pay ratio. Everything a proxy would carry comes from 20-F Item 6, IFRS Note 38h and the Taiwan annual meeting agenda. Individual compensation is disclosed for exactly two people, the chief executive and the chief financial officer; every other executive officer is inside a single aggregate row. The 20-F figures are an accrual basis (cash plus stock awards plus long-term incentive credited to a trust), while US summary compensation tables use grant-date fair value for equity, so the peer comparison below is directionally usable.

Who runs the company

C.C. Wei, aged 71-75, is Chairman and Chief Executive Officer with 28 years at TSMC. He joined in 1998 from Chartered Semiconductor and STMicroelectronics, held operations, mainstream-technology and business-development roles through 2012, was co-chief operating officer from 2012, President and co-CEO alongside Mark Liu from 2013, sole CEO from 2018, and took the chairmanship on Mark Liu's retirement in June 2024. He is an internal promote with a 26-year climb. Revenue went from NT$851bn in 2013 to NT$3,809bn in 2025.

The operating structure below him is deliberately plural, not a designated successor: two co-chief operating officers (Y.P. Chyn, 39 years; Y.J. Mii, 32 years), two deputies (Cliff Hou, 29 years; Kevin Zhang, 10 years, formerly Intel), a chief financial officer of 27 years' tenure, and a general counsel of 31 years. Of 28 executive officers listed, six joined from outside within the last decade.

2025 was the heaviest year of senior departures in the archived record. Five executive officers left within four months and a sixth in April 2026: J.K. Lin (retired April 2025), Rick Cassidy (role change July 2025), Douglas Yu (retired July 2025), Vanessa Lee (resigned July 2025), Wei-Jen Lo (retired July 2025) and Lora Ho (retired April 2026). Douglas Yu is the architect of TSMC's advanced-packaging platform, and he retired at the moment management was telling investors packaging capacity was the binding constraint on customer growth. Vanessa Lee is the only resignation in the list; she had been promoted to vice president in August 2024 and left roughly eleven months later. TSMC gives no reason for either. The bench was rebuilt in one action: eight promotions on 10 February 2026, four to senior vice president and four to vice president, with a mean tenure of roughly 24 years.

Board. Ten directors, seven independent, all terms expiring 2027. Six features matter, in descending order:

  • No executive sessions of non-management directors and no lead independent director. The 20-F states that "Taiwan law does not contain such a requirement" and does not allow separate board meetings of part but not all of the board. Combined with a Chairman who is also the CEO, the independent directors have no structural forum in which to meet without him.
  • The CEO sits on the committee that selects independent directors. The Nominating, Corporate Governance and Sustainability Committee is by charter "composed of the Chairman of the Board and three to six independent directors." NYSE rule 303A.04 requires this committee to be entirely independent; TSMC discloses the deviation.
  • The CEO-succession mandate was deleted from that committee's charter description. The FY2022 20-F described the committee as assisting the board "in selecting candidates for nomination to be elected as independent directors to the Board, developing a Chief Executive Officer succession plan, making recommendations to the Board for the next Chairman, and advising on corporate governance and sustainability matters." From FY2023 onward the succession-plan and next-Chairman language is gone. The deletion appears in the first annual filing after the decision to combine the two roles. TSMC gives no explanation.
  • Two of seven independent directors have Applied Materials ties. Michael Splinter, who chairs the Compensation and People Development Committee, was chief executive of Applied Materials from 2003 to 2012 and chairman to 2015; L. Rafael Reif is currently co-chair of Applied Materials' Growth Technical Advisory Board. Applied Materials is one of TSMC's largest equipment suppliers.
  • A sitting government minister sits on the board. The National Development Fund of the Executive Yuan holds 6.38% and has held a seat since founding; its representative since September 2025 is a Minister without Portfolio who also chairs the National Development Council.
  • F.C. Tseng is a related-party node. He received NT$12.1m of director fees in 2025 plus NT$18.6m from non-consolidated affiliates and NT$19.9m of advisory fees from TSMC, and is simultaneously Chairman of TSMC China, Chairman of Global Unichip and Vice Chairman of Vanguard.

Succession. Chairman succession was discussed at length on the record: Mark Liu announced his retirement in prepared remarks on the January 2024 call and the nomination committee recommended C.C. Wei as Chairman while continuing as CEO. What has not been discussed on any archived call is what happens after Wei. There is no named successor, no President, and the CEO-succession mandate was removed from the nominating committee's disclosed charter after FY2022. That combination is the largest governance exposure in this section.

How compensation is built

The spine is statutory, not designed. The Articles of Incorporation provide that "not more than 0.3 percent of our annual profits... may be distributed as compensation to our directors and at least one percent of our annual profits may be distributed as profit sharing bonuses to employees, including executive officers," with directors who also serve as executive officers not entitled to director compensation (20-F FY2025, Item 6). Note 29 states the accrual is based on a percentage of net income before income tax, profit sharing and director compensation, so the base is pre-tax income before those items, not net income. Neither statutory limit binds in practice: 2025 director remuneration was NT$157.4m, and employee bonuses were NT$206,146m, 12.2% of net income against a 1% floor.

The base metric is absolute annual profit. Not earnings per share, not return on invested capital, not return on equity, not total shareholder return, not free cash flow. Executive bonus comes from the same profit-sharing pool as every employee's.

Three further layers apply on top.

Employee restricted stock awards (2021-2024 vintages). Granted free of charge, vesting 50/25/25 over three anniversaries, subject to performance and explicitly to ESG conditions. For executive officers the vested count is set by TSMC's total shareholder return relative to the S&P 500 IT Index, with 2.5 percentage points of vesting per point of outperformance above 50%, capped at 100%, then modified up or down 10% for ESG achievement (Note 28a). The chief executive proposes the grant sizes, including his own, and the committee approves. The forfeiture rate is the most informative number here and it collapsed:

Vintage Issued Vested Reclaimed Reclaim rate
2021 Rules 1,387,000 — 766,216 55.2%
2022 Rules 2,110,000 996,560 1,113,440 52.8%
2023 Rules 2,960,000 2,102,106 155,394 5.2%
2024 Rules 2,353,000 1,102,000 132,000 5.6%

The 2021 and 2022 vintages, granted into the 2022-23 downturn, lost more than half of their shares to unmet conditions. The 2023 and 2024 vintages, vesting into the AI boom, have lost about one twentieth. TSMC discloses neither the specific conditions nor the assessment against them, so a real bar met and a loosened bar cannot be separated from the filings. Either way, forfeiting half of two consecutive executive equity vintages is an unusual outcome for a large-cap board.

The 2025 long-term incentive plan. Adopted effective 2025, participants are granted a target notional cash amount "tied to a comprehensive set of performance metrics. These metrics include annual individual performance, as well as company-level financial indicators, total shareholder return performance relative to a peer group and ESG achievements," with the final result credited to a trust for the purchase of common shares (20-F FY2025, Item 6). The metrics are named. What is not disclosed is the peer group's constituents, the weight on each metric, threshold, target and maximum, the vesting schedule of the trust shares, the actual achievement, or the payout as a percentage of target. Under foreign-private-issuer rules none of it has to be. The plan is inside "All Other Compensation" alongside pensions and company cars.

What is not there. No stock options outstanding and none held by any director or executive officer. No change-of-control or golden-parachute arrangements disclosed. "No benefits are payable to members of the Board upon termination." A clawback policy adopted in August 2023 with no recoveries required. Directors are paid entirely in cash with zero equity.

Chief-executive pay grew 3.4x over two years while net income grew 2.0x. In aggregate the numbers remain small — total board plus key-management pay is 0.54% of net income — but the ratio rose in both years. Note also that share-based payments to key management declined 10.5% in 2025 while short-term cash benefits rose 80.0%: the 2025 step was cash, even though the long-term incentive ultimately buys shares through a trust.

Against a peer set drawn from US summary compensation tables (basis warning above), the size of the one-year move stands out. In 2024 C.C. Wei's US$28.9m sat at the peer median, level with the chief executives of Applied Materials, Lam Research, Qualcomm and KLA. In 2025 his US$77.2m is above NVIDIA's Jensen Huang (US$49.9m) and Apple's Tim Cook (US$74.3m), below only Broadcom's Hock Tan (US$205.3m) and a new Intel chief executive's recruitment package (US$93.0m). One plan change moved TSMC's chief executive from median to top-decile in a single year.

Combining the chairman and chief-executive roles also moved money across a line. Mark Liu, as non-executive Chairman, was paid NT$630.4m in 2022 against C.C. Wei's NT$643.4m as chief executive, 98% of what the CEO was paid, out of the director-compensation bucket. Director remuneration collapsed from NT$507.1m (2024) to NT$157.4m (2025) while executive compensation rose from NT$5,298.0m to NT$9,060.0m. The mechanism is obvious once both tables are read together; TSMC never explains it.

Where the profit pool goes

For 2025: employees' business performance bonus NT$103,073m plus employees' cash profit-sharing bonus NT$103,073m, a total of NT$206,146m, 12.2% of net income against a statutory floor of 1%. Across 90,557 employees that averages NT$2.28m, roughly US$72,600, of bonus per employee [estimate: total pool ÷ year-end headcount; headcount grew 8.0% during the year so the true per-head average for a full-year employee is modestly higher]. The pool grew 46.6% in 2025, almost exactly matching net income's 46.4%, and management told the 2026 annual meeting to expect more than 30% growth again in 2026.

Two ratios follow from that pool. The executive bonus line of NT$4,880.7m is 2.4% of the pool while the roughly 30 executive officers are 0.033% of headcount, so an executive officer's profit-share per head is roughly 72x the average employee's [estimate]. And total board plus key-management pay is 4.5% of what the broad workforce receives in bonus alone. The sharing is broad-based. It is also a large, non-discretionary claim on profit that scales with earnings, and it enters operating leverage.

Insider ownership

As of 2026-03-18, the National Development Fund holds 6.38%, F.C. Tseng 0.11%, C.C. Wei 0.03% (7,452,349 common shares) and all directors and executive officers as a group 0.23%. The disclosure explicitly excludes shares held by related parties, shares in the employee stock purchase or long-term incentive trusts, and unvested restricted shares, so it understates true exposure. C.C. Wei's stake at the NT$2,425 share price cited at the June 2026 annual meeting is roughly NT$18.1bn, about US$577m, or about 7.5x his 2025 total compensation [estimate: 7,452,349 × NT$2,425 at ~31.4 NT$/US$].

The independent directors own almost nothing: three hold zero, three hold 2,000-7,565 ADSs, one holds 126,826 common shares. Combined they hold well under 0.001% of the company, are paid entirely in cash and receive no equity grants. The chair of the Audit and Risk Committee has served 24 years and holds zero shares.

The group's decline from 0.32% (Feb 2023) to 0.23% (Mar 2026) is almost entirely composition, not selling: Mark Liu's 12,967,192 shares left the table on his retirement and five executive officers exited it in 2025. The one real sale window is calendar 2021, when C.C. Wei sold 1,300,000 shares (18.1% of his holding) and F.C. Tseng 5,000,000 (14.5%), in a twelve-month window containing the then-record share price. Mark Liu did not sell. Wei's holding has since been rebuilt from 5.88m to 7.45m, and that recovery is restricted-share vesting, not disclosed open-market buying.

Candor

Where the record is strong. Self-inflicted failures are sized and disclosed: the Q1 2019 photoresist contamination was disclosed in a February 2019 press release ahead of the call and then quantified on it in two dimensions, about 2.6 points of gross margin and about 3.5% of quarterly revenue. Forecast errors are owned in the chief executive's own voice: the Q1 2023 call contains three explicit admissions of a wrong call in six sentences, with the prior forecast restated so the listener can score it. Structural guidance has been held stable, not reset when convenient: the overseas-fab dilution guidance has been repeated in materially identical wording from Q2 2024 through Q1 2026, and the 53%-and-higher gross-margin target was not lowered during the 2023 downturn when lowering it would have been easy. Non-answers are given as non-answers: asked at the 2026 annual meeting when capital spending would plateau, C.C. Wei answered "Honestly, I don't know" [web].

Where it is weaker. The headline growth metric was redefined at the same moment its growth rate was restated. In April 2024 the metric was "server AI processors narrowly defined as GPUs, AI accelerators and CPUs" at a low-teens percentage of revenue with a 50% five-year compound rate; in January 2025 it became "AI accelerators, which we now define as AI GPU, AI ASICs and HBM controller," at close to a mid-teens percentage with a mid-40s% rate. CPUs were dropped and HBM controllers added, the base moved, and the rate moved, all in one step with "we now define as" as the only signal. Neither definition corresponds to any line in the annual filing, whose disaggregation is by node, by product and by platform. That forward number is defined by management, revised by management, and auditable by nobody.

The company-wide long-term revenue target lapsed and was re-based, not scored. The 15-20% target for 2021-2026 was abandoned mid-window on the Q3 2024 call ("I don't have a long-term CAGR number to update") and replaced three months later with a new one on a new base year. On the underlying numbers the old target was beaten: 2021 revenue of US$56.8bn to 2025's US$122.42bn is a 21.2% US$ compound rate, above the top of the range. Nothing was being hidden, but re-basing a multi-year target onto a fresh start year each time it approaches its test date removes the ability to score it.

The annual meeting figures do not tie to the SEC figures and TSMC does not reconcile them. The 2026 annual meeting business report gives 2025 net income of NT$1,717.88bn and diluted EPS of NT$66.25; the 20-F gives NT$1,695,124.9m and NT$65.47. Revenue ties exactly. The gap runs about 1.2% and, checked across three years, runs in both directions.

Competitor commentary hardened in 2026. On Samsung's stated 2030 goal: "I'll say that is totally a pipe dream." On competition generally: "We have always won. The future will be no different" [web]. That is a change in register from the studied neutrality of earlier years, made at the top of a cycle by a chief executive whose new incentive plan pays on relative total shareholder return.

TSMC's investor relations director restates every analyst question in his own words before management answers it, which across the transcripts routinely narrows a two-part question to the part management wants. Hostile questions do get answered, but the restatement layer gives management a filter no US call has.

Alignment

The base metric is a size metric, and size metrics normally reward dilutive expansion. Here they largely do not, for three checkable reasons: the share count is frozen (25,930,380,458 in December 2021 to 25,932,524,521 in December 2025, a change of about 0.008%, with restricted-share grants diluting roughly 0.01% a year and no options), there is no material acquisition anywhere in the archived period, and there is no buyback to manufacture earnings per share with. With no dilution, no M&A and no buyback, absolute profit growth and per-share profit growth are the same number.

What the metrics do not reward is return on capital. Management commits publicly to a sustainable return on equity above 25%, restated as high-20s through the cycle in January 2026, and that commitment is not in the compensation disclosure. For a company spending US$60-64bn a year against roughly US$122bn of revenue, where a single wrong capacity decision destroys more value than a decade of executive pay, no return-on-capital gate is disclosed. The 2025 long-term incentive's "company-level financial indicators" may include one; TSMC does not say.

The direction of travel is mixed. The 2025 plan introduced relative total shareholder return, the first pay metric measured against anything outside TSMC's own income statement, and its payout buys shares through a trust. In the same year chief-executive pay rose 156% on a plan whose weights and thresholds are undisclosed, the CEO took the chairman's seat, the board lost its split-leadership structure, the CEO-succession language vanished from the nominating committee's charter description, and that committee now includes him. On the mechanical anti-shareholder devices that dominate US proxy criticism — options, repricing, megagrants, severance, change-of-control — TSMC has none of them.

Over ten years TSMC deployed 63 cents of every operating-cash dollar into its own plant, 24 cents into dividends, nothing into acquisitions, effectively nothing into buybacks, and retained about 13 cents. Dividends absorbed 65.7% of cumulative free cash flow. Cumulative capital spending was 1.73x cumulative depreciation, which on that proxy puts roughly 42% of the programme into new capacity and 58% into replacement, with 42% a floor because leading-edge tool cost per wafer rises with each node. The menu is one growth channel, one return channel, and no third option ever exercised.

Two behaviours point the same way. TSMC over-delivers in up-cycles and cuts in down-cycles. The 2022 and 2023 cuts, 14% and 10% below the initial midpoints, came in the two years when revenue growth decelerated and then declined. That is the flex a foundry needs. And the only multi-year commitment TSMC ever made — US$100bn for 2021-2023, confirmed by the CFO as "a CapEx number" — was delivered at 96.8%.

Buybacks. One programme in twelve years. The board resolved on 5 June 2024 to repurchase shares "in order to offset the dilution from the increase of outstanding shares due to Employee Restricted Stock Awards issuance"; 3,249,000 shares were bought between 14 and 28 June 2024 for NT$3,089m at an average NT$950.81, 0.01% of shares issued, and cancelled in August [web, TSMC 2025 annual meeting agenda]. The question has been asked and refused three times: Q2 2018 ("our shareholder prefers cash dividend than buyback"), Q3 2022 ("our cash on hand will be better kept to invest in our capital expenditure") and Q1 2025 ("Our conclusion stays the same"). The Q3 2022 refusal was made with the Taipei line trading between NT$371 and NT$683 for the year; the stock closed at NT$2,280 on 2026-07-28. The 2025 surplus alone (operating cash flow less capital spending less dividends, NT$535,786m) would have retired 1,037.8m shares at the 2022 average price of NT$516.2, 4.0% of the share count, against 234.9m shares or 0.9% at the 2026-07-28 close.

Dividends. The policy language is fixed and has not changed: "sustainable and steadily increased cash dividend per share on both an annual and quarterly basis." The Articles require distributions "preferably by way of cash dividend." The board, not the shareholder meeting, approves quarterly dividends.

TSMC declares a quarterly dividend roughly two quarters before it pays it, so the declared-basis and paid-basis per-share figures for a calendar year are never equal. Both are shown. The observable consequence is a payout ratio that keeps declining while the headline per-share dividend keeps rising: from 73.2% of net income in 2019 to 27.5% in 2025, tracking near 23% in 2026. The 33% dividend increase for 2026 is smaller than the earnings increase behind it.

The return on the programme has risen, not declined, as the programme has grown, which is unusual for a capital-intensive business scaling capital spending 4.4x in a decade. It makes no attribution between capital spending and the pricing and mix improvements that also lifted operating income.

Per-share outcomes. Because the denominator is fixed, absolute and per-share growth are the same number. Revenue compounded at 16.3% over 2015-2025 and 23.3% over 2020-2025; earnings per share at 18.8% and 27.1%; free cash flow per share went from NT$10.50 (2015) to NT$38.66 (2025). The one place per-share growth lags is the dividend, at 12.5% over 2020-2025 against 27.1% earnings growth, and that gap is where the retained cash comes from.

Funding sources outside the operating-cash-flow arithmetic. Government grants received in cash went from nil through 2019 to NT$47,545m (2023), NT$75,164m (2024) and NT$76,259m (2025), now roughly 6% of annual capital spending. Beyond cash received, TSMC Arizona "is also eligible to apply for a 25% investment grant for its qualified investments," and the November 2024 Direct Funding Agreement provides up to US$6.6bn of direct funding plus up to US$5bn of loans, with TSMC guaranteeing its subsidiary's obligations. The non-cash reconciliation also shows that reported cash capital spending is not the economic addition to property: FY2025 additions of NT$1,160,978m became NT$1,272,411m of cash paid, with a NT$93,113m movement in "changes in other receivables" in 2025 after NT$140,290m in 2024, a NT$233bn two-year receivable build consistent with the US investment-credit receivable. TSMC earned NT$1,612m of interest on "Government grants receivable" in 2025 against nil in 2023 and 2024, so that receivable is both large and newly interest-bearing.

Stated framework versus revealed behaviour. The gap is narrow, and it opens in two places. The capital-intensity claim — "we do not expect in the next several years, a sudden surge in capital intensity" (Q1 2026 call) — was reversed one quarter later. And the argument that cash is better kept to invest in capital expenditure has not stopped the cash pile from compounding faster than either capital spending or dividends: capital spending absorbed 55.9% of 2025 operating cash flow, not all of it, and cash and marketable securities rose from NT$1,560,413m at end-2022 to NT$3,068,595m at end-2025 and NT$3.5 trillion at 30 June 2026.

The record capital budget does not strain the funding capacity. First-half 2026 operating cash flow was roughly NT$1,529bn against NT$847bn of capital spending and NT$286bn of dividends. On a full-year operating cash flow of roughly NT$3.6-4.4 trillion, capital spending at the guided US$60-64bn absorbs 43-57%, against a twelve-year range of 48.6% to 76.5% and 55.9% in 2025. The largest budget ever guided consumes a lower share of operating cash flow than the average year of the last decade, because earnings are growing faster than the budget. The surplus after both capital spending and dividends widens from NT$535,786m in 2025 to roughly NT$0.95-1.90 trillion in 2026 [estimate: second-half revenue extended from the Q3 guidance midpoint with Q4 flat to +8% sequentially; second-half net margin 52-56%; operating-cash-flow conversion of 1.30-1.50x from the realized 2023-2025 range]. The constraint on TSMC's capital allocation is not the supply of cash.

Two things remain open. The first is accumulation: cash and marketable securities compound while the payout ratio compresses, with no target cash level ever articulated. And the concentration of the forward commitment: Arizona now totals US$265bn with overseas fabs guided to dilute gross margin 2-4 points, government grants offsetting roughly 6% of annual capital spending under milestone and clawback conditions that are never sized, and the customer prepayments that helped fund the 2021-2024 buildout now unwinding at roughly NT$100bn a year. None is a problem at a 67.7% gross margin. All of them make the return on the next NT$7 trillion harder to earn than the return on the last one.

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

TSMC is not a serial acquirer, and the serial-acquirer grading does not apply. Across fifteen years it completed exactly one business combination, a NT$3,930.8m step-up to control of an affiliate it already part-owned, and recorded NT$52.7m of goodwill on it. Total goodwill at 31 December 2025 was NT$5,891.1m, 0.155% of FY2025 net revenue, and almost all of it predates 2014, arising from the TSMC-Acer absorption in 2000 and the WaferTech joint venture founded in 1996 (stated in the FY2016 through FY2018 filings and dropped from FY2019 onward). There has never been a goodwill impairment. Identifiable cash spent on acquisitions, supplier stakes and acquired fab assets across the entire period is roughly NT$66bn: 0.9% of the NT$7,588,035m of capital expenditure over the same window and 2.3% of the NT$2,930,192m paid in dividends. The growth was built, not bought.

The record splits four ways. The two diversification attempts failed and were exited within about eighteen months of management concluding they could not reach profitability. The supplier co-investment produced a good nominal return and a very large opportunity cost. The legacy minority stakes are being monetized and are worth far more than book. And there is no impairment record to grade because there is almost no goodwill.

Intel ended FY2025 with US$23.9bn of goodwill, 45.2% of its revenue, took a US$2.8bn Mobileye goodwill impairment in Q3 2024 and US$3.1bn of goodwill and acquired-intangible impairments in 2025, and paid Tower Semiconductor a US$353m fee to walk away from a deal it could not clear. ASE ended FY2025 with NT$52,541.9m of goodwill and impaired NT$132.8m of it in the first half of 2025. TSMC's foundry rivals consolidated; TSMC did not, and gained share anyway.

The ASML exit

Inputs, all disclosed: 21.0 million shares (5% of ASML) bought on 31 October 2012 at €39.91 for €837.8m, with a separate €276.0m R&D funding obligation over 2013-2017; forward contracts over 2013-14 covering the full position at an average €62.59, locking a profit of €483.5m; lock-up expiring 1 May 2015 and all shares disposed by 8 October 2015 for NT$56,176m and a NT$22,070m book gain.

Scale: €27.8bn is roughly 27% of FY2025 net revenue and roughly 80% of FY2025 capital expenditure. A fair view of the decision: TSMC's stated purpose was strategic, the Customer Co-Investment Program was joined to accelerate next-generation lithography, and that objective was met, since EUV entered TSMC production with N7+ in 2019 and enables every node since. The hedge that capped the return was placed in 2013-14, before EUV's commercial success was established, and locking a €483.5m profit on an €838m position was defensible on the information then available. The 2023 IMS Nanofabrication purchase repeats the structure at US$430m and is marked slightly below its 2024 carrying value.

Deals considered and declined

The stance hardened over the decade. Q1 2019: "we don't have any plan of M&A right now." Q1 2020, Mark Liu: "We do have continued scouting about the possible fab, but those are mostly only mature fabs... overseas fab acquisition is unlikely to be a leading fab." Q3 2024, asked directly about acquiring Intel fab capacity, C.C. Wei: "are we interested to acquire one of IDM's fab? The answer is no. Okay. No, not at all." Q1 2025, in prepared remarks and unprompted: "TSMC is not engaged in any discussion with other companies regarding any joint venture technology licensing or technology transfer and sharing."

On a cash basis TSMC has been a net seller of equity interests: over 2022-2025 partners paid NT$47,785.4m into TSMC's own subsidiaries while TSMC spent about NT$30bn on stakes and assets.

12. Capitalization and balance sheet

TSMC's balance sheet is not a constraint on anything it is trying to do. At 31 December 2025 gross debt was NT$1,032,988m against cash of NT$2,767,856m, a net cash position of NT$1,734,868m; on management's broader "cash and marketable securities" measure the pool was NT$3.1 trillion at the end of 2025 and NT$3.5 trillion at 30 June 2026. Gross debt is 0.39x EBITDA and 16.1% of total capital. Ratings are AA− (S&P) and Aa3 (Moody's), unchanged since at least FY2022. There is no revolver, no commercial-paper programme, no meaningful covenant, no pension problem and no refinancing wall worth the name. The fixed obligations that matter here are industrial, not financial.

The stack is unusually granular: 96 outstanding tranches — 79 NT$ domestic, two US$ "Formosa" tranches issued in Taiwan and 15 US$ overseas — all fixed-rate, all unsecured, all bullet or two-equal-instalment.

Weighted-average cost of debt is computed principal-weighted at face across all 96 tranches, with US$ tranches translated at NT$31.37. Because the entire stack is fixed-rate, the coupon and the cash rate are the same. Cross-check: FY2025 gross corporate-bond interest of NT$19,148.2m over average bonds payable of NT$987,893m gives 1.94%, within 7 basis points of the computed 2.01%.

The 2020-2021 vintage was issued at 0.36%-1.375% and the 2022 vintage at 3.875%-4.625%; the US$ stack shows the rate regime change far more sharply than the NT$ stack. The US$8,000m of TSMC Arizona notes are guaranteed by TSMC and rank equally with its other senior unsecured obligations. Debt is 52.1% US$-denominated by face, deliberately: the 20-F states TSMC uses "foreign currency denominated debts and foreign currency deposits, to protect against currency exchange rate risks associated with non-NT dollar-denominated monetary assets and liabilities." The US$ debt reduces balance-sheet currency risk.

Maturity wall and refinancing cost. NT$120,620m matures in 2026, NT$173,946m in 2027 and NT$119,733m in 2028, so NT$414,298m over three years, 41.7% of face, at a weighted coupon of 1.42%. Refinanced at TSMC's own March 2026 NT$ print (1.72% and 1.78% on the 115-1 issue) and an assumed 4.40% for AA− US$ paper [estimate: the NT$ leg is TSMC's own recent issue; the US$ leg is an assumption, since TSMC has issued no US$ paper since July 2022], annual cash interest on that slice rises from NT$5,892m to NT$11,715m, an increase of NT$5,823m a year. That is 0.22% of FY2025 EBITDA and 0.30% of operating income. The refinancing wall is a rounding item.

Security, covenants, seniority. No security; pledged assets are NT$129.4m of certificates of deposit collateralising building leases. Covenants exist only on part of the long-term bank loans and are at a subsidiary: a subsidiary equity floor, a subsidiary debt-to-equity cap and a group debt-to-EBITDA cap, none of the three thresholds disclosed. Group debt/EBITDA is 0.39x so headroom is presumably large, but the absence of numbers means the subsidiary equity floor at JASM cannot be tested. Structural subordination is minimal in practice: the obligor group holds 95% of total assets.

Leases, pensions and other obligations

Right-of-use assets are NT$43,918.9m, of which NT$39,873.4m (91%) is science-park land in Taiwan leased from the state on terms of one to 36 years; lease liabilities are NT$35,428.0m, 0.7% of equity. Financially immaterial, structurally notable: TSMC does not own the ground under most of its Taiwanese fabs. Eight of the nine Hsinchu fabs sit on land whose leases come up for renewal between December 2026 and December 2044, and the Kaohsiung site where the 2nm Fab 22 operates is on agreements up for renewal by December 2026. TSMC discloses the dates and not the terms.

Pensions are a non-issue: the Taiwan plan is defined contribution with NT$6,707.5m of expense in FY2025, and the legacy defined-benefit plan is a net liability of NT$6,012.3m, 0.1% of equity.

The off-balance-sheet position is where the disclosure is thin. Note 36 discloses long-term purchase agreements for materials and supplies, manufacturing services, waste disposal, equipment and maintenance, and energy, stating that "the relative minimum fulfillment quantity and price are specified in the agreements" and quantifying none of them. MD&A meanwhile states that "There are no off-balance sheet arrangements that have or are reasonably likely to have a current or future effect on our financial condition." Those two statements sit awkwardly together. The long-term energy purchase agreements in particular are a multi-decade fixed obligation at a company whose annual filing devotes a risk factor to Taiwanese power availability and price.

Two contingent claims are on capacity, not cash. Under the 1987 technical cooperation agreement with the Industrial Technology Research Institute, "the R.O.C. Government or its designee approved by TSMC can use up to 35% of TSMC's capacity provided TSMC's outstanding commitments to its customers are not prejudiced," automatically renewing every five years and never invoked in 39 years. And under the SSMC shareholders agreement TSMC and NXP must in aggregate purchase at least 70% of SSMC's capacity. The first is a sovereign call option on roughly a third of the world's leading-edge foundry capacity.

Share count and dilution

Total share-based payment expense was NT$1,550.2m in FY2025 (equity-settled restricted shares NT$1,246.1m, cash-settled units NT$304.1m), 0.04% of revenue and 0.09% of net income. Restricted shares go to executive officers only, each vintage under 0.012% of shares outstanding. Weighted average diluted shares moved from 25,927.8m (2013) to 25,928.3m (2025), +0.002% in twelve years.

Cash, not stock, is how TSMC pays employees: accrued profit-sharing bonus to employees was NT$103,073.0m in FY2025 against NT$70,296.3m in FY2024, 2.7% of revenue and 5.0% of pre-tax income, running through the income statement without touching the share count. Comparing TSMC's margins to a US peer that runs 5-10% of revenue through share-based compensation requires adjusting for this; TSMC's reported operating margin already absorbs the full cash cost.

The capital structure moved through three regimes.

  • 2016-2019: shrinking debt, with gross debt down 28% while revenue rose 9%.
  • 2020-2022: deliberate pre-funding of the 5nm and 3nm build, with gross debt up 4.8x at coupons of 0.36%-1.375%, a decade of capital borrowed at the bottom of the rate cycle and locked out to 2060.
  • 2023-2025: debt unchanged, up 8% over three years, while EBITDA rose 81% and cash rose 89%.

TSMC levered up when money was free and stopped when it was not. Net cash has never gone negative in ten years, and the equity base compounded 4.0x since FY2016 on an almost unchanged share count, which is retained earnings, not issuance.

Interest and the capitalized-interest question

FY2023 FY2024 FY2025
Gross interest 18,329.1 19,805.7 19,986.3
Less capitalized into PP&E (6,329.7) (9,310.3) (7,615.9)
Reported finance costs 11,999.4 10,495.4 12,370.4
Interest income 60,293.9 87,213.4 105,739.1
Net interest income 48,294.5 76,718.0 93,368.7
EBITDA / gross interest 79x 100x 131x

Coverage is not a meaningful metric here: TSMC earns 5.3x more interest income than it pays in gross interest, and net interest income is 4.8% of operating income. Between 35% and 47% of the gross interest bill is capitalized into property each year, so the reported finance-cost line understates the economic interest bill by NT$7.6-9.3bn a year and moves that cost into depreciation with a multi-year lag. Reported finance costs understate the economic interest bill by roughly 60%.

Liquidity

Cash and financial assets were NT$3,202,932m at 31 December 2025, 40.4% of total assets, against total debt of NT$1,032,988m at 13.0%. The stated investment policy is principal preservation and liquidity support, investment-grade only, with per-issuer credit limits; the realized pre-tax yield on the pool was 3.30% in FY2025. Total undiscounted non-derivative financial liabilities due inside twelve months were NT$767,298.5m, which cash alone covers 3.6x. There is no revolver and no commercial-paper programme because liquidity is held on balance sheet.

The quarterly trend confirms and extends the annual picture: cash and marketable securities went NT$3.1 trillion (Q4 2025) to NT$3.4 trillion (Q1 2026) to NT$3.5 trillion (Q2 2026) while quarterly capital spending accelerated to NT$496.00bn, and long-term interest-bearing debt declined to NT$864.27bn with total liabilities at 30.9% of total assets, the lowest in the sampled period [deck: Q2 2026 earnings conference, slide 7]. Record capital spending is being funded without leverage.

Structural risks

1. Foreign-exchange translation of the earnings stream, and the disclosure that omits it. Substantially all revenue is US$-denominated and reporting is in NT$. TSMC's own long-standing rule of thumb, stated on the Q3 2015 and Q4 2015 calls and never withdrawn, is that a 1% currency move changes gross margin by about 0.4 percentage points, and rebuilding it from FY2025 figures reproduces 0.41 points of gross margin and a NT$38,091m gross-profit effect, or NT$32,034m after tax, 2.2% of net income for every 1% the US dollar weakens against the NT dollar. The FY2025 20-F's own risk-factor sensitivity is approximately 0.3 percentage points of operating margin per 1%. The financial-statement sensitivity note, by contrast, says a 10% adverse move would have decreased net income by NT$1,987m, NT$199m per 1%. That note is not wrong — it measures a monetary balance sheet TSMC has hedged almost perfectly, partly with the 52% US$ share of its bonds — but it measures the exposure TSMC has eliminated, not the one shareholders bear. The two figures differ by roughly two orders of magnitude and they are measuring different things. Nothing hedges the revenue translation, and management says so: "we have no control over the foreign exchange rate."

2. The equipment-order wall, not the debt wall. Capital purchase and other purchase obligations of NT$1,534,575m, with NT$1,220,393m due inside twelve months, are 54% of FY2025 operating cash flow and 4.9x the year's contractual debt service. Nothing in the disclosed agreements suggests they are non-cancellable take-or-pay, and TSMC cut capital spending in 2022 and 2023 without any disclosed penalty. The leading indicator is "payables to contractors and equipment suppliers," NT$177,730.3m at FY2025 and declining.

3. Undisclosed subsidiary covenant thresholds. Small in size (NT$40,954m of bank loans, mostly yen at JASM) but a subsidiary-level equity floor at a fab that has publicly struggled to fill capacity is the one covenant in the group that could plausibly be tested.

4. Government-grant clawback. NT$198,968m received over three years against undisclosed conditions and construction timelines, with clawback named as a risk factor and never sized. TSMC guarantees TSMC Arizona's obligations to the Department of Commerce.

5. Structural subordination and jurisdiction. Minimal in accounting terms, but every meaningful claim ultimately runs to assets in Taiwan. A geopolitical event does not breach a covenant; it removes the assets, and no disclosed instrument mitigates that.

6. The R.O.C. government's 35% capacity right. It has never been invoked in 39 years, and it is the largest undisclosed contingent claim on the productive assets.

7. Refinancing and floating-rate exposure. Effectively nil, as computed above. The larger interest-rate exposure runs the other way: a 100 basis point rate rise cuts other comprehensive income by NT$4,081m through the fixed-income portfolio, and a rate fall would cut the NT$105,739m of interest income that currently offsets 4.8% of operating income.

Peer contrast. Intel has US$46,585m of debt against US$37,416m of cash and short-term investments, was downgraded to BBB from BBB+ in August 2025 with the agency "citing execution risks tied to our technology roadmap and foundry strategy, delayed deleveraging and weaker than expected demand," and more than doubled non-controlling interests from US$5,762m to US$12,079m in FY2025 to fund its buildout (INTC 10-K FY2025). Debt to total capital: TSMC 16.1%, Intel 26.9%, UMC 12.8%. Whatever competitive contest is being run at 2nm, it is not being run with equal balance sheets.
