What the history shows

The FY2025 row is already stale by four to ten margin points. Trailing four quarters to Q2 2026 gross margin is 64.2% and operating margin 56.1% against FY2025's 59.9% and 50.8%; the June quarter alone printed 67.7% and 60.3%.▪ Revenue growth accelerated: +36.0% year over year in NT$ in Q2 2026 against +31.6% for the full year. The drivers management names are higher leading-edge utilization, cost improvement and a weaker NT dollar, and the mix moved hard behind them: advanced technologies 74% to 77% of wafer revenue, 3nm 23% to 30%, 2nm appearing at 3%, and HPC from 57.6% of FY2025 revenue to roughly 66%.

Growth is priced and mixed, not shipped. Blended ASP per 12-inch-equivalent wafer rose 149% in US dollars from 2018 to 2025 while shipments rose 39.7%, and 2025 shipments of 15.0 million remained below the 2022 peak of 15.3 million while wafer revenue was 64% higher.

Return on invested capital set a decade high of 51.0% in 2025, against a 2023 trough of 32.2% and a 2019 trough of 28.6%. Three-year rolling return on incremental invested capital of 55.2% over 2022-2025 exceeds the terminal-year figure, so the NT$7.0 trillion spent on capital over the decade earned more than the existing base.

The effective tax rate roughly doubled, from 8.7% in 2018 to 17.0-17.7% in 2024-2025. That is the single largest structural drag on net-margin expansion relative to operating-margin expansion, and it looks permanent, not cyclical. Non-operating income moved the other way, from NT$7,964m in 2016 (2.1% of operating income) to NT$105,563m in 2025 (5.5%), driven by interest income on the cash pile.

Working capital tightened sharply in 2025 and then reversed. Year-end days sales outstanding of 26.7 was the lowest in the series and inventory days of 68.8 the lowest since 2019, with inventory flat in absolute NT$ while cost of revenue rose 20.3%. On the disclosed quarterly series, inventory days then went 74 (Q4 2025) to 80 to 87 and receivable days 26 to 29, both attributed to the N2 ramp. The prior peak of 99 days in 2Q23 came with revenue declining 10.0% year over year and shipments 23.2% — a demand miss. This build comes with revenue up 12.0% sequentially, so the two episodes are not the same thing.

One quarter's earnings include a large item below the operating line. Q2 2026 pre-tax income grew 74.9% year over year against operating income up 65.4%, on NT$95,827m of non-operating income versus NT$29,613m a year earlier, a NT$66,214m swing, and NT$28,834m in Q1 2026. Roughly NT$67bn of the quarter's pre-tax income is below the operating line with unverified recurrence, about NT$2.6 per share pre-tax. The deck presents three facts in the same document and links none of them: the non-operating jump, a NT$61.4bn sequential increase in long-term investments, and a recent-events bullet dating the sale of 8.1% of Vanguard to 2026-05-15. Operating margin of 60.3% is the clean comparison for that quarter; net margin of 55.6% and return on equity of 45.9% are not.

Restatements and basis breaks that matter for any series built from these numbers. Packaging and testing revenue was reclassified from wafer to non-wafer revenue in 2017, so wafer-revenue percentages before and after are not comparable. IFRS 15 and IFRS 9 were both adopted in 2018, which is why the revenue-disaggregation note begins with FY2018 and why the current-financial-assets line used in net debt and invested capital is not comparable across the 2017/2018 boundary. Platform disclosure replaced application-type disclosure in 2019, so the HPC / Smartphone / IoT / Automotive / DCE series cannot be extended back. Billing utilization was disclosed for 2016-2020 (92%, 91%, 87%, 81%, 94%) and never again. Earthquake losses of NT$3.0bn (Q2 2024) and NT$5.3bn (Q1 2025) are inside cost of revenue. Government grants are recognised as reductions of PP&E cost, not income, so they never touch revenue, gross margin or operating income.

The discontinued metric is the consequential one. TSMC now discloses capacity and shipments on bases it explicitly says are measured differently and publishes no utilization percentage, while management names capacity utilization as the first of the six factors driving gross margin. Utilization, the largest single input to operating leverage, is therefore not disclosed.

The first of two inflections is the volume regime change in H1 2026 after three years in which price and mix did all the work. The second is the backend share reaching a record 16.0% in Q2 2026 after eight years in which advanced packaging moved corporate mix by one percentage point; that is the mix shift the market has been forecasting since 2023 arriving in 2026, not 2024.

14. Expectations: internal, external and base rates

Consensus is below the company on the current year and far above the historical distribution on the years after it. Management guides FY2026 US$ revenue growth to "slightly above 40%" while the sum of first-half actuals and quarterly consensus implies +38.9%; three years out, consensus asks TSMC to compound revenue at 32.0% a year from a US$122,556m base, and no company at or above US$100bn of revenue has achieved 30% for three years in the 403 observations available since 1990.▪

The guidance record

TSMC guides three numbers one quarter forward and has done so on every call in the sample: US$ revenue as a range, gross margin as a 200 basis point range, and operating margin as a 200 basis point range, the latter two against a stated exchange-rate assumption. It does not guide earnings per share.

Metric Beat the midpoint Met Missed Average deviation
Revenue (US$) 26 / 33 (79%) 4 3 +1.5%
Gross margin 26 / 33 (79%) 4 3 +113bp
Operating margin 27 / 33 (82%) 4 2 +160bp

Across Q2 2018 to Q2 2026. Revenue landed above the high end of the guided range in 15 of 33 quarters and has not printed below the low end since Q1 2019, twenty-nine consecutive quarters. Every quarter in the sample that finished outside its original range did so because of a discrete, disclosed, physical event, and in three of the four cases TSMC pre-announced a revised guide mid-quarter. There is no instance in twelve years of a quarter missing its range because demand simply came in below the company's own forecast.

The bias widened inside the AI cycle. Over the last ten quarters the average revenue beat against the midpoint was +2.5% against +1.5% across the full sample, the gross-margin beat +157 basis points against +113, and the operating-margin beat +246 against +160. Operating margin beats gross margin by roughly 90 basis points on average because a 2.5% revenue beat drops through a fixed operating-expense base.

Consensus has been revised in one direction for four consecutive quarters, and nothing in the series is a cut.

The 9.5-point upgrade to the FY2026 gross-margin forecast is a larger change than the 17.7% revenue upgrade and is what produced the 46.6% earnings upgrade. Part of it is currency: the exchange rate embedded in the street's own estimates moved from 29.71 to 32.40 over that window, a 9.0% NT dollar depreciation, which at the disclosed sensitivity is worth roughly 2.7 percentage points of margin [estimate: 9.0% × the disclosed 0.3pp operating-margin sensitivity, applied to a gross-margin series; the exposure is in NT$-denominated cost of revenue so it maps across, but it is not an exact transfer]. So roughly 2.7 points of the 9.5-point upgrade is the currency and roughly 6.8 points is price, mix, utilization and cost improvement.

The upgrade impulse is decelerating. Each of the last three prints produced a smaller upgrade than the one before: FY2027 EPS +21.8% after Q4 2025, +14.5% after Q1 2026, +8.6% after Q2 2026, with the gross-margin upgrade going +3.7 points, +2.3 points, +0.7 points. The revisions remain positive and large; the second derivative has turned. That matters because the margin line is now within 1.6 points of where the street models it for 2028, so there is little upgrade left in the margin lever unless price does more than the announced 5-10%.

2026 is closed: a 9.1% revenue spread and a 3.3% earnings standard deviation across 44 contributors, with two quarters reported and the third guided. The 2027 disagreement is about revenue, not margin — scaling the mean EPS by the high-revenue contributor's revenue explains roughly 87% of the top-end earnings gap — so the street has converged on about 66% gross margin and disagrees about how many wafers at what price. Capital spending is where there is no shared view at all: a 2.3x spread on FY2027 against 1.33x on revenue, with even the FY2026 low contributor at US$37.0bn against a company guide of US$60-64bn, which is far enough out to suggest a definitional difference, not a view.

What the street is not modelling

Five items go unaddressed in the covering reports.

  1. The fully-depreciated node band and its mechanical shrinkage. N5 and N7 were 44% of wafer revenue in Q2 2026 and both are past the five-year machinery life; reproducing a 67.7% consolidated gross margin requires that band to run at roughly 73-85%. It declined from 50% of wafer revenue in FY2025 to 44% in Q2 2026 and keeps declining as N2 and N3 take share. Both covering houses bridge gross margin with pricing, mix, loading, productivity and overseas dilution; neither lists the depreciation schedule.
  2. The mature and specialty franchise declining in absolute terms, 22% of revenue and NT$936bn (2022) to NT$839bn (2025), with no published note giving a separate forecast.
  3. The temporary-receipts decline, 34.8% in the year management described demand as most acutely exceeding supply, addressed in none of the eight most recent calls and in neither digest report.
  4. Upstream cost inflation as a claim on TSMC's volume. Hyperscaler budgets are set in dollars, so memory and substrate inflation displaces units. The covering models treat hyperscaler capex growth as a demand input and component inflation as someone else's margin problem.
  5. The street's own 2029. Consensus has FY2029 revenue growth decelerating to +8.4%, gross margin fading to 62.3% and earnings up only 5.7%. No published note discusses 2029; the notes stop at 2028. That tail depends on four to six contributors and its aggregates are not internally consistent, so it is weak evidence, but it is the only place the consensus model states where its visibility window ends.

Base rates, and where they bind

The reference classes were computed from Bloomberg panels: 43 semiconductor, semicap, OSAT and EDA names with annual fundamentals 1990-2026, and 68 large global companies over the same period. The mega-cap class is deliberately biased toward fast growth by including Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, NVIDIA, Tesla and Microsoft, which makes the resulting base rate conservative in TSMC's favour.

Threshold, from a ≥US$100bn revenue base Hits / 403 observations Share
≥15%/yr for 3 years 31 7.7%
≥20%/yr for 3 years 10 2.5%
≥25%/yr for 3 years 4 (all Amazon) 1.0%
≥30%/yr for 3 years 0 0.0%

Consensus asks TSMC for 32.0%/yr for three years from a US$122,556m base. Absolute dollars tell the same story: consensus implies +US$159,382m of revenue between FY2025 and FY2028, and in the whole panel only seven three-year windows added more — Amazon four times, NVIDIA once and Exxon twice on oil price.

Three things run the other way, and none is small. TSMC's own record after a boom year is a median forward three-year rate of about 15% with a best of 17.3%, which is far below consensus but also far above the cross-sectional median. NVIDIA has already produced a 99.6%/yr three-year revenue compound rate inside this same supply chain and inside the forecast window, which is a direct violation of the class. And TSMC has beaten every multi-year target it has set since 2018 while holding return on invested capital in an 18-29% band for twenty years through four capital programmes.

The buffer has narrowed. Management's multi-year targets were beaten by +5.2, +11.1, +6.9 and +4.2 percentage points across four completed cycles, and consensus now sits only +2.6 points above the current stated target. The conservatism that made prior consensus safe is largely gone.

Two other base rates constrain things other than growth. On returns, the consensus operating income of US$163,477m in FY2028 against a balance sheet rolled forward on its own capex and free-cash-flow assumptions implies operating income over total assets of 32.6% to 44.2% [estimate: consensus capex, EBITDA and free cash flow rolled onto the FY2025 balance sheet], against a TSMC all-time high of 24.7% and a 2015-2025 average of about 19.5%. And on the cycle, 19% of panel years since 1995 were down-years and a negative industry year arrived within three years of five of the seven boom years above 20%. The consensus path embeds no such year through 2029.

15. Market pricing and valuation history

This section is descriptive only. Historical multiples are stated as fact; forward multiples are the price divided by a consensus estimate on a stated date. There is no judgment about whether any multiple is deserved, no fair value, no price target and no buy or sell view. Where a cited source states such a judgment, it is reported as that source's view and not adopted.

TSMC's shares trade on two lines: Taiwan Stock Exchange ordinary shares (2330 TT, NT$, per common share) and NYSE ADSs (TSM US, US$, one ADS equals five common shares). All per-share figures in the annual filing are per common share. The two lines do not move together, and the ADR premium is a second, unhedged position (see below).

Diluted EPS here is the Taiwan IFRS series that ties to the Bloomberg fundamentals used for the price statistics; the 20-F basis is lower by roughly 1.2% (Section 13). EPS per ADS is US$ net income divided by weighted average common shares divided by five, a full-year translation [estimate] that is not identical to the sum of the four per-ADS figures the quarterly releases publish. Perfect-foresight forward P/E is the FY-end price divided by the next year's actual, which uses hindsight and was not computable at the time. Consensus forward P/E is the December month-end price divided by the contemporaneous rolling twelve-month-forward consensus per ADS, and the 2026 entry is at the 2026-07-28 price on the 2026-07-28 estimate set. Enterprise value is a point-in-time Bloomberg field recorded against each fiscal year, so the EV/EBITDA column is approximate. Price-to-book is the Taipei line, because the ADR line returns none from the terminal.

The record shows three things. Reported EPS per ADS compounded at 20.4% from 2016 to 2025 while the year-end price compounded at 30.0%; the 10.57x price gain can be decomposed into a 5.33x earnings gain and a 1.98x multiple expansion, which on a log basis is 71% earnings and 29% multiple. The trailing multiple on the year-end price has ranged from 11.3x (2022) to 32.1x (2020) and the contemporaneous forward multiple from 12.4x to 28.3x, with both extremes inside the last six years. And the 2019 row is where the two multiple columns disagree most, 27.0x trailing against 17.1x perfect-foresight forward, because FY2020 earnings grew 50%.

Ten drawdowns of 15% or more in twelve and a half years, one of them live at the run date. Two exceeded 35%. Completed episodes recovered from trough in 25 to 489 days.

The major moves, decomposed

Each episode decomposes into what happened to the twelve-month-forward consensus and what happened to the multiple applied to it.

Episode Price 12-month-forward consensus EPS Forward P/E
2018-01-22 → 2019-01-03 (25.9)% (3.9)% 19.0x → 14.6x, (22.9)%
2020-01-14 → 2020-03-19 (covid) (27.2)% +5.7% 22.0x → 15.1x, (31.1)%
2022-01-14 → 2022-11-03 (downcycle) (57.1)% +18.4% 28.3x → 10.3x, (63.8)%
2022-11-03 → 2024-07-10 (recovery) +216.9% +16.5% 10.3x → 27.9x, +172.1%
2024-07-10 → 2024-08-05 (22.6)% +7.9% 27.9x → 20.0x, (28.2)%
2025-01-23 → 2025-04-08 (tariffs) (37.1)% +5.9% 25.2x → 15.0x, (40.6)%
2025-04-08 → 2026-06-30 +237.8% +87.1% 15.0x → 27.0x, +80.6%
2026-06-30 → 2026-07-28 (17.9)% +9.7% 27.0x → 20.3x, (25.1)%

Seven of the eight episodes are multiple moves against flat or rising estimates. Only the 2018-19 episode had estimates declining at all, and by 3.9%.

The 2022 drawdown is the decade's largest. Twelve-month-forward consensus EPS rose 18.4% across the drawdown, from US$4.97 to US$5.88 per ADS, while the forward multiple went from 28.3x to 10.3x. Nothing in the earnings expectation deteriorated during the fall. The dated events in that window are the October 2022 US export controls on advanced computing ICs to China, the October 2022 capex cut for 2023 from US$40-44bn to about US$36bn, and the general repricing of long-duration assets through 2022. FY2022 then printed a record. The de-rating anticipated FY2023, which delivered revenue −4.5% in NT$, gross margin −5.2 points and EPS −17.5%. The market was early by roughly four quarters and right about the direction.

The 2025 tariff drawdown resolved fastest of the large episodes, 80 days from trough to full recovery, with forward estimates rising 5.9% through it. The dated events are the April 2025 US baseline and reciprocal tariffs and the opening of the Section 232 investigation. Consensus target prices were cut in exactly one month across the entire 37-month series, April 2025, and recovered within four months. The ADR premium hit its all-time high of +33.4% one day after the trough.

The live episode is entirely multiple. Consensus twelve-month-forward EPS per ADS rose 9.7% over the 28 days from 30 June to 28 July 2026, from US$17.66 to US$19.37, while the price declined 17.9% and the forward multiple went from 27.0x to 20.3x. FY2027 consensus EPS rose 8.6% and FY2028 rose 10.7% over the same window. The stated reasons in dated reporting are the capex raise to US$60-64bn plus an incremental US$100bn of Arizona commitment, a Q3 gross-margin guide of 65-67% taken as light against buy-side expectations, and a sector-wide repricing in which the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index declined more than 20% that week and Samsung and ASML also drew muted reactions to strong results (Yahoo Finance, published 2026-07-22, accessed 2026-07-28) [web]. The Taipei line declined 5.4% over the same 28 days, so most of the ADR move was the premium compressing from +26.2% to +11.5%.

The ADR premium is a second, unhedged position. Over 2,958 daily observations the premium to the Taipei line translated at spot ranged from −5.1% (2018-04-19) to +33.4% (2025-04-09) with a median of +4.9%. It was +20.5% at end-2024, +23.2% at end-2025, +26.2% on 2026-06-30 and +11.5% on 2026-07-28 [estimate: ADR price ÷ (Taipei price × 5 ÷ USDTWD spot), computed daily]. A US-dollar holder's July 2026 loss was therefore about two-thirds a premium move and one-third a move in TSMC's local share price.

TSMC reports at roughly 01:30 US Eastern time, before the US open, so the reaction is the same US session as the announcement.

Every one of the twelve quarters beat both the guided revenue midpoint and the consensus earnings number, and six produced a negative or flat same-session reaction. The correlation between surprise size and reaction is close to zero: the three largest surprises produced reactions of −2.3%, −1.6% and +3.7%.

Qtr Reaction What the market reacted to
4Q23 +9.8% on the day, +13.2% through five sessions Not the print. The earnings beat was mid-range for the sample. On the same call management guided FY2024 US$ revenue growth to "low to mid-20s" after a year of −8.7%, and paired it with FY2024 capital guidance of US$28-32bn and the statement that "the rate of increase of our capital spending has begun to level off as we capture and harvest the growth." A return to 20%-plus growth with capital spending flattening was the new information
3Q24 +9.8% on the day, +5.6% through five sessions The margin, plus the annual raise. Gross margin beat the guided midpoint by 333 basis points and, in the CFO's words, "exceeded the high end of the range," the largest margin beat in the sample. Management simultaneously raised the FY2024 growth forecast to "close to 30%" and guided Q4 gross margin to 57-59%, holding the new margin level into the next quarter's guide
1Q24 (4.9)% on a +7.9% earnings beat The industry forecast, not the print: "We lowered our forecast for the 2024 overall semiconductor market, excluding memory, to increase by approximately 10% year-over-year, while foundry industry growth is now forecast to be mid- to high-teens percent," down from the roughly 20% given in January. Management also flagged the 3 April earthquake's effect on Q2 gross margin
2Q26 (2.3)% on the day, (0.9)% through five sessions, (6.5)% cumulative to 2026-07-28 The largest consensus beat in the sample with a negative reaction, inside the live drawdown. Three things arrived with the print: the 2026 capital budget raised to US$60-64bn, a further US$100bn of Arizona commitment taking the US pledge to US$265bn, and a Q3 gross-margin guide of 65-67% against a Q2 actual of 67.7%, with 3-4 points of second-half dilution attributed to the N2 ramp. Consensus FY2027 and FY2028 EPS were revised up 8.6% and 10.7% in the twelve days after the print, so the price move was not an estimate move

Across 2014-2026, TSMC beat the pre-print consensus in 45 of 50 announcements, with five misses (Q1 2016, Q1 and Q3 2017, Q1 2019, and Q2 2021 at −1.0%). The current unbroken run is twenty announcements. Mean surprise averaged +1.7% across 2016-2019 and +5.5% across 2022-2025, reaching +9.4% across the two 2026 quarters, which mirrors the guidance record's finding that the beat is a property of the current utilization environment, not of how the company forecasts.

TSM US closed at US$392.31 on 2026-07-28 and 2330 TT at NT$2,280 the same day. Every multiple below is on those prices and on Bloomberg BEst consensus pulled the same day. These estimates have been moving 6-20% per quarter, so the as-of date matters.

On the Taipei line at NT$2,280 the same consensus gives 21.1x FY2026E, 16.2x FY2027E and 12.9x FY2028E; the two lines differ by the ADR premium. Blending FY2026E and FY2027E by the fraction of the fiscal year remaining gives consensus next-twelve-month EPS of US$19.37 per ADS and a forward P/E of 20.3x; Bloomberg's own next-twelve-month field returns 20.54x the same day, which corroborates the blend. Enterprise value to consensus EBITDA is 15.7x FY2026E, 11.6x FY2027E and 9.1x FY2028E on an enterprise value of US$1,956,408m.

Where the current multiple falls in the distribution. From 150 monthly observations of the rolling twelve-month-forward consensus P/E, January 2014 to June 2026:

The full-period median of 17.1x spans two regimes that barely overlap.

Price to book. TSMC is capital-intensive and has traded through deep cyclical troughs, so book value is a relevant second measure. From 150 month-end observations on the Taipei line: minimum 2.93x, 25th percentile 3.66x, median 4.44x, 75th percentile 6.39x, maximum 10.37x (May 2026). At the 2026-07-28 Taipei close against 30 June 2026 book value per share of NT$248.05, price to book is 9.19x [estimate: current price ÷ last reported book value per share]. The 2022 trough print was 2.93x and the 2019 pre-AI level about 5.3x.

What the street's targets say, reported and not adopted. Bloomberg on 2026-07-28 shows 39 recommendations on the Taipei line — 37 buy, 2 hold, 0 sell — with a mean target of NT$3,195.50, median NT$3,190 and a range of NT$2,700 to NT$3,800 against a NT$2,280 price. The ADR-line consensus is contaminated by an unconverted NT$ target pooled into it and is not used. Named ADR targets from dated reporting run US$440 (TD Cowen) to US$650 (Barclays) [web]. The lowest published target on the stock is 18.4% above the market price.

TSMC has almost no wedge between adjusted and GAAP earnings: the Taipei line returns NT$64.74 / 106.79 / 139.14 / 174.71 for 2025A-2028E against adjusted 64.73 / 106.88 / 139.46 / 174.91, a gap under 0.3% in every year. Several peers do have one: Intel's FY2026E GAAP earnings are −US$1.24 against an adjusted +US$1.44, so its GAAP P/E is not meaningful, and Synopsys's FY2026E GAAP earnings of US$2.71 against an adjusted US$14.78 put its GAAP P/E at 142x against 26x adjusted.

17. Forward model summary

TSMC discloses no utilization rate and no per-fab capacity, so the single largest input to operating leverage cannot be observed. The bear case below is therefore sized from the 2023 margin decompression. This section includes no per-geography margin build, so the guided overseas-fab dilution widening from 2-3 to 3-4 points enters only through aggregate cost and depreciation lines.

This is an operating model. It projects revenue through free cash flow. There is no valuation, no multiple, no discount rate and no view on the shares. It uses the 20-F accounting basis, so every comparison to consensus below crosses that basis and understates the model by roughly 1.2% at the earnings line.

Structure

Five identities, in order:

(1)  Wafer revenue (US$)  = 12-inch equivalent shipments × blended wafer revenue per wafer
(2)  Total revenue (US$)  = wafer revenue ÷ (1 − Others share of net revenue)
(3)  Total revenue (NT$)  = total revenue (US$) × USDTWD
(4)  COGS (NT$)           = 0.94 × depreciation + 0.64 × amortisation
                            + shipments × cash cost per wafer
(5)  Depreciation (NT$)   = ratio × trailing five-year average gross capex

Every input is either a disclosed KPI or a tagged assumption. The volume/price split is at the consolidated wafer level: node-level volume is undisclosed, the triangulated FY2025 leading-edge volume band is ±13% and the mature ASP band ±9%, and multiplying those and projecting seven years would produce precision the disclosure does not support. Total shipments and total wafer revenue are both filed figures, so their ratio is a disclosed series; the franchise split is then applied as a mix driver.

The model includes no acquisitions (TSMC has made none in twelve years and has no goodwill to impair), no equity issuance and no buyback of consequence, and no change in gross debt (the stack is entirely fixed-rate and the 2026-2028 maturity wall reprices annual interest by roughly NT$5.8bn).

Assumptions

The right-hand column gives the main objection to each assumption; the ones that matter most are discussed after the table.

Driver Bear Base Bull Objection to the base
Wafer shipments, FY2026 growth +17.0% +17.9% +19.0% Weak. First-half 2026 shipments were +22.0%; the base implies a 7.6-point deceleration in the second half in a year management calls supply-constrained. Continuing the realized first-half rate gives +22.0%, above the bull
Wafer shipments, FY2027-32 CAGR +3.0% +7.5% +11.1% Weak. 2025→2028 implies +13.2%/yr for three years against a best realized three-year shipment rate of +14.9% that began from a down year; every three-year window starting at a shipment peak returned zero or less. Partly rescued because sell-side capacity models independently imply about 2.6m wafers/yr of additions, roughly 7.5% on a 17m base, and the path decays to +4% by 2032
Blended wafer ASP, FY2026 growth (US$) +15.5% +16.2% +16.8% Weak. Realized first-half blended ASP was +8.7%, so the base needs +13.2% half-on-half in the second half. The 1.3-point band is far too narrow on the driver the sensitivity ranks first, and the error does not cancel at the margin line because cost is charged per wafer
Blended wafer ASP, FY2027-32 CAGR (US$) +1.6% +5.6% +7.8% The largest unresolved band. Realized six-year blended-ASP rates are +13.7% (2018-2024) and +15.3% (2019-2025), and no single year since 2018 printed below +6.1%, so the entire bear-base-bull range is below anything realized over a comparable window. After 2027 the path runs 3-5%/yr, below node-rung migration alone at a 10-20% N2-over-N3 premium every ~2.5 years, before the announced January-2027 increase. The downward attack is also real (UMC −5.4%, GlobalFoundries −10.4% in 2025)
Advanced (≤7nm) share of wafer revenue, FY2032 85.0% 88.0% 90.0% Holds. The 85-90% band brackets both the stall case and the trend case, and the driver feeds only the franchise revenue split, touching no margin, cash or capex line
Backend share of net revenue, FY2032 16.0% 19.5% 22.0% Weak. Advanced packaging moved one point of corporate mix in eight years and the whole Others line moved 2.4 points in seven; the base asks for +4 points in six, roughly three times the historical rate. Not refuted because Q2 2026 printed a record 16.0% and the mechanism is arithmetic. The base should probably be 17-18%
USDTWD, FY2027 onward 30.00 32.00 33.50 Weak. Holding 32.00 for six years is the weakest sustained NT dollar in the disclosed record against a ten-year mean of 30.5, and in the last comparable boom the currency appreciated to 29.4 and 27.9. Partly rescued because spot on the run date was 32.487 and management guided Q3 2026 margins on exactly 32.00. Worth NT$624bn of FY2032 operating income against the bear
Cash cost per wafer, FY2027-32 CAGR +7.1% +6.3% +5.2% Weak. The realized series compounded at +11.3%/yr over 2019-2025 and +22.7% over 2021-2025 with annual changes from −16.1% to +28.7%; a 1.9-point band against that amplitude is narrow, and overseas-fab dilution, Taipower increases and rising mask layers all push up. Running the realized 11.3% instead would take FY2032 gross margin from 62.1% to about 56.0%
Depreciation ÷ trailing five-year average capex 0.87 0.82 0.78 Weak. Realized ratios were 1.066 (2021), 0.873, 0.816, 0.851, 0.784 (2025), a five-year mean of 0.878, so the whole forward range is at or below the mean. With a five-year straight-line machinery life the ratio converges on the trailing average whenever capex growth flattens, and the model's own capex path flattens hard. Moving the terminal ratio from 0.84 to 0.95 adds NT$317bn of FY2032 depreciation, 2.6 points of revenue
Capital expenditure, FY2026 US$62.0bn US$62.0bn US$64.0bn Weak because bear equals base, so there is no downside case. TSMC came in below its final in-year guide in 2023 and 2024 and below its initial midpoint by 14% and 10% in 2022 and 2023. Consequence is bounded at roughly US$2bn
Capital expenditure, cumulative FY2026-32 US$414bn US$613bn US$702bn Weak on shape, not total. Base capital intensity runs 36.4% down to 26.1% while every year 2016-2025 printed 30.6% or higher. Holding FY2025's 33.4% through 2032 adds NT$897bn of FY2032 capex and cuts FY2032 free cash flow 18%; the rising free-cash-flow margin is substantially a product of that deceleration
Operating expenses, FY2027-32 CAGR +7.6% +13.5% +15.5% Weak. The base implies opex intensity of 6.4-6.6% against a ten-year record low of 9.1% and a first-half 2026 run rate of 7.7%. Backing out selling and administrative expense at its FY2025 share leaves R&D at about 4.4% of FY2032 revenue against a disclosed R&D intensity that has never been below 6.5%. Holding R&D at 6.5% costs NT$305bn of FY2032 operating income
Effective tax rate, FY2032 19.5% 19.0% 18.5% Weak. Q2 2026 already ran roughly 20% including the accrual on undistributed retained earnings, above the entire forward range. Taiwan levies a 5% surtax on undistributed earnings and the model holds the payout at 22-26%, so roughly three-quarters of earnings stay in the surtax base every year while cash builds to NT$18.0tn. Three points is NT$218bn of FY2032 net income
Dividend per common share, FY2032 NT$36.00 NT$58.40 NT$82.00 Weak. Cumulative modelled dividends are 34.8% of cumulative modelled free cash flow against 65.7% over 2016-2025, which is the mechanism producing the NT$18.0tn terminal cash balance. Even the bull is a 19.7% payout of bull-case FY2032 earnings, below every year in the ten-year record. Materiality is low: dividends drive only the cash balance
Government grants against PP&E, FY2032 NT$40,000m NT$60,000m NT$85,000m Weak. No disclosed mechanism ties the level to anything, and the base path totals NT$590bn over 2026-2032 against NT$198,968m actually received over 2023-2025. Materiality is near zero: grants enter the closing cash balance, not operating income
Inventory days, FY2032 85 82 80 Weak. The base declines through a window the model describes as a continuous sequence of node ramps, when every prior ramp raised days (52 in 2019 to 92 in 2021 on N5; 74 to 87 on N2). The base and the bull are both below the most recent quarter. Materiality is small: five days is NT$64bn, about 1.3% of FY2032 free cash flow
Days sales outstanding, FY2032 30 29 28 Weak on width, not level. The realized series has moved between 26.7 and 49.4 days over ten years, so a two-day forward band is unjustified; reverting to 40 days is NT$369bn of receivables, 7.4% of FY2032 free cash flow
Pre-tax yield on cash and marketable securities 2.5% 3.0% 3.3% Weak on basis. The model applies the yield to average cash, and on that basis realized yields were 3.71% (2023), 4.24% (2024) and 3.85% (2025), so even the bull is below all three. The band is also far too narrow; the difference between 1.5% and 4.0% is NT$405bn of FY2032 pre-tax income
Weighted average diluted shares 25,930.6m 25,930.6m 25,930.6m Holds. The count moved 0.001% over nine years; share-based payment was 0.04% of revenue; the only buyback in a decade retired 0.012% of shares; employees are paid in cash
Cyclical down-year in the window (FY2028 shipments) (8.0)% +10.0% +14.0% Refuted. The base and the bull embed no down-year anywhere in a seven-year window. At the 19% annual down-year rate the run's own base-rate work establishes, the probability of at least one down-year in seven years is 75%; on TSMC's own shipment series it is 81%. The base is therefore the roughly 20%-probability path presented as central. The bear's amplitude is also understated 2.7x: TSMC's actual 2023 shipment decline was −21.3%, modelled here at −8%
FY2026 total revenue (calibration anchor) US$167.2bn US$170.6bn US$175.1bn Weak. Management's "slightly above 40%" implies US$171.4-174bn, so the base is 0.5-2.0% under the guide, and TSMC beat the quarterly revenue midpoint in ten of the last ten quarters by +2.5% on average. Applying that beat rate gives FY2026 at US$173-176bn, at or above the bull. Everything compounds off this anchor

The mature franchise re-accelerates in 2026 and then decays back to roughly flat. First-half 2026 mature revenue grew 22.3% year over year on AI power-management and image-sensor demand plus industry-wide supply contraction, reversing a decline from NT$936bn (2022) to NT$839bn (2025), but TSMC is simultaneously winding down a 6-inch and an 8-inch fab and converting 40-90nm tools to CoWoS interposers, so a price-and-mix recovery on a shrinking merchant tool base does not compound. That assumption is unprotected: because the franchise split used here is by node, not platform, premium smartphone application processors are inside the leading-edge franchise, and no scenario shocks a smartphone content reset or a second-source loss at Customer B.

In the bear, shipments grow 6% in 2027 and decline 8% in 2028; blended ASP grows 5% then declines 3%; the backend share stalls at 16%; the NT dollar appreciates to 30.0; cash cost per wafer grows 9.5-10%; the depreciation ratio moves to 0.88 as committed capacity enters service into weaker demand; and capex is cut to US$55bn in 2028. The 2028 shipment decline of 8% is a milder version of what TSMC has already lived through — 2023 shipments declined 21.3% — and the mechanism that makes the bear's margin worse than 2023's is that the depreciation base is roughly twice as large. Free cash flow stays positive in every year at NT$1.3-2.0 trillion because capex is cut alongside, and TSMC ends the bear scenario with NT$9.5 trillion of cash. There is no solvency case here.

The bull's gross margin of 71-73% is an upper bound, not a forecast. The highest annual gross margin any capital-intensive semiconductor manufacturer in the 43-company panel has ever reported is Intel's 63.7% in FY2014 at roughly half TSMC's capital intensity, and TSMC's own record is the 67.7% it printed in Q2 2026. The bull requires that record to be exceeded by four points and held for six years, and it exceeds the historical best incremental operating margin in every year of the forecast.

Sensitivity

Each driver moved by one plausible increment, holding everything else at base. Swings measured on FY2032 operating income (base NT$6,798,353m) and FY2032 free cash flow (base NT$5,012,697m).

Driver Move tested Δ FY2032 operating income Δ FY2032 FCF
1. Blended wafer ASP growth ±2pp a year from 2027 +1,460,686 / (1,328,738) +1,227,219 / (1,120,236)
2. Wafer shipment growth ±2pp a year from 2027 +1,158,091 / (1,055,175) +955,260 / (874,323)
3. USDTWD 34.00 / 30.00 from 2027 +623,733 / (623,733) +490,196 / (490,196)
4. Backend share of revenue ±3pp +474,535 / (440,437) +422,333 / (392,046)
5. Capex level ∓20% from 2027 +455,820 / (455,820) +618,215 / (618,215)
6. Cash cost per wafer growth ∓2pp a year +254,554 / (279,659) +229,756 / (252,629)
7. Depreciation ratio 0.74 / 0.90 +271,322 / (162,793) (70,728) / +43,409

Price beats volume marginally and both dwarf everything else: a two-point change in annual ASP growth moves FY2032 operating income by 21% and a two-point change in shipment growth by 17%, and together they account for more of the terminal-year outcome than the other five drivers combined. That is the correct shape for a business whose growth has come 94-110% from price and mix, and it means a forward model that gets capacity right and pricing wrong is still wrong. Currency is the third-largest driver. Capital spending is the only driver where the operating-income and free-cash-flow signs agree in an uncomfortable way: cutting capex 20% raises both, which is the trap in reading the later years as a quality signal, because the bear case's FY2032 free-cash-flow margin of 30.0% is achieved by not building anything. The depreciation ratio moves operating income and free cash flow in opposite directions, because depreciation is non-cash; anyone attacking the margin path should attack the ratio, and anyone attacking the cash generation should attack capex and price.

Cross-checks

Incremental operating margin against the realized record. Realized incremental operating margin was 72.1% in 2020, 69.7% in 2022, 67.1% in 2025 and 57.1% cumulatively across 2019-2025.

Base 80% 66% 57% 46% 40% 47% 51%
Bull 81% 77% 74% 68% 64% 64% 68%

The base case exceeds the historical best in FY2026, at 80% against 72.1%. It is defensible because it has already happened: first-half 2026 produced an 87.9% incremental operating margin on the reported half-year, so the model's 80% for the full year is below what the company has already printed. The mechanism is a fixed depreciation base spread over 22% more wafers plus a weaker NT dollar, and it does not repeat: the base decays to 66%, 57% and 46% as the capital programme enters service. The bull exceeds the historical best in every year, which is a real weakness in the bull.

The base case is below consensus on revenue in every year after 2026 and above it on gross margin in every year, and the two roughly cancel at the earnings line. Three structural differences sit underneath.

  • The revenue difference is a base-rate difference. Consensus asks for 32.0% compound revenue growth over FY2025-FY2028 from a US$122.6bn base, and no observation of a company at or above US$100bn of revenue in 35 years achieved 30% a year for three years. The model's 27.8% is at roughly the 99th percentile of that distribution, not outside it. Quantification: US$26bn of FY2028 revenue.
  • The margin difference is a depreciation difference. Consensus models gross margin roughly flat at 66% through 2028; the model has it peak at 67.5% in 2027 and decline continuously thereafter, because the trailing five-year capex average that sets depreciation roughly triples between FY2026 and FY2032. Quantification: depreciation and amortization goes from 14.7% of revenue in 2027 to 19.9% in 2032, 5.2 points of revenue arriving from arithmetic on capital already committed. No published note lists the depreciation schedule.
  • The capex difference is the free-cash-flow difference. Consensus has capital intensity declining to 29.6% by 2028; the model holds 34.4%, closer to the CFO's own statement at the same print that spending over the next three years would run "even more significantly higher." Applied to the model's FY2028 revenue that is roughly US$12.2bn a year of extra spending, which is why the model's FY2028 free cash flow sits US$10.2bn below consensus.

Against management's own framework. The standing target set on the Q4 2025 call is a US$ revenue compound rate approaching 25% for 2024-2029 with gross margin of "56% and higher through the cycle."▪

The base sits 6.1% above management's target and 4.4% below consensus. That placement is deliberate: management has beaten every multi-year revenue target it has set since 2018, but the size of the beat has been shrinking and consensus now sits only 2.6 points above the current target, so the buffer that made prior consensus safe is largely gone. The gross-margin target constrains nothing, 1,050 basis points below the run rate within two quarters of being set.

ROE 35.4% 43.6% 35.2% 26.6% 21.8%

The base-rate objection to consensus is that it requires operating income over total assets of 32.6-44.2% by FY2028 against a TSMC all-time high of 24.4% on this basis. The model's base case requires 29.2%, above the all-time high but well inside the range consensus needs, and it fades below the all-time high by FY2030.

The model does not solve the cash problem, and neither does TSMC. Cash and marketable securities grow from NT$3.1 trillion to NT$18.0 trillion in the base case even after NT$613bn of capital spending and NT$7.6 trillion of dividends, because free cash flow compounds faster than the payout ratio rises. Every year of that build dilutes the reported group return, which is why return on equity declines from 43.6% to 21.8% while return on operating capital stays above 44%.

Contradictions in the disclosures

  1. The FY2026 capital budget disagrees with itself across two TSMC documents: US$52-56bn in the annual filing dated 2026-04-16 and US$60-64bn on the July call. The model uses US$62bn and treats the filing as stale.
  2. Management's FY2026 revenue guide and the quarterly consensus do not meet: "slightly above 40%" implies US$171.4-174bn against US$170.0bn from the consensus sum. The model takes US$170.6bn, so if management's fourth quarter is right the base understates FY2026 revenue by 0.5-2.0%.
  3. N2 dilution changed basis between calls and the change was never reconciled: "2-3 percentage points for full year 2026" in April against "about 3-4 percentage points" in the second half in July. The model embeds the dilution through the depreciation roll-forward and the cash-cost path.
  4. Two independent estimates of the N3 wafer price differ by 30%. The model does not use node-level prices precisely because that gap would change implied leading-edge volume by roughly 25%.
  5. Q2 2026 non-operating income of NT$95,827m against Q1's NT$28,834m is unexplained. The model includes the first-half actual in FY2026 and reverts to a recurring interest-income formula from FY2027, which removes it. Each recurrence would add roughly NT$67bn of pre-tax income, about NT$2.12 of EPS.

18. Risks

Ranked by expected effect on earnings. Each entry states the mechanism, the sized exposure, the leading indicator and the mitigation already in place. One structural note first: the local sell-side store holds two TSMC reports, both Buy, both predating the Q2 2026 print, so every adversarial argument below is constructed from primary disclosure, analyst questions and peer filings.

R1 — One demand driver now accounts for 78% of revenue. Top-ten customers went from 70% to 76% to 78% of net revenue over 2023-2025, with Customer A at 19% and Customer B at 17%. Concentration by count is not the change that matters; the change is that the top of the customer list now shares one demand driver where it previously spanned two uncorrelated ones, with HPC moving from 58% of FY2025 revenue to 66% in Q2 2026 while smartphone declined from 29% to 22%. Tracing HPC to its ultimate exposure gives the capital budgets of six to eight hyperscalers and AI labs. Sized: losing Customer A entirely removes NT$726,974m, 19.1% of FY2025 revenue, and because 41.8% of cost of revenue is depreciation that does not decline with volume, the operating-income effect is larger — on the order of NT$490,000-560,000m, roughly 25-29% of FY2025 operating income [estimate: lost revenue × marginal gross margin, no cost reduction assumed]. The more likely form is a demand reset, not a customer loss, and TSMC's own base rate for that is 2023: shipments −21.3%, NT$ revenue −4.5%, gross margin −5.2 points, operating margin −6.9 points, with an installed base roughly half the current one. Leading indicators, by lead time: hyperscaler quarterly capex guidance, TSMC's monthly NT$ revenue filings, inventory days (74 → 80 → 87), and the annual customer table. Mitigation and its limit: TSMC absorbed the loss of a 14%-of-revenue customer once already, Huawei from September 2020, with no visible dent. Management dismissed the current version on the record while the annual filing says the same fact "may adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition." The filing and the chief executive disagree, and the risk is being accepted, not managed.

R2 — The 2026-2028 capital programme becomes depreciation before the demand it assumes is proven. Capital expenditure was US$29,800m (2024) and US$40,895m (2025); the 2026 budget was guided US$52-56bn in January, near the upper end in April and raised to US$60-64bn in July, with the CFO giving no number beyond "the CapEx in the next 3 years will be even more significantly higher" than the past three years' US$101bn. Arizona alone was raised by US$100,000m to US$265bn total with no schedule. Depreciation converts that into fixed cost with a lag, guided up a high-teens percentage in 2026 off NT$638,014m in FY2025 cost of revenue, and TSMC's own risk factor states the consequence: "Because we own most of our manufacturing capacities, a significant portion of our operating costs is fixed. In general, these costs do not decline when customer demand or our capacity utilization rates drop." Sized two ways: the realized 2023 base rate of a 5.2-point gross-margin decline on a 4.5% revenue decline, which on a FY2026 revenue base is roughly NT$269,000m of gross profit; and the guided dilution of 3-4 points from N2 in the second half of 2026 plus 2-4 points from overseas fabs, which against a Q2 2026 gross margin of 67.7% and management's through-cycle floor of 56% accounts for most of the distance. Leading indicators: the capital-budget revision direction, since TSMC has cut 14% and 10% below initial guidance before; the gap between guided and actual gross margin and the attribution management gives for a miss; and 2nm as a share of wafer revenue. Mitigation: the balance sheet absorbs a great deal, with NT$3.5 trillion of cash against NT$856,228m of bonds. The risk is to margins and returns, not to solvency. Note that the FY2025 filing added "If the market demand does not materialize" to this exact risk factor in the same year the budget was raised.

R3 — Tariff and trade policy, where the legal basis changed twice in six months. Every element of the rewritten trade paragraph is dated inside fifteen months: April 2025 baseline and reciprocal tariffs; a February 2026 Supreme Court ruling declaring them unlawful; a replacement tariff under Section 122; two Section 301 investigations opened in March 2026 naming Taiwan; a Section 232 proclamation imposing a 25% ad valorem tariff on certain advanced computing chips and derivative products, "accompanied by a tariff offset program intended to incentivize the U.S. domestic manufacturing"; and a January 2026 US-Taiwan agreement that "grants preferential Section 232 treatment for Taiwanese semiconductor producers investing in U.S. manufacturing capacity," whose details the filing says "are still unclear." Sized: the direct cost is unquantified — the filing says the 2025 tariffs "nonetheless affected our cost of operations in the U.S." The larger channel is conditionality. Both the tariff-offset programme and the preferential treatment are tied to US manufacturing investment, which is US$265bn in Arizona, and the margin cost of that investment is disclosed: 2-3 points of overseas gross-margin dilution early, widening to 3-4 later (Q2 2026 call). On implied FY2026 revenue of roughly US$170,000m, 3-4 points is US$5,100-6,800m a year [estimate: guided dilution × implied revenue]. Leading indicators: the Section 301 determinations; whether the "designated use in the U.S." carve-out survives; the Arizona ramp pace against the guided dilution.

R4 — Export-control licensing became annual, and the compliance obligation exceeds the information a foundry has. The FY2024 filing described the Nanjing Validated End-User authorization as "a permanent authorization"; the FY2025 filing states it "expired in December 2025" and was replaced by an annual export licence with "no assurance that this annual export license will not be terminated, or we can timely get the license renewed." New in FY2025: "export controls over certain semiconductors often depend on the products' specific features or performance characteristics that foundries may not be able to verify independently." Retained from FY2024: an October 2024 notification to US and Taiwan authorities that one type of a customer's chip "might have been diverted to a restricted entity," disclosed as still open twenty-one months later. Sized: China non-current assets were NT$65,020m at end-2025, down from NT$82,406m, 1.7% of the total and declining; a full write-down is 3.8% of FY2025 net income. China-domiciled customers were 8.6% of revenue. The enforcement exposure from the diversion matter is not estimable and TSMC does not attempt one.

R5 — The binding constraint is TSMC's own packaging capacity, and TSMC is inviting rivals to relieve it. Every CoWoS unit a rival supplies is packaging revenue TSMC does not earn and a front-end wafer TSMC does sell, and TSMC's position is that the two are separate businesses. Sized: advanced packaging is roughly 8-10% of revenue, guided to slightly over 10% for 2026, roughly US$17,000m at implied 2026 revenue. The constraint is being relieved: CoWoS capacity from roughly 35,000 wafers per month at end-2024 to 120,000-140,000 projected for end-2026, with the supply-demand gap narrowing from about 20% to about 10% [web]. When that gap closes, the pricing support in the fastest-growing 8-10% of revenue closes with it. Leading indicator: the annual "Others" line growing slower than consolidated revenue for two consecutive years — and TSMC does not disclose the wafer/Others split quarterly, so that signal arrives only once a year. Disclosure gap: TSMC declined twice, to Citigroup and to Goldman Sachs, to break advanced-packaging capital spending out of the combined bucket, so nobody outside the company can compute a return on this franchise.

R6 — Taiwan concentration increased in 2025, in the year of the largest overseas announcement. As of 2026-02-28 TSMC operated 23 fabs, eighteen of them in Taiwan. Non-current assets by location: Taiwan 77.2% → 80.0%, United States 16.0% → 13.9% (declining in absolute NT$), Japan 3.7% → 3.0%, China 2.4% → 1.7%, EMEA 0.6% → 1.3%. The realized base rate for disruption is small and disclosed: earthquake losses net of insurance of about NT$3,000m in Q2 2024 and NT$5,300m in Q1 2025, 0.4% and 0.6% of those quarters' revenue. The operational version is the August 2018 computer-virus outbreak. Neither is the tail case, and TSMC discloses no figure for the tail case because none exists. Two dated items sit underneath: eight of nine Hsinchu fabs are on land leased from the Science Park Administration with renewals from December 2026, and the Kaohsiung land where the 2nm Fab 22 operates is on agreements up for renewal by December 2026. TSMC discloses the dates and not the terms.

R7 — Three disclosed margin drags arrive together in 2027-2028. The first is N2 ramp dilution, guided at 2-3 points for full-year 2026 in April and restated as about 3-4 points for the second half in July, moving in the adverse direction inside six months. The second is overseas-fab dilution of 2-3 points early, widening to 3-4 later. The third is depreciation, up a high-teens percentage in 2026, with capital cost per thousand wafers per month explicitly higher for N2 than N3 and higher again for A14. Sized: Q2 2026 gross margin was 67.7% and Q3 2026 is guided to 65-67%, already 1.7 points lower at the midpoint; the gap between 67.7% and management's 56% through-cycle floor is 11.7 points and the three disclosed drags account for seven to eight of them at their widest. Offsets, also disclosed: utilization running above plan, depreciation being diluted by revenue growing faster than it, and N3 gross margin expected to cross the corporate level in the second half of 2026 with fully-depreciated nodes running "generally very high."

R8 — Currency. "Substantially all of our sales are denominated in U.S. dollars and over half of our capital expenditures are denominated in currencies other than the NT dollar... every 1% depreciation of the U.S. dollar against the NT dollar would result in an approximately 0.3 percentage point decrease in our operating margin based on our 2025 results" (20-F FY2025). The sensitivity was 0.4 points on FY2024 and FY2021 results, so it has declined with scale without going away. A 10% adverse move is therefore about three points of operating margin, roughly NT$162,000m of operating income on a FY2026 revenue base [estimate: disclosed sensitivity × a third-party revenue estimate]. Management's position: "we have no control over the foreign exchange rate."

R9 — An ITC case whose remedy reaches customers. In February 2025 Longitude Licensing and Marlin Semiconductor filed complaints with the US International Trade Commission and the Eastern District of Texas "alleging that TSMC and its customers infringe five U.S. patents"; the ITC instituted an investigation in March 2025 and the district case was stayed. "The outcome cannot be determined, and we cannot make a reliable estimate of the contingent liability at this time" (20-F FY2025, Item 8). This ranks above its dollar size because the ITC's remedy is an exclusion order barring importation, not damages, and because the complaint names customers, an adverse determination reaches finished products entering the US, where 74.4% of FY2025 revenue by customer domicile sits. The FY2025 filing separately added that recent US Patent and Trademark Office developments limiting access to inter partes review "may result in an increase of such assertions and lawsuits, and hinder our ability to reach a reasonable resolution with patent owners," so the standard defensive tool against a non-practising entity has been narrowed.

R10 — Government grants are material, conditional and parent-guaranteed. Cash proceeds were NT$47,545m (2023), NT$75,164m (2024) and NT$76,259m (2025), NT$198,968m over three years and 6.0% of FY2025 capital spending. The Arizona package is up to US$6,600m in direct funding plus up to US$5,000m in loans, and TSMC "agrees to provide an irrevocable, absolute and unconditional guarantee to the DOC regarding any financial obligations owed by TSMC Arizona to the DOC." Grants are subject to conditions including "restrictions on the expansion of facilities in foreign countries of concern," and non-compliance "could result in a delay or forfeiture of all or a portion of any future amounts to be received, as well as obligate us to repay all or a portion of amounts already received." The grants reduce the carrying value of the assets they fund, so they lower depreciation and flatter the reported overseas-fab margin; any clawback reverses that in a single period. The maximum exposure is never sized.

R11 — The 22%-of-revenue franchise that was supposed to cushion a downturn was already declining. Mature revenue went from about NT$936bn (2022) to NT$839bn (2025) and subtracted 6.3% from the consolidated revenue increase over that window, while UMC declined 14.8% on 12.3% more wafers at 5.4% lower prices and GlobalFoundries 16.2% on 10.4% more wafers at 10.4% lower prices. The exposure is not that this franchise shrinks further — at 22% of revenue declining 3-5% a year that costs roughly one point of consolidated growth annually — but that the diversification argument does not hold. If leading-edge demand resets, the mature leg does not catch it. Leading indicator: UMC's and GlobalFoundries' ASP disclosures, which lead TSMC's own by roughly a quarter and are published more granularly.

R12 — Antitrust and the politics of a 72% share. TSMC accounted for 69.9% of top-ten foundry revenue in FY2025 and 72.3% in Q1 2026 [web]. The FY2025 filing keeps the sentence "With our success in the foundry business and the increasing criticism on the concentration of the semiconductor industry and sometimes directly on us, we are subject to heightened risks of antitrust investigations" while deleting the standalone antitrust risk factor and the history of the 2017 European Commission inquiry closed in May 2020. The live regulatory vector is not a competition authority: it is the USTR Section 301 investigation into alleged manufacturing overcapacity opened in March 2026 and naming Taiwan. Not estimable.

Which risks arrive together

A bad quarter here is never one item from the list; the risks arrive in three clusters.

The AI demand reset (R1 + R2 + R7 + R11). A hyperscaler capex reset reaches TSMC two to three quarters later. Utilization declines against a fixed cost base in which depreciation is 41.8% of cost of revenue and rising a high-teens percentage. The N2 dilution of 3-4 points, underwritten by volume, arrives without the volume. The mature franchise provides no cushion because it is already declining into a price war. Inventory days, already 87 and up 13 in two quarters, rise further. Every element is the same event viewed from a different line, and TSMC's own 2023 gives the amplitude.

The policy cluster (R3 + R4 + R6 + R12). A Section 301 determination on manufacturing overcapacity targeting Taiwan, a Nanjing licence not renewed at the December window, and any Taiwan operating disruption all hit the same 80%-of-assets base and share a political driver, so they are more likely to co-occur than independent probabilities imply.

The margin cluster (R7 + R8 + R2). N2 dilution, overseas dilution, the depreciation step-up and a stronger NT dollar all land in gross margin in the same quarters, 2H 2026 through 2028, and management has guided all four separately without ever summing them. The Q3 2026 guide of 65-67% against a Q2 actual of 67.7% is the first quarter in which the sum is visible.

What does not correlate: the balance sheet. Net cash of roughly NT$2.0 trillion at end-2025 and NT$2.05 trillion at Q2 2026 means none of these clusters produces a financing event.

Peer failure mechanisms, and whether they apply

Peer episode Mechanism Applies to TSMC?
Intel Foundry: US$10,318m operating loss in FY2025 on US$17,826m of revenue, US$307m external Leading-edge capital committed against internal demand that did not materialise, then an attempt to sell external capacity from a standing start The capital mechanism applies; the demand mechanism does not. TSMC's capacity is contracted against external customers with a two-to-three-year engagement lead time. Intel's failure was building for itself
GlobalFoundries abandoned 7nm in 2018; FY2025 revenue 16.2% below 2022 with ASP −10.4% A sub-scale leading-edge programme could not fund the next node, so the company exited Not a TSMC risk at the leading edge. It is the cohort TSMC's own 22%-of-revenue franchise is now in
NVIDIA's US$4,500m H20 charge and US$7,200m of full-year inventory and excess-purchase provisions in FY2026 Export controls stranded inventory and purchase commitments placed forward Directly relevant as the transmission path. NVIDIA's US$95,200m of outstanding purchase obligations is what stands between a demand break and TSMC's order book, and it buys one or two quarters
Micron: gross margin from 37.7% to 84.6% in twelve months on revenue up 346% A commodity layer captured the AI profit pool through price The inverse risk. Evidence that the profit pool inside an AI system can migrate between layers quickly, which TSMC's own chief executive acknowledged
TSMC's own August 2018 virus outbreak A single-vector operational failure propagated across fabs and tools Applies, with disclosed and specific mitigation. The FY2025 version is the AI-assisted attack the risk factor now names

What the risk-factor edits themselves say

The FY2025 risk-factor section grew only 1.7% in words while four named items were deleted: Huawei (removed six years after the event); the R.O.C. restrictions on P.R.C. investment (consistent with the China asset base being run down); the standalone antitrust risk factor together with the European Commission history (while retaining the heightened-risk language); and the quantified Taipower increases of +25% from April 2024 and a further +14% from October 2024, the largest quantified operating-cost disclosure in the prior year's section, removed in the year gross margin reached a record. All of the growth is concentrated in the trade paragraph. Softened wordings include customer concentration moving from "will subject our revenue to seasonal demand fluctuations" to "may subject," and export licensing at 16nm and below moving from "any global destination" to "specified destinations." The section is edited deliberately, which makes the deletions readable as a statement of what management no longer treats as live.

Figures a reader could otherwise misread

Two families of web claim are flagged here at lower confidence and should be spot-checked.

  • Yields and node-timing at competitors. Samsung SF2 at 55-60% and SF2P at about 70%; Intel 18A moving from roughly 65% to over 85% during 2026; SMIC 7nm under 50% and 5nm pilot at 20-40%. No company discloses defect density or yield, all figures are trade press, and the Samsung numbers conflict across sources by 5-10 points on a metric central to whether Samsung becomes a real second source. Tagged [web, unverified].
  • Named commercial arrangements not confirmed in any filing. Tesla AI6 reported as wholly Samsung under a US$16.5bn agreement; Google reportedly selecting Intel EMIB-T over TSMC CoWoS-L for a next-generation TPU; Intel packaging gross margins reported around 40%. Each is single-sourced trade press with no confirmation from any named party. Tagged [web, unverified].

One further web figure is logged as unresolved: a search result reporting a Morgan Stanley target of NT$2,088 is inconsistent with the NT$3,000-3,800 cluster and with Bloomberg's NT$2,700 low, and is almost certainly a stale article surfacing in the index. It is not used above.
