Gaps, failures and discrepancies

Sources that were never retrieved. Daloopa, the designated source-linked fundamentals workbook, was never run, justified by a single line noting that three other sources were available — a weak justification for the one ticker where the shipped XBRL extractor returns zero line items because every concept map is US GAAP while TSMC files IFRS, where SEC company facts had not indexed FY2025 at pull time, and where an unresolved three-source discrepancy in net income and earnings per share remains and the skip is nowhere justified. Bloomberg peer financials were left unused by all six per-franchise competitive agents while the terminal was live, leaving ASE's and Amkor's returns on invested capital uncomputed and no cost of capital pulled, which is why Section 3 uses a stated 9-11% assumption. SMIC's Hong Kong annual report, Samsung's Korean business report and TSMC's own Taiwan annual report and MOPS filings were never attempted. TSMC's quarterly IFRS financial statements, filed as 6-K, were identified and never pulled, which is why the quarterly series has no cash flow, balance sheet, share count or working-capital line for any quarter. The monthly NT$ revenue 6-K series — roughly 40 filings for 2023-04-10 to 2026-07-13 alone — was never pulled, despite being flagged independently by three agents as the instrument that would test the most falsifiable number in the run six to ten weeks before the January print.

Sources that failed. Firecrawl returned HTTP 402 for every agent that tried it, and several fallback targets then returned 403 and were never obtained: SEMI's full historical silicon-shipment table, the Yole advanced-packaging market report, SemiEngineering's and Tom's Hardware's symposium write-ups, and Vanguard's own investor releases. The market sizing in Sections 4 and 6 therefore leans on secondary summaries of paid primary sources.

Sources that do not exist. TSMC is a foreign private issuer: there is no DEF 14A, no compensation discussion and analysis, no say-on-pay vote, no pay-versus-performance table and no chief-executive pay ratio, and the Proxy project store contains no TSMC record. There is no 10-K and no 10-Q. TSMC holds no investor day and no capital markets day, so the presentation layer here is web-sourced write-ups of the annual technology symposium and the shareholder meeting, which rank below filings and earnings calls.

Extraction defects logged. The 10K-redlines section files for this ticker are mis-extracted, because the extractor keys on 10-K Item 1 and Item 1A headings that do not exist in a 20-F; the FY2025 "business" file contains risk-factor text, and the "risk_factors" file begins before the risk factors and includes the exchange-rate section. The archived Q2 2026 earnings transcript contains figure-corrupting errors throughout, and the archived text of the 4Q2025 earnings release transposes the prior-year fourth-quarter operating income. Every figure above that would otherwise have come from those files was taken from the corresponding 6-K, deck or annual filing instead.

Discrepancy log. Six disagreements are stated here: (a) the audited annual filing and every Taiwan IFRS source disagree on income tax expense, net income and earnings per share in all ten years, in both directions, while agreeing exactly on revenue, gross profit and operating income, with the mechanism undetermined; (b) the 2026 capital budget appears as US$52-56bn in the filing dated 2026-04-16 and US$60-64bn on the July call; (c) management gave two different FY2025 advanced-packaging revenue shares one year apart; (d) N2 dilution guidance changed basis between calls without reconciliation; (e) the annual meeting business report and the annual filing disagree on 2024 director compensation, NT$358,989,109 against NT$507.1m, with no reconciliation located; and (f) Bloomberg's FY2025 "actual" earnings line is the stale pre-print consensus, not the reported figure, which is why the comp table's 2025A column holds an estimate for this name.

Claims revised on review

Where a claim was judged overstated or contradicted, it has been revised to what the evidence supports. The most consequential revisions concern the B200 cost decomposition, the consensus-beat streak, the drawdown count, the mature-node peer growth ranking, the "two independent triangulation angles" framing, and the succession discussion in the transcript archive.

Weak assumptions in the forward model

Of the model's 21 assumptions, two held (the advanced share of wafer revenue in FY2032 and the flat share count), eighteen were judged weak, and one was refuted. The refuted one matters most: the base and bull cases embed no cyclical down-year anywhere in a seven-year window, against a 19% annual down-year rate in the run's own base-rate panel and a 75-81% probability of at least one down-year in seven years, and the bear's amplitude of −8% understates TSMC's own realized 2023 shipment decline of −21.3% by a factor of 2.7. Section 17 shows the specific objection against each assumption in the right-hand column of the assumptions table.

External data

One external dataset was identified for this company and none was pulled. It is described in Appendix C. Its absence matters substantively: management named memory price inflation as the reason 2026 PC and smartphone unit growth would be "very minimal," and the WSTS +90% 2026 semiconductor forecast is overwhelmingly a memory pricing event that would overstate TSMC's market denominator roughly six-fold in Sections 4 and 6 if used carelessly.

Internal discrepancies

Twenty-seven figures that contradicted this document's own tables were corrected: three year-over-year operating-income deltas in the Section 1 operating-leverage table, a cash-cost-per-wafer figure that did not foot against its own cost breakdown, a margin-gap-versus-Intel-Foundry figure overstated by 6.6 points, a five-year average ROIC, a wafer-volume growth rate, a peer yield range, and the 2023-2025 government-grant total, which the Section 13.1 cash-flow row settles at NT$198,968m and which had been printing as NT$199,969m in six places, including one line that gave the three components and then the wrong sum.

The conflicts below are the ones visible from the front matter and Sections 1 to 9, which were reconciled line by line against this document's tables. Figures in Sections 10 to 20 and the appendices are not verified to the same standard.

Conflicts this document cannot settle from itself. These are not errors with a known right answer; each needs an outside source or a basis decision:

  • Section 10 net-income basis. The financial history carries both total net income (NT$1,695,124.9m) and net income attributable to parent (NT$1,697,604.0m) for FY2025. Section 10 prints the former; the NT$65.47 diluted EPS belongs to the latter. Section 10 does not state which line its payout and profit-sharing ratios use, and the two are not interchangeable. Section 13.1 and the Reading notes use the parent figure.
  • Accounts receivable at Q2 2026. Section 1 states NT$440.92bn, implying about 32 receivable days, against the 29 days disclosed in Section 13.2. The prior-year figure ties exactly to its disclosed 23 days. Settling this needs the Q2 2026 6-K balance sheet.
  • Depreciation per wafer by node. The Section 1 node cells total roughly US$10.2bn against about US$20.7bn implied by the consolidated row; the residual would place some 61% of depreciation on backend revenue. Either an allocation key is missing or the node column is lifecycle-illustrative and does not foot.
  • D&A versus depreciation-only. Section 1's D&A/revenue row sits 0.3 to 0.5 points below Section 13.1's D&A divided by revenue, and Section 1's Capex/D&A row only reproduces on a depreciation-only denominator. One of the two rows needs relabelling.
  • ADR premium arithmetic. The front matter attributes the Taipei multiples to the ADR multiples "lower by the ADR premium of +11.5%", but 23.8x / 1.115 is 21.3x, not the 21.1x printed; the printed trio implies a 12.8% gap. The trio matches Section 15, so the numbers were left alone and the attribution is what is in doubt — most likely these are a separately collected Taipei consensus set.
  • ROIC window and basis. A "five-year average ROIC 33.0% over 2016-2020" cannot be computed: FY2016 ROIC is not disclosed in either table, and the four disclosed years average 31.7%. Separately, FY2025 ROIC excluding the cash pool appears as both 48.7% and 51.0% in Section 3, which differ by closing versus average invested capital.
  • R&D intensity. "8.5% of revenue in 2023" and "absolute R&D rose 35.1%" are mutually inconsistent on the disclosed R&D figure.
  • SMIC wafer basis. Section 3's "roughly 9.7 million wafers" is an 8-inch-equivalent count; Section 4's 4,310k is 12-inch-equivalent. Both are defensible, neither says which.
  • Utilization quarters. "Above 100% in every quarter of 2025" is followed by three figures, not four.
  • CoWoS capacity path. Section 4's backend peer table and Section 5's constraint discussion give different end-2026 exit figures.
  • Market-share denominators. Section 6's growth table prints a TSMC share that does not equal its own two revenue columns divided.
  • Customer concentration and node ranking. Two Section 8 pressure tests state a top-two customer share and a largest-node-in-bucket claim that the Section 1 customer table and Section 4 node table respectively do not support.
  • Gross-margin target arithmetic. Two Section 8 pressure tests, both inside tagged claims, state a basis-point gap to the 56% target and a revenue-compound-rate history that the referenced sections do not reproduce. Left as filed.
  • Weighted-average share count. Section 9 quotes a 2013-to-2025 share range that matches Section 12 but not Section 13.1's diluted-share row.
  • Two 0.2-point deck-versus-filing gaps in Section 1's incremental-margin arithmetic, both explicitly sourced to the Q2 2026 deck and left as filed.

20. What we still don't know, and the monitoring KPIs

Unresolved gaps in coverage

  1. Geography of production is analysed nowhere. No per-fab or per-country table of capacity, capital spending, revenue, government grants or return exists, despite a US$265bn Arizona commitment, roughly 30% of eventual sub-2nm capacity eventually sitting there, NT$198,968m of grants received over 2023-2025, and guided overseas gross-margin dilution widening from 2-3 to 3-4 points, worth roughly NT$150bn of annual gross profit at FY2026 revenue. This is the largest unquantified swing factor in the Section 3 durability judgment and the Section 17 margin path, and it is flagged at the top of both.
  2. There is no capacity or utilization dimension at all. TSMC discontinued its billing- utilization disclosure after FY2020 and no longer publishes a per-fab capacity table that UMC still files. The Taiwan annual report and MOPS filings, where the Taiwan-mandated capacity disclosure would sit, were never attempted. The single largest input to operating leverage is absent from the Section 13 KPI table, and the Section 17 bear case is sized from the 2023 margin decompression.
  3. The non-packaging half of the backend line has no forward treatment. NT$231,800m, US$7,500m, 6.1% of FY2025 revenue in mask making, wafer probe and final test, design services and royalties — larger than the Automotive and IoT platforms combined — enters Sections 1 and 13 purely as a residual with no revenue driver, growth series or margin estimate, even though ASE's disclosed testing gross margin of 31.0% against 22.1% for packaging suggests it may be the higher-margin activity and therefore mis-centres the 45-55% backend margin band that drives the Section 5 profit-pool table.
  4. The shrinking half of the business has no forward treatment either. Customer B declined from 25% of revenue in 2023 to 17% in 2025 and the Smartphone platform from 39% in 2022 to 22% in Q2 2026, but because the franchise split is by node, premium-smartphone application processors are inside the leading-edge franchise and no scenario in Section 17 shocks a smartphone content reset or a second-source loss at Customer B.
  5. No quarterly cash flow or balance sheet exists for any period. TSMC files quarterly IFRS financial statements as a 6-K and they were never pulled, so Section 13.2 could not be built to the full contract and the Q2 2026 free-cash-flow inflection has no complete series behind it.
  6. The monthly NT$ revenue 6-K series was never pulled. It is the fastest public inflection signal this issuer offers, no US-listed peer publishes an equivalent, and it is the instrument that would test the run's most falsifiable number — the implied Q4 2026 of US$50-53bn — six to ten weeks before the January print.
  7. The filed record starts too late. The archive begins with the FY2016 annual report although EDGAR holds filings back to FY2011, so the capital sunk into TSMC Solar and Solid State Lighting cannot be sized, the pre-2014 cash-flow lines are unavailable, the 2014-2015 16nm share loss is sourced only from a transcript, and the 2008-09 and 2011-12 downturns enter only through Bloomberg.
  8. Two quarters are incomplete and one peer quarter is missing. FY2023 Q3 and Q4 exist only as five-line comparatives inside the 2024 releases, with no diluted earnings per share, margins or node mix, so two of the eight quarters in Section 13.2 cannot show earnings growth. And ASE's and Amkor's 2026-Q2 filings are not archived, so the most recent apples-to-apples packaging comparison is Q1 2026 while the backend inflection being tested is a Q2 2026 event.

Open questions

  • What return do TSMC's customers' customers earn on the roughly US$610-725bn of 2026 AI capital spending, and over what depreciable life? Payback, AI return on investment and useful life are not established anywhere, and hyperscaler server-life extensions — the accounting assumption holding up reported AI returns — appear nowhere. About 66% of Q2 2026 revenue traces to six to eight capital budgets, so if that spending only clears a hurdle on aggressive utilization or extended-life assumptions, the Section 3 durability judgment, the Section 6 secular-versus-cyclical split and the FY2029-32 tail of Section 17 weaken together.
  • What does the disclosed construction-in-progress balance imply for forward depreciation? The FY2025 property note includes a full gross-cost roll-forward by asset class showing NT$1,518,996m of equipment under installation and construction in progress at 31 December 2025, 41% of net property, none of it yet depreciating, alongside the disclosed five-year machinery life. Section 17's model fits depreciation as 0.82x trailing five-year capital spending and calls that its single largest margin lever, while its own open questions state that construction in progress is not disclosed in a modellable form. The filing shows otherwise, and the NT$1,519bn figure appears in no workpaper.
  • Why did the effective tax rate double from 8.7% in 2018 to 17.7% in 2024, and where does it go under the global minimum tax? Pillar Two is not addressed above, nor is any treatment of Taiwan's alternative minimum tax, the undistributed-earnings surtax, US taxation of Arizona profits, or intercompany transfer pricing. One point of tax is roughly NT$57bn of FY2030 net income in the Section 17 model.
  • What is inside non-operating income and is any of it repeatable? Q2 2026 non-operating income was NT$95,827m against NT$29,613m a year earlier, and the quarterly release does not split it between interest income on NT$3.5 trillion of cash, foreign-exchange gains, equity-method income and any gain on the Vanguard disposal. It is worth about NT$2.12 of quarterly earnings per share.
  • What is the maximum government-grant clawback exposure? NT$198,968m was received across 2023-2025 and every workpaper treats it as a clean capital offset, which the model itself calls the optimistic treatment, while the filing references milestone and clawback conditions without quantifying them.
  • Does the employee profit-sharing pool cap operating leverage? The pool was NT$206,146m in 2025, 12.2% of net income and +46.6% year over year, with management guiding more than 30% growth again in 2026. The Section 17 model includes no profit-linked cost driver, and the roughly 90% realized incremental operating margin in the most recent quarter is never reconciled against a claim on profit growing faster than revenue.
  • How much of the 7.8-point gross-margin rise from FY2025 to Q2 2026 is the exchange rate, not operations? Constant currency is a zero-hit string across every workpaper. The disclosed sensitivity is about 0.3 points of operating margin per 1% move, and the base-rate work flags that its own consensus-error series contains currency and that the FY2025 beat is inflated by 2025 NT dollar appreciation by an amount it does not decompose.
  • What settles the CoWoS interposer classification? Whether interposer wafers and the chip-on-wafer step are recognised in the Wafer line or the Others line is unresolved and was flagged by four separate agents. It is bounded at NT$31-63bn, larger than the entire 2022-2025 growth of the 65nm node, and if interposers are booked in the Wafer line then part of what counts here as mature-node revenue is advanced-packaging revenue and the merchant mature franchise is weaker than it appears.
  • What is the actual gross margin of advanced packaging? "Approaching corporate, but not there yet," last updated in October 2024, spans roughly 45-58% on the FY2025 base, and the Section 3 and Section 5 conclusions differ materially at each end.
  • Why did the executive restricted-share forfeiture rate collapse from about 53% to about 5% between the 2022 and 2023 vintages? TSMC discloses neither the conditions nor the assessment.
  • Is there a succession plan? A combined Chairman and Chief Executive aged 71-75, no President, no named heir, and the succession mandate removed from the nominating committee's disclosed charter after FY2022.
  • What are the terms on the Hsinchu and Kaohsiung land leases coming up for renewal from December 2026, including the site where the 2nm Fab 22 operates? Dates are disclosed; terms are not.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

TSMC holds no investor day and no capital markets day. The archive holds six quarterly earnings-conference decks — Q2 2021, Q2 2023, Q2 2025, Q4 2025, Q1 2026 and Q2 2026 — 66 slides in total, three of them consecutive quarters and three isolated. The obvious assumption that an earnings deck repeats the earnings release is wrong here: the quarterly 6-K is a two-page press release containing the income statement, the three margins, next-quarter guidance and the top four node shares, and nothing else. Everything below exists nowhere else in the corpus.

  • Prior-quarter guidance printed beside the actual. Slide 4 of every deck shows the guidance given a quarter earlier next to the result. Neither the release nor the annual filing preserves that pairing. Revenue landed at or above the top of the guided range in five of six sampled quarters, and the operating-margin beat exceeds the gross-margin beat every time there is a beat (4Q25 +1.3 points against +3.0; 1Q26 +1.2 against +2.1; 2Q26 +0.2 against +1.8). Operating expenses are guided more conservatively than cost of revenue. Informs §14.
  • Realized incremental operating margin of about 90%, and rising. From the printed revenue and margins: 2Q25 to 2Q26 revenue grew NT$336,590m while cost of revenue absorbed NT$23,740m and operating expenses NT$14,470m, giving a 92.9% incremental gross margin and an 89.9% incremental operating margin. The same arithmetic over five years gives 69.1% and over three years 71.4%. The opex-to-revenue ratio traces the same path: 12.1% (2Q23) → 9.1% (2Q25) → 7.8% (2Q26). Currency explains about 0.5 of the 10.7 points of operating-margin expansion. Informs §1 and §13.
  • The realized exchange rate against the guidance assumption. Only the deck prints both. The 2Q25 beat was delivered into a 4.5% currency headwind versus the assumption, roughly 1.4 points of operating margin, so the underlying beat was about 2.0 points before currency. Informs §14.
  • Quarterly wafer shipments, and the 81/19 growth split. Dividing net revenue by the deck's shipment line gives a blended revenue-intensity series. Over 2Q21 to 2Q26 revenue grew 3.41x, shipments 1.26x and revenue per wafer 2.72x, a log decomposition of 18.6% volume and 81.4% value per wafer. In the worst quarter of the last cycle, 2Q23, shipments declined 23.2% year over year while revenue declined only 10.0%, because revenue per wafer rose 17.3%. Informs §1 and §6.
  • A continuous 32-quarter series of leading-edge revenue by node. Four instances of the "7nm and Below Revenue" chart overlap and stitch into a series running 3Q18 to 2Q26. The 7nm band has held a NT$88-130bn quarterly band for roughly 24 consecutive quarters through a full boom, the 2023 downturn and the AI boom, while 5nm rose to about NT$355bn, 3nm to about NT$320bn and 2nm appeared at about NT$30bn. Node revenue stacks, not rotates, which is a different capacity and depreciation problem from a rotation model and is why capital spending must rise, not be recycled. Informs §2 and §6.
  • Quarterly platform mix with a growth panel the pie does not show. Applying the printed shares to the printed revenue, HPC added NT$263.2bn between 4Q25 and 2Q26 while the company added NT$224.3bn and everything else in aggregate declined NT$38.8bn. Smartphone is in absolute decline (−11% then −4% sequentially), which the share column alone cannot distinguish from mix dilution. Automotive inflected +15% in 2Q26 after −7% in 1Q26, a reversal the share column conceals entirely because it stays at 4-5% throughout. Informs §1 and §4.
  • The full quarterly mature-node tail. The release discloses only the top four nodes and the advanced aggregate; the deck's pie gives every node every quarter. The mature tail compressed from 51% of wafer revenue in 2Q21 to 23% in 2Q26, but share compression is not revenue decline: the audited node table shows 16nm and 28nm both rising in absolute NT$ between FY2023 and FY2025. Informs §4.
  • Capital productivity at a six-year high while capex sets records and leverage declines. Asset productivity (annualized revenue over average net property) troughed at 0.7x in 2Q23 and is 1.2x now, the highest in the sample, while 2Q26 capex of NT$496.00bn was up 41.4% sequentially and 66.9% year over year, long-term debt declined to NT$864.27bn and total liabilities to 30.9% of assets. Informs §12.
  • Free cash flow declined in 2Q26 despite record operating cash flow, because capex rose NT$145.24bn against a NT$84.39bn rise in operating cash, thinning dividend cover to 1.85x from 2.84x in 4Q25. The 2Q23 quarter shows the downcycle case: free cash flow went negative at −NT$83.28bn while capex kept running at NT$250.53bn. Informs §10 and §12.
  • The 2026 capital-budget cross-check. First-half 2026 capex of NT$846.76bn is US$26.80bn at the deck's own realized rates, so the guided US$60-64bn requires US$33.2-37.2bn in the second half, 24% to 39% above the first-half run rate. Either the step-up is very large or the budget will not be fully spent. Informs §17.
  • What the decks never mention. Across 66 slides spanning 2021 to 2026 there is no slide on advanced packaging, no CoWoS, no SoIC, no InFO and no breakout of the "Others" product line; no customer concentration and no customer named; no revenue by geography; no capacity, utilization or capex by category; no margin bridge; no franchise margin or return; no long-term target, addressable-market slide or roadmap chart; and no competitor by name or category. The single mention of packaging anywhere in the six decks is one bullet in a 2023 recent-events recap. The decks alone give a pure wafer foundry with a 14-16% unexplained residual.

A text-only pass gets two things wrong here, and both were live in an earlier pass on this deck set: the Q1 2026 platform growth panel is dropped entirely by the text extractor, and the Q2 2023 growth bars extract in plot order while the legend prints in a different order, which inverts the sign on HPC. Both were corrected by reading the images.

Appendix C — External data sources

One external dataset is available for TSMC and has not been pulled. This is a menu, not fetched data.

DRAM and NAND spot and contract pricing (memory_spot_pricing) — status: not pulled.

What it is. A mosaic, not a clean series. TrendForce, the primary source for memory spot and contract prices, is a paid subscription, so the dataset is assembled from scattered, dated, cited price points harvested across credible public reporting. Access method is web_mosaic with no coded connector, cadence irregular, and the two mosaic targets are the DRAM contract price trend and the NAND price trend. Any series built this way is partial and would be presented with its coverage gaps stated explicitly, at medium to low confidence, with bounds and a [web] tag, never as comprehensive.

What it measures. The direction and magnitude of memory pricing, which is the single largest price variable in the semiconductor industry in 2026 and the one TSMC does not participate in.

How it would inform this analysis. Three places, each of them currently on single-point evidence.

  • Section 6, secular and industry trends. WSTS forecasts the 2026 semiconductor market at US$1.51 trillion, +90%, "overwhelmingly driven by the Memory segment" with memory at roughly US$800bn, +250%, while TSMC's own Foundry 2.0 market is forecast at +14%. Using the headline semiconductor number as TSMC's market growth would overstate the denominator roughly six-fold and turn a share gainer into an apparent share loser. A dated price series would let the memory component be stripped out properly.
  • Section 5, value chain and profit pools. The memory layer now out-earns TSMC on almost identical revenue: Micron's gross margin moved from 37.7% to 84.6% in twelve months. Whether that is a price event with an expiry or a structural re-rating of the layer is the difference between TSMC losing profit-pool share temporarily and losing it durably, and only a price series answers it.
  • Section 1 and Section 6, the demand drivers. Management named memory price inflation as the reason 2026 PC and smartphone unit growth would be "very minimal," and Microsoft attributed US$25bn of a US$190bn calendar-2026 capital budget to memory and component price inflation buying no additional capacity. Because hyperscaler budgets are set in dollars, memory inflation displaces accelerator units, which is a claim on TSMC's volume, not only on somebody else's margin. A dated price series would convert that mechanism from an anecdote into a quantified drag.
